#3071. Prediction: This Memory Stock Will Be 2027's Best-Performing AI Stock

Micron's AI memory demand, supply constraints, and low forward valuation could make it a standout AI stock in 2027, but cyclical risks remain.

While much of the attention has gone to chipmakers in 2026, the artificial intelligence (AI) boom is creating some unexpected winners, and Micron Technology (MU -2.51%) just might be the next. As models grow more demanding and data centers continue to expand, the need for advanced memory will only accelerate.

Plus, with several major trends working in its favor, this memory stock could turn out to be one of 2027's biggest AI beneficiaries.

Micron is emerging as one of the most important suppliers to the AI build-out, providing the dynamic random access memory (DRAM), NAND, and high-bandwidth memory (HBM) needed to power AI infrastructure. In fact, its fiscal 2026 performance showed how dramatically that position has driven he company's growth, with its cloud and data center products benefiting from strong demand and improved pricing.

At the same time, the company says AI demand for memory is growing faster than the industry can expand supply. To that end, Micron has increasingly focused on higher-value data center products, where demand for HBM and advanced server memory is being driven by hyperscaler spending. Indeed, advanced AI chips require enormous amounts of HBM memory to move data efficiently.

Meanwhile, the company has been expanding its portfolio as AI systems become more complex and demanding. For example, its recent product developments include advanced server memory, high-performance solid-state drives (SSDs) designed for AI workloads, and new memory products for physical AI applications.

Looking ahead, Micron is heading into fiscal 2027 with management pointing to continued AI-driven demand, while its latest guidance and product roadmap suggest that advanced data center memory remains central to its growth strategy.

In fact, memory demand continues to accelerate even as bringing new supply online is neither quick nor easy. That very bottleneck is supporting stronger pricing and profitability across its business.

After all, building leading-edge manufacturing capacity takes years and requires enormous investment. Micron's own expansion plans are proof of that.

Specifically, its new Idaho manufacturing capacity is expected to begin producing DRAM wafers in calendar 2027, while its larger New York expansion will help expand supply over the next 20-plus years.

That combination could make Micron one of the more interesting AI stocks to watch in 2027. That's because, unlike companies whose valuations depend on future promises, Micron is already embedded in the AI infrastructure stack where supply constraints and customer demand are tangible.

On top of that, the company is benefiting from its position as the only major U.S.-based memory manufacturer. Indeed, that's an important strategic advantage as governments and tech companies prioritize supply chain resilience and domestic manufacturing.

But the company still faces meaningful risks.

For one, Micron remains exposed to the cyclicality of the memory industry. In other words, if AI spending slows or manufacturers bring too much new capacity online, memory prices could come under pressure.

Plus, there's the risk that hyperscalers may not earn attractive enough returns on their AI investments. That means any slowdown in data center construction would likely affect Micron's revenue outlook.

Right now, 45 of 49 Wall Street analysts rate Micron stock a buy or strong buy, with an average target price of $1,561.91, suggesting the stock could more than double by this time next year. On top of that, its forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 4.5 offers an attractive entry point for investors who think the AI memory boom still has room to run. The combination of upside and low valuation could help Micron outperform AI peers in 2027.

Looking ahead, with memory becoming increasingly vital to the AI build-out and Micron strengthening its market position, the company could surprise investors as one of 2027's biggest AI stock winners.

#3069. Did a Single Router Ground the Nation’s Flights? Experts Express Doubt

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Federal Aviation Administration officials say the outage stemmed from an industrial-grade router that began flooding its system.

The humble internet router is at the center of another national firestorm.

Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said Sunday that a single router in Arkansas was to blame for the nearly 5-hour-long ground stop on Friday. It was only the second nationwide halt to US air travel since Sept. 11, 2001, leading to the cancellation of 12,462 flights on Friday alone.

FAA investigators zeroed in on a routine network upgrade at a radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, where a copper wire line was being upgraded to fiber optic cable by the contractor L3Harris. A new router that came online during the upgrade may have overwhelmed the older equipment, investigators say.

“Either through contractor error or a faulty piece of equipment, that router that was being replaced as we switched from copper to fiber, it started flooding other routers in our air traffic control system,” Duffy said in an interview Sunday.

This sent a barrage of data through the FAA’s internal communication system — about 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds – that air traffic controllers use to help guide pilots through the country’s airspace. When that new router was turned on, agency officials noticed the same issues at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, which had undergone similar work weeks before, Duffy said. The routers at the Arkansas and Texas facilities led to 17 out of the FAA’s 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers experiencing network instability, according to the agency.

But some aviation experts say this official explanation strains credulity.

“I don’t think it’s plausible,” Robert W. Mann Jr., the founder of airline analysis and consulting firm R.W. Mann & Company, told CNET. “Given the network architecture, which is fully duplicative and has fallback capabilities on every link and every piece of physical hardware, it’s not credible that one or even two routers would be an issue.”

The impacts of the nationwide ground stop are reverberating on the other side of the weekend. As of 3:30 p.m. EST, 333 flights within, into or out of the US have been canceled Monday, according to flight tracking website FlightAware, and more than 3,800 have been delayed.

The FAA router that grounded tens of thousands of flights looks a lot different from the one that sits in your home. These industrial-grade devices, called switches, are much larger than home Wi-Fi routers and built to withstand harsh conditions. While the agency pointed to the single router in Arkansas as the cause of Friday’s issues, it says it disabled 60 similar units as a precaution.

FAA Administrator Brian Bedford said Saturday that the agency is in the process of replacing around 2,000 Cisco routers with 600 Juniper routers. Could any one of those routine equipment upgrades suddenly overload the FAA’s communications system?

“What surprised me most is the redundancy part for this type of national infrastructure,” Ilia Rabinovich, vice president at the cybersecurity firm Sygnia, told CNET. “This is one of the first things we discuss with clients in terms of preparedness – having backups, having redundancy connectivity, having different connections that you can migrate to different places.”

Mann thought the timing and symptoms pointed to a new $875 million AI-supported air traffic management tool called Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories, or SMART.

“What they did starting in September at Baltimore-Washington is at a very low level, for about 60 days. It had managed about 180 flights in total over 60 days,” Mann said. “And then suddenly in November, they announced they would implement that system across all 22 continental US air traffic control centers.”

“You went from subscale to superscale based upon 60 days of very, very limited testing, and within two days, you had the meltdown that they should have known was likely to occur,” Mann said.

On Oct. 13, more than 25 lawmakers sent a letter to the FAA asking it to pause the rollout of the tool, citing a lack of transparency and training for air traffic controllers.

“We have heard from several sources that frontline aviation safety workers were notified of the SMART tool rollout mere days in advance or not at all, giving them no time to learn how the system works, how it is incorporated into their workflow, and what oversight and accountability mechanisms maintain aviation safety standards,” the letter says.

The FAA says in an FAQ page on the incident that the SMART system wasn’t responsible for the issue. A representative for the agency didn’t immediately respond to CNET’s request for comment.

The FAA’s acting CTO, Rebecca Guy, said at a press conference Saturday that the FAA identified the routers in Arkansas and Texas and disabled “both of those right away and were able to stabilize our network.” But the Transportation Secretary’s interviews over the weekend didn’t instill a lot of confidence in the FAA network’s resilience.

“We have old switches, old routers. We use 1980s little copper lines. It’s an old system that went down and went down everywhere. It got overloaded,” Duffy said at a Friday night news conference.

The FAA has upgraded over 3,500 of its communication lines to fiber, but more than 5,000 copper lines are still scheduled to be replaced by the end of 2028. It’s eye-opening to see how reliant the FAA still is on copper lines, a technology that the Federal Communications Commission has for years deemed insufficient for average home internet users.

It didn’t take long for officials to point to funding as the ultimate cause of Friday’s groundings. Duffy repeatedly called for more funding over the weekend in order to upgrade the outdated system.

“The government and FAA are looked on as the piñata here because every time you beat on FAA or beat on the government for not doing a good job, money falls out,” Mann said. “It didn’t take, what, 6 hours, before we had a cabinet secretary basically saying if we gave him $50 billion, he would fix all this.”

Duffy had asked for $30 billion for the FAA in September. After Friday’s fiasco, he increased his request by $20 billion.

#3068. Bank of America vs. JPMorgan Chase: Which Financial Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Bank of America trades at 1.1 times book value versus JPMorgan's 2.5, but JPMorgan's scale and net margin may justify the premium for some investors.

Investors often look to Bank of America (BAC -0.45%) and JPMorgan Chase (JPM -1.26%) when seeking stability. These banking titans dominate the financial landscape, but choosing the better buy for 2027 requires a closer look.

Bank of America focuses on a balance of consumer banking and wealth management while maintaining a vast digital footprint. JPMorgan Chase operates as a global financial powerhouse with unparalleled scale across investment banking and retail services. This comparison evaluates their financial health, growth trajectories, and valuation to determine which better fits your long-term goals.

Bank of America offers a wide range of financial services across segments such as consumer banking, wealth management, and global markets. Among diversified bank stocks, it currently serves roughly 69 million consumer and small business clients across more than 35 countries. Its strategy focuses on digital integration, operating approximately 3,500 retail financial centers and 15,000 ATMs to maintain local presence while expanding its online capabilities.

Reliable recent quarterly figures for at least one of these companies aren't available, so this comparison uses each company's latest full fiscal year. In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $113.1 billion, representing growth of roughly 6.8% over the previous year. The company reported net income of approximately $30.5 billion, resulting in a net margin of close to 27%.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was roughly 1.2, calculated by dividing total debt by shareholder equity. The current ratio stood at approximately 0.4, and free cash flow for the year reached nearly $12.6 billion. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 31.7% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

JPMorgan Chase is a global financial leader serving millions of individual customers, corporations, and governments across more than 100 markets. The firm operates through major segments including consumer and community banking, the commercial and investment bank, and asset and wealth management. Its scale is extensive, with the Chase brand providing national coverage through more than 5,000 branches across the 48 contiguous states.

In fiscal 2025, the bank generated revenue of approximately $182.4 billion, representing nearly 2.8% growth over the prior year. Net income reached close to $57 billion for the same period. This resulted in a net margin of roughly 31.3%, showing the amount of revenue that remained as profit after all expenses.

As of JPMorgan's December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 2.6, illustrating that the company uses more debt relative to its equity than its peer. The current ratio was roughly 0.5, and free cash flow for the fiscal year 2025 was nearly negative $147.8 billion. Free cash flow represents cash from operations minus capital expenditures, showing the surplus cash available after maintaining operations.

Bank of America deals with significant regulatory and legal risks, highlighted by a December 2024 consent order regarding its anti-money laundering compliance. The company is also managing ongoing securities fraud class action lawsuits with deadlines extending into late 2026. Market instability and competition from other large institutions like Morgan Stanley (MS -0.48%) also pressure the bank's long-term outlook.

JPMorgan Chase faces legal and regulatory risks, including ongoing investigations and a cash sweep lawsuit that was partially allowed to proceed in early 2026. Credit risk remains a factor, particularly given concentrations in industries such as commercial real estate, alongside operational risks posed by emerging technologies. The company competes intensely with major rivals such as Wells Fargo (WFC -0.94%) to maintain its dominant market position.

Bank of America appears to be the more value-oriented choice, trading at a lower multiple of both its future earnings estimates and its book value.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

The forward P/E compares a stock price to its future earnings estimates over the next year. The P/B ratio compares the stock price with the company's book value (its assets minus its liabilities, roughly what shareholders would own on paper), and investors lean on it for insurers and banks. A lower P/B ratio means the stock costs less relative to book value.

I think these two stocks are pretty conservative investments. It's obviously not impossible for banks to blow up, but these are massive, established institutions, and they've been bailed out by the U.S. government before. So, in that sense, they strike me as relatively safe investments.

Bank of America's recent revenue growth was stronger, but JPMorgan has a higher net margin. Bank of America's dividend yields more, but on an absolute basis, JPMorgan's payout is higher.

Let's see how both stocks have performed:

Bank of America badly trails JPMorgan, but more importantly, the former hasn't even kept pace with the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.39%). The whole point of investing in individual stocks is to beat the market's average return. B of A is not making a strong argument for itself here.

Past performance, of course, is no indication of future results. The next 10 years may look very different than the past. But if I'm buying a bank stock for 2027 and beyond, JPMorgan gets my vote.

Personal finance writers and editors share their favorite ways to be resourceful.

Have you ever thrown away groceries that spoiled before you got around to using them? Or bought a new jacket despite already having half a dozen in your closet?

It’s easy to let things go to waste and accumulate more than we need.

Use Less Stuff Day, which lands on Nov. 19 this year, encourages us to rethink our consumption habits and make more mindful, environmentally friendly choices.

That might mean squeezing every last drop out of what you’ve got, finding creative ways to reuse things or simply buying less.

I keep a couple of simple tricks up my sleeve to extend the life of my family’s clothing: OxiClean soaks and basic sewing skills. You’d be surprised by how many things you can salvage with a little cleaning and mending.

I asked my fellow Nerds to share some of the ways they reduce waste and unnecessary spending. Maybe you’ll pick up an idea or two.

Pamela de la Fuente, managing editor: My husband grew up with a “make what’s in the house” kinda family. I didn’t. But this weekend while looking for spaghetti I found some crispy rice cereal, and I knew we had marshmallows from a bonfire a few weeks ago so I said, “I’m going to make crispy rice treats with this for the kids and get rid of this cereal.” (Surprisingly, it was not stale.) I still had cereal left, so I added it to some chocolate protein bars I love to make and my son said, “These are 9 out of 10. Usually they are 7 out of 10!”

Karen Gaudette Brewer, head of content: I’m a big “make big batches of food and freeze it” person, so I can drive everyone nuts reminding them that we really do have food at home. That freezer also holds grated lemon zest and cubes of those last little bits of chicken broth and wine so that I can easily make pan sauces and not waste that last half cup of goodness.

Jessica Cano, content coordinator: I save the tops from strawberries after cutting them for my kids. We use some to make strawberry balsamic vinegar, some to make strawberry syrup and the rest go in the freezer to be used for smoothies. Keeps me from having to buy frozen fruit and multiple vinegars.

Pantry shopping can result in less food in the trash and fewer trips to the grocery store. It can also make experimenting with new recipes a little more exciting. Take a page from Managing Editor Athena Cocoves, who says, “Sometimes we pretend we're on ‘Chopped.’”

Ryan Brady, lead writer: Rotating toys with our kids has helped them get more enjoyment out of the same toys versus constantly buying new toys. We put a bunch of toys they're bored with in a bin, and months later, take one out and bam — it's like a new toy all over again!

Kim Lowe, head of content: I invested a whole $12 in a lint remover last winter that transformed all my old sweaters into almost new!

Laura McMullen, editor: Almost all of my kids’ clothes are thrifted or hand-me-downs. My friend group of parents has kids from age 2 to 7, all of whom are about six months apart. We’ve developed a hearty clothing exchange. It’s fun to see my friends' kids wear hand-me-downs that we got from my brother’s family almost 10 years ago.

Look for other ways to salvage your belongings or get them secondhand. That might include watching a vacuum repair tutorial on YouTube, borrowing books from the library or purchasing used tools from Facebook Marketplace. The goal: Keep more stuff in circulation and out of landfills.

Abby Doyle, lead writer: Composting isn’t as fussy as it seems. Once you get into it, you start seeing would-be waste as stuff to feed your new backyard buddy. Junk mail, paper bags, slimy spring mix … it’s all food for my “pet dirt.” And my garden has legit never looked better.

Yuliya Goldshteyn, editor: Instead of throwing away kid art, I reuse it as wrapping paper throughout the year. Bespoke gift wrapping for everyone! I haven’t bought gift wrap for five years now.

Caitlin Constantine, editor: I repurpose glass jars and plastic containers. It always seemed like such a pity to throw perfectly good containers into the recycling after one use, so now I reuse them before I recycle them.

Before you toss something, ask yourself, “Is there another way I can use this?” An old T-shirt makes a good cleaning rag, for example.

Being resourceful often means getting as much mileage as possible out of what you have.

For all that, it helps to look beyond short-term noise and focus on stocks with strong long-term growth potential.

Top Wall Street analysts' recommendations can help investors gain clarity, as these experts conduct in-depth research to pick stocks with attractive growth prospects.

Enterprise software and cloud infrastructure company Oracle (ORCL) recently announced better-than-expected results for the first quarter of fiscal 2027. The quarter benefited from solid growth in cloud infrastructure revenue.

After hosting a series of investor meetings with Ken Bond, Oracle head of investor relations following Q1 earnings, Guggenheim analyst John DiFucci reiterated a buy rating on the stock with a price target of $400. Oracle remains a Guggenheim Best Idea, he said.

"We continue to believe ORCL is a decade stock, driven by the massive (and profitable) opportunity ahead for AI training and inferencing," said DiFucci. He also cited the traditional Public Cloud business and additional AI-enabled cloud database and cloud applications for his bullish stance. DiFucci expects all the factors to drive revenue and profit acceleration over the next few years.

While Oracle delivered 850 MW of data center capacity in Q1 FY27, Bond cautioned that Infrastructure as a Service revenue in any quarter depends more on the timing of when that capacity comes online, than on the headline MW number. DiFucci expects IaaS growth to stay strong, with full-year growth expected above Q1 FY27's 120% constant currency rate. Management expects total revenue growth to accelerate sequentially throughout fiscal 2027, as the faster-growing infrastructure business makes up a larger share of the mix.

DiFucci addressed concerns regarding customer concentration, saying OpenAI's share of total remaining performance obligations has dropped from 80% last June to about 50% now, and is expected to keep falling as new contracts are signed with new and existing customers.

DiFucci ranks No. 263 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 62% of the time, delivering an average return of about 17.5%. See Oracle Insider Trading Activity on TipRanks.

Space systems and launch services provider Rocket Lab (RKLB) was recently initiated as a buy with an $80 price target by Raymond James analyst Brian Gesuale.

"RKLB has assembled launch, spacecraft, components, payloads and optical communications, with Neutron and Iridium completing medium-lift and applications/spectrum in 2027," said Gesuale.

The 5-star analyst highlighted that with the completion of the Iridium acquisition, Rocket Lab will become the only vertically integrated space company with positive free cash flow (FCF). The deal will add a deployed constellation valued at more than $3 billion, globally coordinated L-band spectrum and about $500 million in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) and $300 million in free cash flow (FCF).

Gesuale highlighted RKLB's strong revenue and backlog growth and progress toward positive EBITDA and FCF in 2027/2028. Rocket Lab is moving from a heavy investment phase into monetization, with estimated revenue growth of 59% in 2026, the analyst said, noting that RKLB's backlog has more than doubled to almost $2.4 billion from $1.1 billion in Q3 2025.

Given strong growth projections, the analyst expects RKLB's gross margins to expand from about a 35% trough in 2027 to about 47% by 2030, while R&D spending is estimated to decline from ~35% of sales in 2026 to about 10% in 2028, creating substantial operating leverage as the platform matures.

#3063. This 8%-Yielding Dividend Stock Pays You 16 Times a Year. Here’s What a $25,000 Investment Deposits Each Month.

Main Street Capital is an income-generating machine.

Most dividend stocks pay you four times a year. Main Street Capital (MAIN +0.08%) pays you four times as often. The business development company (BDC) pays a regular monthly dividend around the 15th of each month and a supplemental quarterly dividend near the last day of each quarter, for a total of 16 payments each year.

Here's a look at how much dividend income you'd collect each month if you invested $25,000 in the high-yielding dividend stock.

Main Street Capital pays a regular monthly dividend of $0.27 per share ($3.24 annually). At its current share price of around $56, the BDC has a 5.8% yield based solely on its regular dividend. The company has never cut or suspended its regular monthly dividend since its 2007 IPO. It has raised its monthly payment by 3.8% over the past year and by 145% since coming public, including 13 increases since the fourth quarter of 2021.

Additionally, the BDC pays a supplemental dividend of $0.30 per share each quarter. The supplemental dividend brings its annualized dividend to $4.44 per share, pushing its yield to nearly 8%. The company has declared a supplemental dividend for 21 consecutive quarters, paying the current rate since early 2024. However, it has reduced and suspended this payment in the past, so it's not as bankable as the monthly dividend.

Based on its recent share price, a $25,000 investment would purchase about 446 shares. This investment would generate $120.53 per month in dividend income (roughly $1,446 per year). Additionally, investors would receive another $133.93 in quarterly supplemental dividends (about $535 per year). That works out to around $165 in dividend income each month.

That base income stream should steadily rise. Meanwhile, the BDC should continue to pay meaningful supplemental dividends, as long as market conditions remain healthy. Those dual income streams make Main Street Capital an attractive passive income investment.

#3062. School Campuses Emerge as the Latest Battleground for Flock Safety Cameras

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Over the last year, a backlash against surveillance technologies from companies like Flock Safety has caused agencies in communities, including Los Angeles and Dayton, Ohio, to reevaluate or cancel their contracts for tools such as license plate reader cameras and drones.

A recent story in The Guardian points to dozens of schools, mostly college campuses, where contracts with Flock have been discontinued or where student protests and activism are pressuring administrations to cut ties. Some of the schools that have walked away from Flock include Cornell University, Emory University, Penn State University and Stanford University, where a coalition called Safe Stanford successfully organized to convince school officials. At Stanford, the university chose to switch from Flock to technology from Genetec, which stores data for only an hour and doesn’t share information with third parties.

Some of the most recent campus protests against using Flock technology have been on the University of Iowa campus, where 2,000 petition signatures were delivered to campus police, and at the University of Kentucky, where student groups chanted, “Flock out! Flock off!”

Flock, which is one of several companies, including Axon Enterprise, Motorola Solutions and Palantir Technologies, that provide surveillance hardware and software to law enforcement, has been heavily criticized for license plate reader failure rates and abuses within law enforcement.

In an email to CNET, the Atlanta-based company declined to offer the number of colleges or schools it works with, though a recent research paper published in Policing & Society put the number at around 150.

Flock stressed in its email to CNET that customers it contracts with own and control their own data.

“Students deserve to feel safe at school, and Flock license plate reader technology has a measurable impact on helping to solve crimes and increase public safety,” the spokesperson said. “Flock LPR cameras capture a point-in-time image of the rear of a vehicle. Flock does not use facial recognition, cannot identify who is inside a vehicle and cannot determine who the vehicle is registered to.”

When government agencies like police departments or county sheriff’s offices employ a company like Flock to provide surveillance services, it typically involves installing cameras in public locations and pointing them at street intersections or on buildings.

College and high school campuses may have different rules for on-campus surveillance and for public schools. They might also be bound by state laws that also apply to government agencies.

Peikoff said that most courts have allowed the collection of the types of data Flock Safety collects. However, Peikoff said that problems can arise regarding how long agencies such as police departments or schools can retain the data they collect. In the past, activists have pointed to abuses that have occurred when law enforcement workers inappropriately accessed or shared information collected by Flock, in some cases, using it for stalking.

“Maintaining a vast, queryable database of location histories of individuals about whom there’s no particularized suspicion not only presents an opportunity for abuse, but is in itself, I believe, a Fourth Amendment violation,” Peikoff said.

#3061. iPhone Duo 2 prototypes suggest Face ID, Action Button, other potential 2027 features

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

With manufacturing deadlines looming, it's unclear which of several feature upgrades may have to wait until the foldable's third generation.

Although the iPhone Duo was released just this fall, Apple is finalizing the foldable’s second generation. According to a Bloomberg report, Apple has already created prototypes for the second iPhone Duo, codenamed V78, and some include a sought-after feature: Face ID.

Apple reportedly wants to bring Face ID to the foldable, potentially integrating it into the outer display. However, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman notes that Apple appears to be running out of time to finalize its plans for the Duo ahead of a fall 2027 launch.

Also: iPhone Duo review: Hard to recommend, even harder to put down

iPhone launch events typically take place in early September, when Apple releases its new smartphone lineups. To have the iPhones ready for sale on the heels of their announcement, Apple must manufacture the new models well before the launch event.

Because of this timeline concern, Face ID isn’t guaranteed for the iPhone Duo 2, though it could come to a third generation instead.

Other planned uogrades — including an Action Button, a telephoto camera, and a thinner, lighter construction — are also noted in the report.

Apple reportedly wants to add an Action Button, the customizable button that performs an action when pressed. The iPhone Duo 2 may combine the Action Button and the Camera Control buttons into a single button, providing a useful physical shortcut instead of adding a new button.

The report indicates that many users don’t use the camera control button as often as Apple expected. Combining the camera and action buttons gives Apple the real estate necessary to add both options in an already constrained space.

Apple also wants to incorporate a telephoto camera into the iPhone Duo, though this is likely to happen in one of the next couple of generations. A telephoto camera would give users greater flexibility to zoom in and capture clear photos of distant objects, which would be an upgrade to the Duo’s photography features.

Technically, equipping the Duo with a telephoto camera is feasible, but the biggest obstacle is space constraints. A telephoto camera needs more room than a wide-angle one, since it requires additional optical elements to magnify distant objects.

Apple already uses a tetraprism design in its Pro iPhones, which allows a longer optical path without too much physical depth.

Apple also wants to reduce the weight and thickness of the iPhone Duo, which is legitimately clunky and cumbersome. To do this, Apple needs to balance the large internal and outer displays, battery capacity, camera array, and the hinge mechanism.

Also: The iPhone Action Button you’re hardly using has a superpower

For many users, reducing the weight and thickness of a passport-sized foldable could matter more in buying decisions than adding another button or camera.

Gurman’s latest report doesn’t mention any planned changes for the iPhone Duo’s hinge mechanism, even after concerns with the first generation’s durability. With manufacturing deadlines fast approaching, however, it’s unlikely that Apple will be able to make changes to the Duo 2 based on consumer feedback. More than likely, these changes would come with the third-generation model.

CNET tested the iPhone Duo’s hinge mechanism and found that, after around 440,000 cycles, the hinge stopped opening flat on its own. Loosening and other signs of wear were evident after 390,000 folds.

Also: The best iPhone Duo cases: Expert recommended

Given the thinner, lighter construction of a future Duo model, one could assume that changes to the hinge and the foldable’s internal structure are imminent, but this has not been confirmed.

Because Apple will not have enough time to gather feedback on the iPhone Duo before the manufacturing deadlines for the iPhone Duo 2, I don’t expect the second-generation iPhone Duo to be significantly different from its predecessor. We do expect a thinner iPhone Duo 2 and a way to incorporate the Action and Camera buttons.

#3060. This Magnificent Growth Stock Just Entered the Artificial Intelligence (AI) Cloud Race, and It Looks Dirt Cheap

This company has never been cheaper, despite delivering blistering growth and unveiling an exciting new cloud business.

Singapore-based Sea Limited (SE -1.68%) operates the largest e-commerce platform in Southeast Asia, in addition to a booming digital financial services business and a mobile game development studio that owns some of the world's most popular titles.

But Sea just announced a brand-new business called Sea Cloud, which will offer a range of artificial intelligence (AI) services to enterprise customers. The company is uniquely positioned to make this venture a success, and it could result in significant long-term returns for investors.

Sea stock is currently the cheapest it has ever been by one widely used valuation metric, and in fact, it's trading at a steep discount to most other AI cloud stocks. Read on.

Shopee is Sea's hybrid business-to-consumer and consumer-to-consumer e-commerce platform, and it has a dominant presence in Southeast Asian countries like Indonesia, Malaysia, and Singapore. Shopee processed 4.5 billion orders worth a combined $39.7 billion during the recent third quarter of 2026 (ended Sept. 30) alone, with those figures growing by 25% and 23% year over year, respectively.

Then there is Monee, Sea's digital financial services platform. It offers buy now, pay later loans to consumers to boost their purchasing power, and it also lends money to Shopee merchants to help them grow their businesses. It had 44 million active borrowers during the third quarter, and its loan book grew by a whopping 60% to $12.6 billion.

Over the last two years, Sea has invested heavily in AI capabilities to make those platforms more efficient. The company is now running AI software at scale in areas like fraud detection, customer service, and content generation, and it has mastered the art of squeezing the most value out of data center computing hardware.

Developing those capabilities cost Sea a lot of money, but it will start profiting off them by offering them to enterprise customers through Sea Cloud. Unlike most other cloud providers, Sea's strategy won't involve building expensive data centers unless specifically requested by customers, with prepayments attached.

In fact, Sea is entering the AI cloud race with a rock-solid balance sheet. It boasts a whopping $9.5 billion in cash (and cash equivalents) with under $1 billion in debt, whereas many other companies in this space have borrowed truckloads of money with an uncertain path to profitability.

The Sea Cloud business is still in the formation stage, so it hasn't generated any revenue just yet. But even without it, Sea delivered $8.6 billion in revenue from its existing businesses during the third quarter, up by an eye-popping 43.4% from the year-ago period. It blew away Wall Street's average forecast of $8.1 billion.

Sea also delivered a great result at the bottom line, so its rapid revenue growth wasn't a result of burning through significant amounts of cash. It generated $931.3 million in adjusted (non-GAAP) earnings before interest, tax, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA), up 28.6% from the year-ago period.

Despite Sea's incredible operating results, its stock is actually down 40% this year. It's mainly because management floated the idea of spinning Monee off into a separate company, and investors are still unsure what the structure might look like. However, the deal will have to satisfy regulators in multiple countries, and Sea's chief executive Forrest Li says the process could take up to three years, so nothing is set in stone just yet.

Following its sharp decline, Sea stock is trading at a price-to-sales (P/S) ratio of just 1.5 as I write this on Nov. 15, which is the cheapest level in its history. Moreover, Sea is significantly cheaper than other AI cloud providers like CoreWeave, IREN, and Nebius Group.

With a portfolio of highly successful existing businesses, a rock-solid balance sheet, and an incoming AI cloud platform, I think Sea stock could be a great long-term buy at the current level.

#3059. CNET Survey: $75 Billion in Holiday Packages Could Be Vulnerable to Lurking Porch Pirates

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The average package value nears $300, yet 20% of US adults don't use security devices to help protect their deliveries due to costs.

Imagine patiently waiting for the special-edition Legend of Zelda Nintendo Switch 2 console or the new iPhone Duo to be delivered to your door — only for it to disappear seconds after arrival. That’s the risky reality we’re facing this holiday season because of porch pirates.

Online holiday shopping has become the go-to way for many US adults to conveniently find, compare and buy must-have gifts. But leaving those pricey gifts at your door gives thieves a better chance of snagging them in seconds if you don’t have a plan to store them out of sight.

CNET’s annual package theft survey polls US adults about their experiences with porch pirates and how they try to prevent it. This year, the average package value is close to $300, and 28% of US adults have had a package stolen, know someone who has or caught an attempted theft within the past year. Yet 20% of US adults don’t use security devices due to hardware costs or monthly subscription fees.

But leaving your packages unguarded could be a big risk — especially during the holidays. On the other hand, bad actors have been caught in the act on home security cameras. Is it really enough to deter bad actors, and what more can you do to protect your deliveries?

CNET’s findings show that some US adults have dealt with porch theft firsthand: 8% had packages meant for themselves or their households stolen within the past year, and 5% had a delivered gift stolen. Very few (1%) caught a theft in the act on a video doorbell or security camera.

Meanwhile, many US adults know someone who fell victim to package theft — 13% know a neighbor or community member who had a package stolen within the past year, and 12% know someone who doesn’t live in their community who has.

“Close to a third of our respondents are personally acquainted with package theft, which is still a high number compared to other issues like break-ins,” said CNET’s senior home security editor, Tyler Lacoma. “Thieves generally look for crimes of opportunity, and few things are easier than a package left on a doorstep, especially if nobody is home.”

Surprisingly, most US adults (72%) haven’t experienced package theft or know anyone who has.

Even though the percentages above may seem low, Lacoma said that package theft typically increases during the holidays when thieves know more deliveries are likely, and new porch theft tactics are always on the horizon.

There are reports of thieves trying Wi-Fi jamming to disable live security camera footage while they steal packages. And findings show that some are installing spy cams in high-value neighborhoods to learn your home’s layout and habits to take your packages shortly after they’re delivered. In recent years, pirates have even tracked shipping labels for high-value tech, like iPhones, to steal the package within minutes of arrival.

So while the majority of US adults haven’t fallen victim, that shouldn’t be a sign to shrug off the concern or relax your home security measures. Instead, now’s the time to plan how to safely store your packages if they’re delivered while you’re away.

Online shopping and deliveries to your door can be a convenient way to check off holiday wish lists, but the average package value this holiday season is less than last year. CNET found that US adults plan to have an average of $276.24 in holiday packages delivered during this holiday season. That’s $23.82 less than last year’s average of $300.06.

By generation, Millennials also have a lower estimated average package value than last year, with an average of $227.25, compared to their 2025 package value of $307.47 — an $80.22 difference, while Gen Z’s package value is only about $7 less than last year. But any package’s value is still worth taking precautions to help prevent it from being stolen.

Lacoma has thoughts on why that might be. In short, lower spending could mean fewer packages.

“I wonder if people have also simply gotten fewer packages in general this year due to tariffs, inflation and tech prices. That could pull these numbers down,” said Lacoma. But there’s a high chance that could be the case considering CNET’s 2026 annual holiday survey, which found that US adult tech spending is down to $808 — which is $123 less than last year’s average of $931.

Thieves may not always know what’s in boxes they’re stealing but they’re willing to take a chance. We asked US adults which items were stolen in package thefts in the past year to give you a sense of what’s at risk.

Among the items stolen, apparel and accessories were the most common goods stolen (40%). That’s followed by toys and games (23%). Then there are everyday home basics, like decor, cookware and small appliances (19%).

But personal tech devices and accessories are still among the items stolen. Small accessories like phone chargers and cases are most common (16%) among tech-related packages stolen. They are followed by audio gadgets like headphones and Bluetooth speakers, along with streaming devices and soundbars (11%, respectively).

Still, more costly tech like gaming consoles (10%), computers and laptops (9%) and smart home devices (6%) are among devices stolen.

You shouldn’t leave your packages up to chance. That’s why Lacoma recommends a few safer options to ensure your packages are stored securely after they’re delivered, even beyond keeping an eye on your doorbell or security camera. Instead, keep your packages out of sight with tactics like a delivery box with a code or key or ask for an in-garage delivery.

“Delivery boxes have reached a new level of popularity in recent years as an effective way to stop porch pirates completely. However, Amazon’s Key service that delivers to your garage is an alternative,” said Lacoma. “Either way, you’ll need to trust delivery people to handle your shipments, unless you want to arrange for pickup at a nearby shipping center, which some people like to combine with other holiday errands.”

If you don’t want to install a new security feature, try scheduling your packages to arrive when you know you’re home, requiring a signature from someone you trust or changing your delivery location to a pickup spot, like UPS’ Hold for Pick-Up locations or Amazon Lockers.

Home surveillance, like outdoor security cameras and video doorbells, can deter package thieves who don’t want to risk getting caught on camera. But US adults have mixed feelings about their effectiveness in protecting against package theft.

“Fortunately, the right home security picks can solve both these problems,” said Lacoma. “Brands like Tapo, Eufy, Aqara and even Google Nest offer package detection and alerts for free, so you don’t have to worry about extra fees.”

Among all US adults, only 14% have security devices with a monthly subscription that lets them save or playback video. By comparison, 12% have security devices but no subscription.

Those percentages could be low for a few reasons, including the overall perception of how helpful surveillance and security really are against porch theft. Eleven percent of US adults don’t think security devices deter porch thefts. It’s a valid concern since 4% fell victim to package theft or an attempted theft despite having security devices. And some US adults (9%) use security devices to get proof of a theft after the fact — not to prevent it.

But that doesn’t mean you should ignore the possibility of package theft — especially during the holidays. Even if you don’t want to install cameras or new security devices, make a plan to protect your packages and avoid the headache of package theft over the holidays.

“Remember, the simple presence of a security camera is enough to make many thieves look elsewhere – interviews have confirmed it,” said Lacoma. “And with today’s phone alerts about package detection, you can usually check on a package only seconds after it appears, or bring up footage if it unexpectedly vanishes, letting you take action fast. New practices like delivery boxes or in-garage delivery help address risks in concrete ways, too.”

CNET commissioned YouGov Plc to conduct the survey. All figures, unless otherwise stated, are from YouGov Plc. The total sample size was 2,016 adults. Fieldwork was undertaken between Oct. 23–27, 2026. The survey was carried out online. The figures have been weighted and are representative of all US adults (aged 18 plus).

The $75 billion figure was calculated by multiplying the average value of deliveries each US adult expects to receive by the 2025 US population of adults ages 18 and over calculated by the US Census Bureau.

#3058. 5 ways AI will change how you defend your business in 2027

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Security leaders reveal the future consequences of AI outpacing human defenders.

At the beginning of the year, few organizations were utilizing large language models (LLMs) and AI agents in their cybersecurity workflows, including for discovering and patching vulnerabilities. According to Google, this is now happening at scale.

Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?

The capabilities of agentic AI are fast outstripping the speed and scale at which traditional security operations centers (SOCs) can operate. Like it or not, AI has an integral role in the new reality — for the defenders and threat actors.

Speed and scale are the main reasons enterprises consider adopting AI in SOCs and for security more broadly, and these factors underpin Google’s new security forecast for 2027 — Cloud CISO Perspectives. However, without the right precautions, AI security adopters could inadvertently increase their attack surface rather than shrink it.

With this in mind, these are five ways AI will change the security industry over the next year and what CISOs need to consider going into 2027.

Alert fatigue is well-known across SOC teams. Alert after alert needs to be trawled through; many are irrelevant or false positives, tying up skilled staff with the mundane, tedious, time-consuming task of triaging them.

Now that autonomous, AI-driven threats can probe a network, gain entry, and move laterally across it in minutes, chasing threat data and security alerts from multiple systems logged days or weeks ago can’t help a business mitigate them — and certainly not at the speed of the threat.

According to Google’s forecast, AI will mean the alert queue quietly disappears. Ramya Chitrakar, VP of engineering at Google Cloud Security, believes that “2027 is the year analysts stop chasing alerts and start shaping outcomes.”

Also: AI is both a cyber weapon and a massive target

How? CISOs must change the alert model itself. Instead of human defenders triaging alerts at the start of a cybersecurity incident, the alert becomes final output, with autonomous agents handling “data enrichment, correlation, and triage automatically, surfacing a verified conclusion rather than a raw ticket,” according to Google.

This means cybersecurity experts can oversee alert handling and verify automated actions, potentially freeing them to focus on other tasks.

Custom agentic AI is often designed — or at least intended — to work autonomously, with human oversight. However, having thousands of individual agents working across multiple environments can create high-value entry points into corporate networks that cyberattackers target.

We need to think of agentic AI as more than a tool: each one needs its own identity, like a human employee, to operate within a zero-trust architecture, retain control, and reduce the risk of compromise.

Also: Your enterprise AI access can be sold for pennies – beware ‘LLM Mixers’

However, Heather Adkins, VP of security engineering at Google, thinks this needs to go further and suggests the zero-trust concept shouldn’t stop at the network layer. Instead, Adkins believes it needs to reach the transaction layer.

A paper trail for each agent needs to be established, which is impossible to handle manually, and even within a zero-trust framework, AI agents could be given too much scope. Instead, implement verification for each transaction and for every authorization, and assign each AI agent its own least-privilege set of credentials that can be revoked if there is a security incident or the agent is no longer required.

“When backed by real-time autonomous reasoning, we can dynamically allow a transaction on Tuesday and block the exact same request on Wednesday if conditions look anomalous,” the report notes.

AI is being used to speed up the development and deployment of new software, and in 2027, security will have to become a continuous system embedded in the software delivery pipeline, according to Google.

Threat actors have carried out software supply chain attacks over the years, one of the most notable being the SolarWinds incident of 2020. Sandra Joyce, VP of Google Threat Intelligence, says cybercriminals are now poisoning everything from open-source code to software libraries, which AI coding assistants often pull automatically into codebases.

Also: How AI security failures are endangering your supply chain

Bug-fix tickets that take days to respond to and security appearing at the end of a software development cycle no longer work. Instead, writing and securing code must happen simultaneously, with the help of agentic AI, so speed doesn’t compromise security.

“It’s also crucial that we link live production environments directly back to source code so that defenders can trace a real-world exposure to the exact line of code, validate whether it is genuinely exploitable, and deliver a pre-tested fix at machine speed without breaking production,” Google added.

As organizations rush to implement AI into their applications and services to appear “AI-first,” innovative, and modern, security may be ignored or treated as an afterthought.

As a result, we may face a new, broader attack surface than we realize, as AI introduces new security issues, including software vulnerabilities, misconfiguration, bypasses, and indirect prompt injection attacks. Now that AI is also in the hands of all cyberattackers — from script kiddies to state-sponsored groups — auditing corporate networks and infrastructure is crucial.

Also: Who’s responsible for catching rogue AI agents? You are

Penetration testing and red team exercises now need to cover agentic AI. This wasn’t in scope for many red teams only a few years ago, but now that businesses have run with the idea of implementing AI in their workflows, processes, and products, organizations need to identify and fix security issues introduced by AI before threat actors take advantage of them.

CISOs should task pen testers with auditing before an autonomous workflow hits production, then combine the results with threat intelligence to ensure defenders have the information they need to bolster network defenses and harden classifiers against new and novel attacks.

The final significant trend we are likely to see in 2027 is tackling agent sprawl to create coordinated teams of AI agents that can rapidly handle security tasks at scale.

Single AI agents given general instructions won’t cut it when AI-assisted attackers can compromise endpoint devices, enter networks, move laterally, or start stealing data in a far shorter timeframe than before. Instead, CISOs should replace these “generalist” AI agents with specialized, orchestrated teams of AI agents that can meet the demands of defending against AI-driven attacks by employing specialist tooling and skill sets.

Also: AI agent kill switch urged by Okta-led alliance

CISOs also need to ensure that each agent has its own domain training and understanding, memory, and dedicated tools, and can act on its own within set limits, with a central coordinator that knows when to hand a decision to a human. This requires oversight, but in return, organizations will avoid agent sprawl, which the tech giant believes is the next iteration of shadow IT and its associated threats.

Legislators must act quickly if they want to avoid a shutdown that would land in the midst of the holiday season.

With the midterm election in the rearview and a new Democrat-controlled Congress about to be sworn in Jan. 4, the current class of legislators finds itself working to avoid an impending government shutdown that would start after Dec. 11.

Over the summer, the House of Representatives passed a stopgap bill that would extend government funding at its current level through the December deadline, in a bid to push the funding battle until after midterm elections. The government had been set to run out of money after Sept. 30.

Disagreements over spending priorities could once again leave the government facing a shutdown. Lawmakers face a deadline, with little time to negotiate a longer-term spending deal before the extension expires on Dec. 11. The lame-duck session — the period between the November elections and the start of the new Congress — gives outgoing lawmakers one final opportunity to reach a long-term agreement or extend the deadline into 2027.

Some Senate Democrats are threatening to withhold support for a deal unless it includes restrictions on funding President Donald Trump’s war with Iran. Meanwhile, Trump is urging Senate leaders to use budget reconciliation to fund an additional $350 billion in supplemental defense spending.

However, leaders in both parties are publicly supporting a short-term stopgap that would keep the government funded until after the current lame-duck session ends.

Every year, Congress is supposed to pass 12 spending bills to keep the government’s lights on. These appropriations bills fund those programs already approved by Congress, including defense, the IRS, food assistance, veterans’ benefits and national parks.

The deadline to fund programs for the next fiscal year is always Oct. 1. Without passing appropriations bills or approving a stopgap that kicks the deadline down the road, the government shuts down.

In the past few funding cycles, Congress has relied on multiple short-term continuing resolutions to keep the government temporarily running.

In 2025, the government shut down for the longest period in U.S. history (Oct. 1 to Nov. 12, 43 days) while this year was marked by the longest partial shutdown ever (Feb. 14 to April 30, 76 days). Why didn’t Congress pass the funding bills in 2025? The two parties were deadlocked over Democrats’ ultimately unsuccessful efforts to permanently extend expiring Obamacare subsidies and roll back recent Medicaid cuts in the One Big, Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA).

A second shutdown — this one partial — began on Feb. 14. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) shut down after lawmakers failed to reach a deal to reform Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) tactics. DHS funding became a flashpoint following the fatal shootings of Renée Good on Jan. 7 by an ICE agent and Alex Pretti on Jan. 24 by a CBP agent, both in Minneapolis. The DHS shutdown followed a four-day partial shutdown that ended Feb. 3.

On April 30, the House passed a bill approved by the Senate to fund most of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The deal fully funded all DHS offices with the exceptions of ICE and Border Patrol. Democrats supported the deal, despite it lacking any of the restrictions on the two agencies that they had been demanding throughout the shutdown.

» MORE: How to prepare for the next government shutdown

At 43 days, the 2025 government shutdown was the longest in history. There have been 22 shutdowns since 1976 and most are short-lived — a few hours or days, at the most.

Before then, there hadn’t been a shutdown since 2018-2019. That shutdown, which lasted 35 days, arose in a dispute over funding for Trump’s border wall in his first term.

Before that there was a 16-day shutdown in 2013, as negotiations over the Affordable Care Act dragged on. In 1995 and 1996, two shutdowns totaled 26 days.

Federal workers bear the brunt of impact from government shutdowns.

During a shutdown, there are ripple effects on delivery of government services and programs.

National parks may close or operate without services.

Federal student aid application processing could be delayed.

Food and drug inspections will be delayed.

The IRS can’t verify income and Social Security numbers, which could cause delays for some mortgages and other loan approvals, as well as tax refunds.

Flights will still operate, but there could be delays if TSA agents and air traffic controllers, who are considered essential employees, decide to call out of work, leading to staff shortages. Even small shortages can have a big impact: During a 2019 government shutdown, the absence of just 10 air traffic controllers at two airports grounded flights and caused delays for the Eastern Seaboard. (Read more on how the shutdown affects travel.)

Social Security and Medicare will keep going, but some administrative functions may be suspended, and telehealth appointments may be interrupted.

Unemployment benefits will continue — states administer compensation — but there could be application processing delays if the shutdown lasts long enough.

Food benefits through Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and the accompanying WIC program will continue — both run on contingency funds. WIC funding will only last one month, and SNAP could be strained after 30 days, as well.

The postal service — the USPS is not funded by the federal government.

Federal student loan payments — accounts are serviced by private companies.

Public schools will remain open — they’re funded by state and local governments.

Amtrak will continue operations — it is operated by a for-profit company.

See more details on how a government shutdown could impact you. The shutdown has had trickle-down economic effects. One immediate and direct impact during the previous shutdown was a suspension of federal economic data. Most of that data wasn’t released during the shutdown. That’s a problem because the government’s official data releases guide the markets, the Federal Reserve and business decisions.ent’s official data releases guide the markets, the Federal Reserve and business decisions.

#3056. Walmart Has Raised Its Dividend 53 Straight Years. Why I'd Buy It Before December and Never Sell.

Walmart's 53-year dividend streak points to a durable business. Advertising, memberships, and global growth could keep it expanding for decades.

Some stocks stand out because they've proven they can reward shareholders for decades, and Walmart (WMT -0.23%) is one of those stocks, having raised its dividend for 53 consecutive years. Looking ahead, with new growth opportunities emerging across advertising and e-commerce, here's why investors might consider buying this retail giant before the new year and holding it forever.

The latest increase brought the company's annual dividend to $0.99 per share, up from $0.94 in the previous fiscal year, just as it's done for the past 53 years.

But Walmart's dividend history is about more than returning cash to shareholders. It's proof of something more important: the durability of its business, as Walmart is built around supplying necessities at competitive prices, regardless of whether the economy is booming or slowing.

On top of that, its enormous scale, established customer relationships, and extensive distribution network make it difficult for competitors to replicate what it has built. Instead of relying on its traditional retail business, Walmart has spent years expanding into faster-growing areas that could support decades of future growth.

Retail has traditionally been a relatively low-margin business. Walmart moves enormous volumes of products, but selling groceries and household essentials leaves limited room for profit growth. That's why growing advertising and membership businesses have become increasingly important.

From there, it's important to consider Walmart Connect, the company's advertising platform. Since Walmart has direct relationships with millions of shoppers and access to valuable shopping data, it can offer brands opportunities to reach consumers much closer to the point of purchase.

In fact, that strategy is already driving growth.

Walmart's global advertising business grew 38% in the second quarter of fiscal 2027, while its U.S. advertising business grew 43%, excluding VIZIO. Plus, the acquisition of VIZIO gives Walmart an opportunity to expand its advertising reach into connected television, creating another channel where it can monetize customer relationships.

Meanwhile, memberships offer another opportunity. For example, Walmart+ and Sam's Club memberships encourage repeat purchases while creating recurring fee revenue.

Plus, they give customers more reasons to consolidate their shopping with Walmart rather than spending across several retailers. With that, global membership fee revenue rose 17% in the second quarter of fiscal 2027.

Meanwhile, beyond advertising and memberships, Walmart is expanding globally to drive the next phase of its growth.

These days, Walmart's growth isn't limited to the U.S. In fact, the company operates across multiple international markets, including Mexico, Canada, China, India, and several countries in Central America and Africa. These businesses provide exposure to different markets and give Walmart more opportunities to expand.

On top of that, its international strategy opens up opportunities in digital markets. In India, for instance, Walmart has a significant stake in Flipkart, one of the country's major e-commerce platforms. As India's digital economy and consumer markets expand, it offers a long-term opportunity that's difficult to replicate through traditional U.S. retail operations.

Likewise, Sam's Club is another important part of this opportunity, as its membership-based warehouse model generates recurring revenue and encourages customer loyalty and repeat spending. In particular, the format is seeing significant potential in markets such as China and Mexico, where membership growth and digital adoption can support expansion.

Still, investors should weigh that growth potential against the stock's valuation and risks.

The vast majority of Wall Street analysts covering the stock rate it a buy or strong buy, with an average price target of $131.45. These days, the stock trades at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of about 38, so many investors are already expecting meaningful growth. Still, Walmart's strong competitive position and growth opportunities help justify that premium.

That said, owning Walmart isn't without risks. For one, its enormous size makes growth challenging, while competition from other retailers could pressure margins and market share. Despite that, Walmart's staying power comes from sticking to the business model that has sustained it for decades, while finding new ways to grow and adapt.

Ultimately, Walmart has spent 53 consecutive years proving it can continue to reward shareholders. Looking ahead, with e-commerce, advertising, and memberships creating new opportunities, its growth runway is far from over. And that's why investors might consider buying shares before the new year and holding them for life.

#3055. Oura Ring Adds a Jet Lag Feature for Time Zone Travelers

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Traveling to new places is good for the soul, but then there’s jet lag, which can cause fatigue, headaches, insomnia and even nausea during your trip. Oura, maker of the Oura Ring, wants to help you combat these effects with its latest feature, Jet Lag Plan, which launched on Tuesday.

A press release explained that Jet Lag Plan was developed using a March 2025 study conducted by the National University of Singapore. The study analyzed de-identified data covering 1.5 million nights of sleep from over 57,000 Oura members to determine how sleep shifted before and after about 65,000 long-distance trips.

Jet Lag Plan is specifically designed for users who travel across at least three time zones and is based on typical sleep patterns, flight itinerary and chronotype. The latter describes whether you’re a morning person, a night person or somewhere in between.

Oura uses 40 to 90 days of sleep timing and activity and average body temperature trends to assign users one of six chronotypes: early morning type, morning type, late morning type, early evening type, evening type and late evening type. This can change over time.

Both your chronotype and sleep history also inform your circadian low point. Usually around 4 a.m., this is when your body temperature is at its lowest and you’re the most ready for sleep.

In the Oura app, you can start a Jet Lag Plan in one of four ways: by adding travel from the Today tab, selecting “Jet Lag” from the app menu, asking the AI-powered Oura Advisor to create a plan for your upcoming trip or responding to a prompt when Oura detects that your phone has changed time zones.

In addition to your flight details, you’ll also want to share the reason for your trip, as a work-related Jet Lag Plan will differ from a vacation one.

Your Jet Lag Plan will then populate with a recommended schedule for sleep, caffeine, activity and light exposure before, during and after your trip, with reminders and the ability to mark actions as complete. You can request adjustments to this plan using Oura Advisor.

During your trip, you’ll be able to compare your readiness score to the typical score for similar trips. This is based on data from 10 million trips already taken by Oura members.

Once your trip ends, you’ll receive a report comparing your sleep and readiness scores before and during your trip.

Jet Lag Plan is now available to Oura members whose language is set to English. It works with an Oura Ring 3 or newer on both Android and iOS.

The latest Oura Ring 5 starts at $399, while a membership is $6 per month or $70 per year.

#3054. Apple could build its AI health chatbot from this study – how to enroll

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Apple is leaning into AI-powered health tools with the launch of its Apple Health AI Usage Study.

Apple is exploring how people use AI for their health, presumably to build its own AI health coach. On Sunday, it launched the Apple Health AI Usage Study, which could contribute to the next AI health experience Apple builds by measuring the quality of AI health responses, comprehension, and everyday health behaviors, according to a press release.

Apple is conducting the study in collaboration with OpenEvidence, a clinical AI platform widely used by healthcare professionals. The study examines the relationship between conversational AI tools, like chatbots, and the people who use them.

“Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey,” Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness, said in the press release.

Also: Apple Watch Series 12 review: Finally, the health tracker I’ve been waiting for

Participants are encouraged to share their HealthKit data and query the health app with questions. The study will also explore how AI tools can best prepare patients ahead of clinical visits. Apple will monitor the AI’s clarity and approachability when providing medical information, and each response or recommendation will be linked to peer-reviewed clinical citations. Responses could be unclear or incomplete, which is why Apple is rolling this out as a study to explore a responsibly designed AI health assistant.

Apple often launches studies for features it would like to develop in the future. For example, many of the hearing health features launched on the AirPods were a direct result of the findings from Apple’s Hearing Study.

Also: Athenahealth patients can ask Claude about their medical records now

The AI usage study comes on the heels of the revamped Health app’s debut, which launches officially next month. It also arrives amid a bevy of AI health coaches, popping up alongside companion health devices. Google launched its AI Health Coach in Google Health Premium last year, and Oura launched a proprietary AI model for women trained on medical standards and research from Oura’s in-house team of board-certified clinicians.

A growing number of Americans are relying on AI for medical advice. A recent survey from Pew Research Center found that 34% of US adults have talked with a chatbot for medical advice. As AI proliferates, that percentage will only increase.

“Patients and clinicians are both turning to AI, but the tools they use are being built and tested in separate worlds,” said Robert M. Wachter, M.D., UCSF’s professor and chair of the Department of Medicine, in the press release.

Apple and other tech companies are building for this new health normal, and the AI usage study indicates that Apple isn’t taking the responsibility lightly.

If you’re interested in participating in Apple’s study, it’s open to 200,000 eligible participants age 21 and older in the US. You’ll need a phone with Apple Intelligence enabled (the iPhone 15 Pro or later), running iOS 26 or later. You can download the study app to learn more and enroll.

#3053. Eaton vs. Vertiv: Which Industrials Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Eaton and Vertiv both ride the electrification wave, but their growth profiles and valuations diverge sharply heading into 2027.

As the energy transition and data center demand accelerate, choosing the right infrastructure play is vital. Should you bet on Eaton Corp. (ETN +0.39%) or Vertiv Holdings Inc. (VRT +1.33%) for your portfolio?

Eaton is a global giant managing power across diverse industrial sectors, while Vertiv specializes in cooling and power systems for the booming data center market. Both companies benefit from massive electrification trends, but they offer different levels of diversification and growth potential for investors looking to capitalize on modern infrastructure needs.

Eaton operates as a massive power management company, serving markets ranging from utilities and data centers to aerospace and mobility. In its latest annual report, filed for FY 2025, the company noted that six major customers account for approximately 22% of revenue in its Electrical sectors. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, particularly as the firm seeks to expand its reach in specialized industrial segments.

In FY 2025, revenue reached about $27.4 billion, which represented growth of approximately 10.3% over the prior year. The company reported a net margin of close to 14.9%, resulting in net income of roughly $4.1 billion. This growth reflects strong demand for electrical infrastructure as global power needs continue to rise.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 0.6x. This ratio shows that total debt is equivalent to 60% of shareholder equity, indicating a moderate level of borrowing. The current ratio, which compares short-term assets to short-term liabilities, was roughly 1.3x, while free cash flow reached about $3.6 billion after subtracting capital expenditures from operating cash.

Vertiv specializes in providing the cooling and power infrastructure required to keep data centers and communication networks running. The company serves prominent hyperscale and cloud providers including Microsoft Corp. (MSFT -1.65%) and Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN +0.39%). It also maintains a strategic partnership with Infineon Technologies (IFNNF +0.35%) to supply power semiconductors for high-performance computing.

In FY 2025, revenue reached approximately $10.2 billion, reflecting significant growth of about 27.7% compared to the previous year. Vertiv reported net income of around $1.3 billion, which corresponds to a net margin of roughly 13%. This rapid expansion highlights the company's leading role in providing critical digital infrastructure within the industrial stocks sector.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was roughly 0.8x. This metric indicates that the company carries $0.80 in debt for every dollar of shareholder equity. The current ratio stood at approximately 1.5x, and free cash flow for the period reached about $1.9 billion, representing the cash left over after the business pays for its necessary capital projects.

Eaton faces operational integration risks because it frequently uses strategic acquisitions to expand its business. The company is also exposed to global supply chain disruptions and inflationary pressures that could impact the cost of raw materials and labor. Furthermore, cybersecurity threats and potential challenges from spinning off its Mobility business segment could affect its operations.

Vertiv carries risks related to its heavy reliance on the growth of data centers and overall spending on artificial intelligence. The company competes against large global manufacturers like Schneider Electric (SBGSF -0.38%) and Legrand (LGRVF -4.42%) for market share in power and cooling solutions. Additionally, the long-term, fixed-price nature of many contracts means that any errors in estimating costs could reduce its future profitability.

Eaton looks cheaper with a lower Forward P/E using future earnings estimates and a lower P/S ratio based on sales over the past twelve months.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

Eaton is a blue chip industrial company that is benefiting from megatrends, including energy transition, electrification, digitalization, and infrastructure spending. The company has been experiencing strong orders and record backlogs, which has led investors to believe top-line sales and profits should steadily increase. In particular, data centers have been a high-growth area for Eaton, with orders up more than threefold in 2026 and an order backlog that extends out 12 years. Management also anticipates strong growth in the aerospace and utility end markets.

In its third quarter, reported in early November, Eaton saw sales rise 28% to $8.9 billion, with net income up about 30% to $1.34 billion. Eaton is expected to finish 2026 with sales up more than 20% over 2025 and improved net income. For 2027, Wall Street analysts expect sales and net income to rise about 12%.

Vertiv has been a specialist in computer cooling systems since World War Two, and it also offers complementary products for mission-critical technological infrastructure, such as uninterruptible power supplies. The AI-driven data center boom presents a long-term opportunity for Vertiv, especially for its liquid cooling systems. Liquid cooling is better for quickly removing heat from high-powered chipsets. Vertiv believes one-third of the total addressable market for data center cooling will eventually use liquid solutions (technically, some air-cooling and heat-dissipation systems will always be needed to work in tandem with liquid systems).

For 2026, Vertiv revenue should rise 44% to $14.7 billion, with net income shooting up about 90% to $2.5 billion as AI data center demand powers the business. Those figures are much stronger than anticipated just a few months ago. For 2027, analyst consensus has Vertiv revenue jumping about a third, with net income up more than 40% to $4.6 billion.

These are both traditional industrial businesses that have tapped into the trends of electrification and AI, and are posting exceptional growth as a result. Which is the better buy? It may be a toss-up, so Eaton's slightly cheaper P/E and P/S ratios win the day.
