An estimated 1.5 million travelers had their flight plans upended on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, after the Federal Aviation Administration announced a rare nationwide ground stop. That number comes from the flight data firm Cirium, which tracked passengers scheduled to depart U.S. airports that day after the stop was declared. The ground stop lasted more than four hours.

That ground stop lifted at 8:15 p.m. ET on Friday, but the ripple effects could be massive. Planes are out of position for the weekend, and some travelers are still trying to reach their destinations or get refunds on flights and other expenses.

NerdWallet travel writer Craig Joseph was among those affected. He was flying out of Asheville, North Carolina, for a one-night trip to a college football game, and learned his flight was delayed by three hours. Because it was a quick trip, and he had booked with frequent flyer miles that could be redeposited into his account, he canceled. Moments later, his flight — and every other one on the departures board — was canceled.

He canceled his hotel before the deadline, too, so his only sunk cost was the football ticket. But not all travelers will be so lucky.

If your travel plans were impacted, here's how you can get your money back.

Don’t count on calling customer service. Major airlines have been overwhelmed with customers asking for help.

As of Friday night, Southwest’s automated phone number said it would take several hours to get a callback from a human. American Airlines’ automated line said it would take at least two hours to reach a human. Frontier Airlines wouldn’t even let us speak to a human, and instead sent us to a chatbot.

Skip the chatbots and long waits. Instead, do this:

Check the airline’s app or website, and look for any emails or other alerts. Most airlines are proactively notifying affected passengers with rebooking options, and you may be automatically rebooked.

Get a refund or rebook online or through the airline's app. Every major airline has issued a travel waiver due to the ground stop, which gives you more flexibility to rebook without a change fee, often without charging for fare differences. More on that below.

Check your travel insurance. Because the ground stop was outside the airlines' control, they may not offer vouchers for hotels or food. If you paid these costs out of pocket, you might be able to get reimbursed from your travel insurance policy, if you purchased one, or your card's coverage. More on that below, too.

Under U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) rules, you are entitled to a full refund if your flight is canceled or significantly delayed — no matter the reason — and you decide not to travel and turn down other forms of compensation like travel credits. The money must be delivered to your original payment method, even if you bought nonrefundable tickets.

If your flight disruption meets the DOT criteria, make sure you're getting a full refund. Some airline waivers offer a travel credit as a default option. Credits typically expire, and you won't get value from them until you redeem them. With a refund, you can get your money back within days.

If you booked with points or miles, you'll generally get those redeposited to your loyalty account, plus a refund of any taxes and fees you paid.

But if you still want to forge on with your travels, most airlines are allowing affected passengers to rebook new flights without owing a change fee or fare difference, which is more generous than usual. If your original travel dates were Nov. 13 or 14, and you purchased your tickets on or before Nov. 12 or 13, you're likely eligible for these flexible change policies.

Depending on the airline, you might have even more flexibility. For example, Southwest’s more generous rebooking policy applies to flights scheduled through Monday, Nov. 16.

Just note that each airline has its own limitations on when you must take that new flight, so check with your airline to ensure you book within the allowed window. Here are the waiver pages for major airlines:

Right now, you and everyone else who was supposed to be on that Friday afternoon flight are vying for limited seats on aircraft flying the same route over the next few days. Get creative if the flight you need is booked up. Think about whether a nearby airport might be possible. You might also opt for a train or rental car.

If your flight disruption also cost you a hotel night, a rental car, a concert or sports ticket, or some other prepaid piece of your trip, here's your best chance at getting that money back, too:

Call the hotel or rental property directly. Although not guaranteed, your host may waive a cancellation penalty or no-show fee for a documented flight disruption like this one. Have your canceled or delayed flight confirmation handy, and ask kindly.

For nonrefundable event tickets like concerts or sports games, you’re unlikely to get a direct refund. Check the specific event's refund policy first (and it never hurts to ask!), but your best bet in most cases is reselling the ticket through a platform like StubHub, SeatGeek or Vivid Seats rather than counting on a refund from the original seller.

Keep every receipt and email confirmation. Whether you're asking a hotel for an exception or filing an insurance claim, having your original flight confirmation, the cancellation or delay notice and your other prepaid reservations documented in one place will make every one of these conversations faster.

If you have a standalone travel insurance policy: Travel delay and missed connection benefits may cover you for a disruption like this one, according to the insurance marketplace Squaremouth. If you already hold a policy, contact your provider's 24-hour emergency assistance line directly rather than waiting to file a claim after the fact.

If you don't think you bought travel insurance, check your card terms. Many premium travel credit cards include travel insurance for covered events as a card benefit, assuming you paid for the trip with your card. But in this case, trip cancellation and interruption coverage likely wouldn't apply, because covered events are limited to things like illness, injury and inclement weather.

But trip delay coverage (which typically applies after a delay of 6 to 12 hours) often covers "equipment failure," so it's more likely to apply here — if the ground stop is deemed to be an equipment failure. This coverage would reimburse "reasonable" expenses during a delay, like meals and lodging. Save your receipts so you're ready to file a claim, but keep in mind that card terms vary and the claim might be denied.

The backlog from Friday's ground stop is expected to keep disrupting flights through the weekend. If you have a flight in the coming days, recheck your specific flight status before heading to the airport even if things looked fine an hour ago.

And whatever you were counting on — a refund, a rebooking or an insurance payout — make sure you move fast, document everything and don't assume you only have one option. With airline waivers, DOT refund rules and travel insurance, you might have more ways to get your money back than you think.

As for Joseph, he’s still trying to resell his football ticket.

Nov. 15, 2026: This article has been updated to clarify how credit card travel insurance benefits might apply here.

#3051. Google’s Xreal Aura, Reviewed: The Weird Evolution of VR Into Glasses Is Already Underway

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Computing > Gadgets > VR/AR Productivity

The most fascinating and frustrating device I've used in a long time pushes at the edges of where headsets are heading, and glasses are evolving.

Let me tell you about a strange, fascinating and rough tweener product called Xreal Aura.

There are VR headsets, and there are smart glasses. And there’s a new class of devices that’s falling right in between. What do we call these things? I have no idea. The category includes the Meta VR Glasses coming next year and now the Aura, a collaboration by Google and Xreal.

The Xreal Aura shoots for the moon, aiming to bridge glasses and VR, and to shrink everything down on the go. It’s often fascinating, and more often frustrating. At times, it almost feels like a VR headset. At other times it feels like a superpowered version of the tethered display glasses that Xreal and several others already make, that act like wearable monitors for your phone or laptop or almost anything else.

I think it’s actually an experimental bridge to a future where phones will play nicer with advanced smart glasses. Those future glasses could create floating displays and workspaces all around you, if you wish. Consider the Aura, in a way, Google’s early attempt to get there.

Emphasis on early. Right now, the Xreal Aura’s features, OS and especially inputs feel rough to use at times and sometimes hard to get into a natural flow with. But it shows what something of this size could be capable of with more software and input-flow tweaks. And when it does work, it feels wildly like a portable VR/AR headset in a way I’ve never really seen before.

The Aura aspires to be a shrunk-down version of last year’s Samsung Galaxy XR, an expensive mixed-reality headset similar to Apple’s Vision Pro. Like the Galaxy XR, the Aura runs Android XR, a variant of Android that floats apps all around. It even runs VR apps. At times it gets close. Other times, it’s not nearly close enough.

What’s wild about the Aura is that it folds down into a case that’s truly small enough to slide into my bag. But setting up and using the Aura often involves patience and experimentation. When it works, it’s a heck of a peek at a future that’s likely around the corner. But the hoops you have to jump through to make it happen sometimes make me want to hop out.

Android XR is Google’s OS for AR/VR/AI devices and wearables, and aims to connect glasses and headsets of all shapes and sizes to Google and Gemini services and apps. The Samsung Galaxy XR, released last year, was the first. Coming up next, in just a few weeks, are Google and Samsung’s Warby Parker- and Gentle Monster-designed AI smart glasses.

The Xreal Aura is more Galaxy XR than smart glasses, in concept: It’s an AR/VR headset that you can take on the go. The glasses connect with a USB-C cable to an included processor puck that runs Android XR. It can display Android apps in both 2D and immersive 3D.

The Aura supports hand tracking and can allow full spatial movement to place floating 3D objects or play immersive games. It can float apps all around you, and you can navigate apps at the same time. You can use hand tracking to open or tap those apps, or a trackpad that’s built into the top of the processor puck. You can also pair a Bluetooth keyboard, or game controller, or a mouse, like I’m doing.

The kit tucks into an included carry case that’s smaller than the one I carry my Nintendo Switch 2 in. It’s easy to pack away for travel. I love this part of the Aura so, so much.

It’s $1,279 for the version with 256GB of storage and 12GB RAM or $1,499 for 512GB/16GB, but it’s on sale until the end of the year for $1,099/$1,299. That onboard storage is all you get, though. There’s no expandable microSD card slot. I reviewed the 256GB version.

The display tech in the Aura is an enhanced version of what’s already on Xreal’s other tethered display glasses, and similar to what Viture and TCL RayNeo use. The twin micro OLED displays are impressively bright and crisp, projected via prisms to look like they’re floating in the room with you. The “birdbath” display tech means the lenses are chunky and odd-looking, but they’re also a lot bigger and better-looking than what’s possible on display-enabled wireless glasses like Meta’s Ray-Ban Displays.

They have a 70-degree field of view, something that beats out previous generations of AR glasses like Magic Leap or the upcoming Snap Specs. The fidelity, although capping at 1,920×1,200 pixels per eye, is also really crisp and great for movie watching or games (up to 120Hz refresh). It’s enough to feel like a big movie screen is projected across the room or to lay out a virtual computer monitor, but there are clear edges where the image is still cut off compared to VR headsets (which tend to have 90 degree or better fields of view).

When running VR apps, which this can shockingly do, the graphics look sharp but narrowly framed. It’s good enough to use VR in a pinch, though: I floated through 3D Immersive Google Maps, dragging and scrolling with my fingers in the air, or played the VR role-playing game Demeo, exploring a tabletop board game dungeon, or played back 360-degree videos on YouTube. But the limits of the viewing field become a lot more stark in these modes, making me wish I had a VR headset instead. Then again, I never travel with VR headsets, and I’d travel with this.

The display’s visuals seemed to tear a few times while playing YouTube videos. Tracking, using the built-in cameras, also sometimes drifted. Mostly, the displays stayed where I put them, but sometimes they’d shift slightly out of alignment.

The processor puck means the Xreal Aura can open up most Android and Chrome-based apps I can think of, but not all of them. The Qualcommm Snapdragon Reality Elite chip on the puck seems more than zippy enough to handle whatever multiple games and apps (even VR ones) I throw at it, but not all Android apps are available: Developers can choose not to opt in, as with Netflix and Disney Plus, but they can be loaded up in-browser.

Other apps aren’t necessarily optimized for the fluid way the Aura can open an app in any size. I watched a Jets game on Paramount Plus on the Aura, and it stayed in a fixed window size. I could move closer or further away, but it wouldn’t enlarge.

The whole Aura interface feels new-ish, even if you’ve used VR. The glasses enable hand tracking that’s surprisingly OK: Tapping and pinching works, and an extended pointer can reach at a distance and click and drag or adjust windows. When my hand passes in front of the Aura’s display, it even gets overlaid with a virtual hand mapped onto mine, like VR.

There’s no eye tracking, though, something Apple Vision Pro, Samsung Galaxy XR and Meta VR Glasses do. Eye tracking is helpful: It means you can lock into something and click it without lifting your hand. Here, I found I had to lift and aim my hand a lot, like an interactive remote. Hand tracking does work somewhat below the display’s field of view, but you often won’t know if you’re interacting until that hand’s lifted up higher. This is where the Aura’s smaller-than-VR viewing area becomes a problem.

It’s particularly an issue when playing some VR games. I tried Synth Riders, a popular fitness music movement game that’s also on Android XR. I could see what was further off in front of me, but the limited viewing area meant my hands were out of sight when in my peripheral vision, so I couldn’t reach for targets near me or off to the sides.

There’s a second way to control Aura: The processor puck itself has a touchpad across its whole top. Hold it and it’s a touch remote: I can drag my finger and touch-click. On a table next to a paired keyboard, it’s a trackpad.

That’s super clever, but the trackpad’s performance ranged from OK to poor depending on the apps I ran. There are some multitouch elements too, but it still felt less effective as a headset control than I wanted.

The puck has discrete volume controls and a power button with a fingerprint sensor for secure logins. But the side button wasn’t always in an easy place to press, depending on how I held the puck.

You could also just use voice to control things: Saying “Hey Google” or launching live Gemini can open apps, handle dictation and feel like a control system of sorts. But Gemini can’t always do things in apps. It’s more of a launcher.

There aren’t a ton of unique immersive Android XR experiences, unfortunately, even a year after the Samsung Galaxy XR debuted. The Aura can technically run almost all of those same apps, including many 2D ones that show up on the Google Play store in-headset. On the plus side, VR apps working at all on glasses this small feels like magic, despite some limits.

Demeo, one of several VR games I found that run on these glasses, looks great and is surprisingly playable. I can cast up a virtual tabletop RPG game in front of me, and my hands bring up cards that I can pick and play on the field. An included Galapagos immersive 3D documentary app looks lovely.

YouTube and Google Maps are once again stars of Android XR, just like they were on Galaxy XR when I reviewed it last year. YouTube has plenty of 3D and 360-degree videos you can view, and Google Maps’ immersive 3D earth modes and, occasionally, 3D scanned interior locations are still great to browse on the Aura’s smaller screens.

I fell in love with a demo of Sock Puppet Superstar, too. It’s a hand-puppet-singing VR game that works well on the Aura.

Mixed reality VR experiences that try to project a few simple things into a room work best, effectively turning the glasses into augmented reality. Cubism, a hand-tracking enabled puzzle game I’ve played on other VR headsets, works well here too. The accuracy of the hand tracking isn’t always great for precision gripping the corners of the virtual floating blocks, though.

The refresh rate on these VR apps isn’t as ultrasmooth as on Quest 3 or Steam Frame, but they do look sharp. Except, as I said before, the viewing area ends up clipped more narrowly, so immersion feels blindered.

Some VR apps didn’t run at all, though. A VR air hockey game on Android XR wouldn’t let me use my hands to control the pucks, for some reason. I know this is a prelaunch review of the Aura, but expect some apps to act oddly. You can sideload APKs of other VR apps, which is great. Google’s AI Studio tools also work in spatial 3D in these glasses, which means you could vibecode experiences on them.

Think of the Aura as a pair of super-powered Xreal glasses with a better viewing area and an included processor puck. Xreal’s existing line of other display glasses float microOLED displays via a USB-C tether in a similar way. The Aura glasses have similar Xreal controls on the arm, but they’re modified to Android XR interface controls that are a little different. There are volume buttons, a button that changes the dimming level of the electrochromic lenses from clear to nearly full black, and a top button that brings up the home app grid when clicked once, or launches live Gemini when held.

There’s also an array of three built-in cameras that handle room tracking, visual awareness for Gemini and hand tracking. Two are in the corners of the frame, one’s above the nose. Xreal’s other glasses, for the most part, are camera-free unless you buy a snap-in module.

The prism-like lenses that reflect the microOLED displays from the top of the frame are flatter like the Xreal One Pro line, and prescription lens inserts snap in the same way – I used the ones from the Pro and they work fine.

The display’s field of view, at 70 degrees, is bigger than Xreal’s largest size on the One Pro (57 degrees), and it feels like a larger projected display in front of me. The resolution is still just the same as Xreal’s other recent glasses, but things still look crisp, even for reading.

Sizewise, they’re like many other tethered glasses: bulkier and weirder than normal glasses, but a lot lighter than any VR headset. Three sets of nosepads are included for fit adjustment, and the arms bend at several angles, too.

I’m writing this review now in the Aura, at my dining room table, with a separately sold folding wireless keyboard made by Xreal. The keyboard performance in Chrome and Docs is fantastic. The trackpad, not quite as much. But I really feel like I can write on this.

Navigating Chrome and work apps also is possible: Logged into my office’s Google-based system, I’ve been handling emails and chats and little needs fine.

Getting files on and off the Aura is the trick. I’m Mac- and iPhone-based, so I’d need to put things in Drive and Google apps to triangulate more easily.

But what’s also impressive is that I can plug in other devices, including my MacBook, and use the Aura as a virtual screen. I can float my MacBook and the Aura apps side by side.

Here’s the catch: My MacBook keyboard only controls my Mac, and the Aura’s keyboard and hand tracking only work for the Aura apps. So I need two keyboards side by side to multitask.

To be clear, no one’s handled handing off of peripherals between connected devices well, not even Apple. But it points to the biggest thorn in Aura’s device-bridging dreams.

Connecting to lots of other devices via the Xreal Aura is a wild experience. You just need to cable in with a DisplayPort-ready USB-C cable to do it. The second cable included in the Aura box won’t do it; oddly, that’s just a charging cable.

Right now, I’m connecting the new iPad Mini and casting a second display up in the air. I’m typing on a Logitech keyboard and mouse paired to the iPad, because the Xreal inputs won’t control it. But the point, mainly, is that it connects. And Gemini can still give me feedback on what it sees on my iPad’s virtual screen.

Whatever you plug in can cast a virtual monitor in-glasses: MacBook, iPhone, Steam Deck. Shockingly, even a Nintendo Switch 2 works, something Xreal’s team has been excited about. There are caveats: The Switch 2 goes into docked mode and needs the Joy-Cons detached, and only certain higher-fidelity DisplayPort USB-C cables work. I played Ocarina of Time on the Aura’s screen and it looked great, but the framerate was a bit lower than what I get on the Switch 2 normally. But again, I can ask Gemini questions about the game as I’m playing, and it sees and gives me answers, provided I’ve clicked a little on-screen toggle to share my screen with Gemini’s visual mode.

Bridging between devices is exciting to me, but it’s really just limited to treating the input like a video-in that pops on a second screen in-glasses. Meta’s VR Glasses will do this too. It’s a great bonus addition, but having to cable both my glasses and my other device to the Aura puck means too many cables for my comfort.

The glasses also work on their own without the puck, defaulting to standard Xreal glasses firmware and controls. That’s great if I want to use them with my laptop/phone/etc on the fly without needing the Aura puck, at least.

Turning on Gemini Live with a press of the top button on Aura’s glasses means you can have Gemini in your life constantly, if you wish. Toggle a little upward-arrow icon to share your camera feed and on-screen apps, and suddenly Gemini can also describe YouTube videos for you, or read what you’re writing, or tell you what’s in your hand.

It’s an all-seeing assistant that can even work with Google’s circle-to-search, although that feature’s hard to trigger (press and hold my fingers and click to bring it up, it seems). But I can then circle something in front of me, capture it, and Google AI search brings up results instantly (a book I’m holding, a freezeframe on TV or something on one of my virtual screens).

This is a step beyond the type of live, camera-enabled AI modes in smart glasses. It can see the world via its cameras and all the virtual apps that get conjured.

That being said, it’s hit or miss. The video feed quality isn’t great, so the AI can’t always read things at a distance. But I wore the Xreal Aura across my kitchen, making coffee while floating a YouTube window in front of me and talking to Gemini, and it felt like some sort of cyberpunk future I’d only experienced in bits and pieces before. It’s something you could walk around with, technically, but not a device I’d wear all day (nor is it designed to be).

Xreal promises four hours of battery life on the Aura, which is more than most VR headset claims of 2 to 3 hours. In practice, it feels good. I can use it for several hours and still have a fair amount of battery left, which seems promising. I’ve only been testing for a week, though.

But the processor puck can overheat. The puck has venting fans that can pump very warm air, and it’s not meant to be put in a pocket, even though that’s exactly what I want to do with it when I’m wearing Aura on my face. Instead, there’s an included belt clip. I tried putting it in my pocket, and pretty soon I got an overheating warning pop-up message. Don’t put it in your pocket.

I don’t think I’ve ever been as fascinated and borderline overwhelmed as I have with the Xreal Aura. It points in all sorts of directions for where phones, AI assistants and glasses can be heading. Could this little tweener device be my portable workstation eventually?

Right now it’s more of an experiment with fascinating side benefits. It can’t replace a standard VR headset, though parts come close.

The Xreal Aura tested even my new-device tolerance, although I see amazing glimmers. It’s coming with me on my next trips for sure, and I’ll let you know what happens when I do. But it’s not yet the true fusion solution I’m waiting for. And yet, I’m still convinced that the concept, remixed and refined, will be.

#3050. Visa and American Express Both Raised Their Dividends 16% This Year, but Only 1 of the Stocks Is Up in 2026

Not all payment card giants are created equal.

Was it coincidence or a keeping-up-with-the-Joneses strategy?

Last month, payment card giant Visa (V -0.92%) announced a 16% dividend raise. That came less than eight months after longtime rival American Express (AXP -0.25%) declared its own 16% hike. And those increases followed a nearly 15% dividend raise trumpeted by their veteran peer Mastercard as 2025 came to a close. Despite the matching 16% bumps, the stock prices of Visa and Amex have traveled in strikingly different directions this year.

To put it briefly, Visa stock is up, and Amex is down; the former has risen by nearly 22% year to date, well higher than the S&P 500 index's 8% gain, while Amex has fallen by almost 14%. For the curious, Mastercard is also in index-beating territory, with a nearly 16% increase. Here's how that looks on a handy graph:

One big factor in that divergence is recent quarterly performance. Both Visa and Amex routinely post very healthy growth rates on both the top and bottom lines. After all, paying for basically anything by card -- from snacks to utility bills to large pieces of furniture -- is the rule rather than the exception for consumers these days. Marry that with a still-thriving economy (despite some pull-back due to rising prices), and you've got a fine source of organic growth for payment card companies.

With this, investors expect Visa, Amex, and Mastercard to not only perform well, but to outperform. For the most part, all three deliver... well, at least they did, until Amex's last two reported quarters. In both its second and third frames, it missed -- if only barely -- the consensus analyst estimate for revenue. Technically, the company underperformed, which was a psychological blow to investors.

Amex also struggled to contain expenses; one reason its competitive moat is high is the many perks it offers cardholders through its vaunted Amex Rewards program. These aren't free for the company to provide, plus in our current age where consumers often value experiences over material items, uptake of those goodies has been brisk lately. In the second quarter, total expenses grew by 12% year over year, outpacing the 10% rise in revenue. The subsequent quarter was a wash, with both increasing by 9%. Investors are far more comfortable when revenue growth eclipses spending.

With Visa, Amex, or Mastercard, it's important to be aware of the difference between an open-loop and closed-loop operator. Visa and Mastercard are the former; this means they act only as facilitators of transactions made on the cards bearing their logos. They extend none of the credit; instead, this is done (typically) by banks or other financial institutions.

Closed-loop operators, exemplified by Amex, span the entire credit card ecosystem. They are both the transaction facilitator and the issuer, so when you swipe with an Amex, the company is also lending you the money.

There are pluses and minuses with each model. Very briefly, I'll sum up my favorite advantages: Open-loopers are asset-light, collecting a tiny percentage of every transaction from their massive volume -- after all, who doesn't have at least one Visa or Mastercard these days? Closed-loop operators, unlike their rivals, don't have to split transaction fees with intermediaries such as issuers. Also, they earn revenue from card fees and the interest charged to folks who don't pay their balances on time.

Two other developments are negatively impacting Amex, as a closed-looper, and benefiting the two others. One is the federal government's long-simmering Credit Card Competition Act (CCCA), which would require large banks to use more than one payment network to process credit card transactions. This means no more exclusivity for Visa or Mastercard, which is currently common industry practice. Closed-loop companies would be exempt from this requirement, to the obvious advantage of Amex.

The fact that this act has essentially gone nowhere in Congress -- despite President Donald Trump promising more than once he'd sign it into law if it's passed -- is a drag on Amex stock and a boon for Visa and Mastercard.

The second of the two developments is the Federal Reserve's interest rate hike in September and, given the persistence of inflation, the possibility that more raises are on the way. Again, Amex acts as an issuer, so it's interest rate sensitive. Yes, it'll earn more revenue from cardholders carrying over balances, but those people could rein in their spending as their APRs rise.

While I believe Visa fully deserves that index-topping rise in its share price, I don't feel Amex is being treated fairly with the decline in its equity.

The latter company -- a longtime favorite of beloved master investor Warren Buffett, by the way -- boasts an enviable set of advantages. Despite having many ambitious competitors, its plastic is still considered to be the most prestigious by many consumers, who are willing to fork over the often high annual "membership fee" for the privilege of holding it. Meanwhile, the average Amex cardholder is relatively affluent and likes using their Centurion or Platinum card to buy things. It's telling that even through lean economies, Amex has usually managed to post healthy top- and bottom-line growth.

On top of that, its dividend yield beats Visa's, at 1.1% versus 0.7%, and its forward P/E is far lower (less than 16 against 28).

I've been bullish on both companies for quite some time, but with Amex's recent downward trajectory, I'd be more inclined to buy that stock than I would Visa.

Stock markets remain volatile as investors weigh uncertainty in the Middle East, rising interest rates and concerns about the artificial intelligence (AI) trade.

Given this volatile backdrop, investors seeking a stable income stream can enhance their portfolios with the addition of dividend stocks. In this regard, tracking recommendations of top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend stocks that are backed by strong financials.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Integrated oil and gas giant Chevron (CVX) is the first dividend pick. Earlier this month, the company paid a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share. At an annualized dividend of $7.12 per share, CVX offers a dividend yield of about 3.5%.

After a meeting with senior leadership, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on CVX and raised his price target to $240 from $225. Among the key takeaways Mehta emphasized was that Chevron is building a solid pipeline of promising international exploration projects across Latin America, the Middle East, West Africa and the Eastern Mediterranean. In particular, he mentioned the focus on Venezuela, where Chevron expects to more than double gross production to 600 kbd from about 280 kbd by 2031, using three joint ventures.

Mehta also noted Chevron's efforts to deploy new technologies, especially in shale and tight-oil operations. CVX is focused on boosting productivity and efficiency to maximize free cash flow, he added.

Initiatives such as artificial lift optimization, AI and machine learning, and advanced chemical treatments are expected to improve recovery by about 10% in new wells. Consequently, capital spending per barrel in U.S. shale is projected to fall 25% in 2026, with total Permian spending dropping below $3.5 billion.

Enterprise Products Partners (EPD) is a master limited partnership (MLP) that provides midstream energy services to producers and consumers of natural gas, natural gas liquids (NGLs), crude oil, refined products and petrochemicals. With a quarterly cash distribution of 56 cents per common unit ($2.24 per common unit annualized), EPD offers a yield of about 6%.

Following a recent call with the company, RBC Capital analyst Elvira Scotto reiterated a buy rating on EPD with a price target of $42. The analyst slightly lowered her estimates for the second half of 2026, citing margin and volume normalization, though demand dynamics remain strong.

While the 5-star analyst expects a sequential decline due to normal seasonality and normalization following high spreads in the first half of the year, she still expects EPD to report another solid quarter (Q3 2026) and enter 2027 with a favorable setup. Ahead of Q3 earnings, Scotto expects investors to focus on export demand durability, EPD's ability to profit from spot cargo sales and growth in Permian volumes.

Scotto continues to expect $150 million of common unit buybacks per quarter in the second half of 2026. She expects buybacks to increase to $200 million per quarter in 2027, as capex spending declines and free cash flow improves.

In total, Scotto is bullish on EPD and views it as a core MLP holding that has both offensive and defensive characteristics. The analyst praised EPD's diverse asset base as ensuring stable cash flows. "Furthermore, the partnership's multi-year organic growth backlog helps provide visibility on long-term distribution growth," Scotto said.

Scotto ranks No. 199 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 67% of the time, delivering an average return of 15.9%. See Enterprise Products Partners Financials on TipRanks.

Brookfield Infrastructure Partners (BIP) operates a diversified portfolio of high-quality utilities, transport, midstream and data assets. The company declared a quarterly distribution of 45.5 cents per unit, payable on September 29. At an annualized distribution of $1.82, BIP offers a yield of 5.2%.

Recently, BMO Capital analyst Devin Dodge reaffirmed a buy rating on Brookfield Infrastructure with a price target of $47. The analyst cited improved visibility into BIP's growth and views its corporate simplification as a potential catalyst.

"Layering in the benefits from the proposed corporate simplification, a multiple well below historical levels and an attractive yield, we believe BIP offers a compelling risk/reward and it remains a preferred idea," said Dodge.

With more organic growth projects in the pipeline and new partnership investment opportunities, Dodge believes that BIP has clearer visibility into where it will deploy capital. That should support continued double-digit growth in funds from operations (FFO) per unit.

#3047. The Crypto Fear & Greed Index Is in "Extreme Fear" Territory. History Says This Happens Next.

Periods of fearfulness like this one are rarely reversed quickly, but conditions still improve eventually.

The Crypto Fear & Greed Index, a high-level measure of market sentiment, is, as of Nov. 16, at an "extreme fear" reading of 13, marking a reversal from the widespread bullish mood this summer that saw the index at 80 on Aug. 25. Bitcoin (BTC +0.90%) traded at $78,565 on Aug. 25, versus $64,931 on Nov. 16.

Wild volatility and extremes of sentiment have been common for Bitcoin. Here's what history suggests will happen next, given the fearful market.

In an analysis in February 2026, Coin Bureau co-founder Nic Puckrin found that when crypto's Fear & Greed Index fell or lingered below 25, Bitcoin's average 90-day returns afterward were just 2.4%. For example, when the index was at 24 on Jan. 21 of this year, Bitcoin's price was $89,364, and it has fallen 26% since then.

Part of the reason this dynamic exists is that extreme market fear usually occurs during crypto bear markets or immediately after crashes or hacks that destroy investor confidence. But even if the 90-day returns aren't that great on average, waiting longer -- perhaps even a lot longer -- tends to give way to a recovery eventually.

In the coronavirus crash of March 2020, the index sank to 3. Despite plunging along with everything else during that period, Bitcoin is now up nearly 1,190% since then. Buying during that panic took confidence in the asset, but it paid off.

Nearly two-thirds of 2021's 100 largest altcoins — esentially all cryptos aside from Bitcoin — were down by more than 90% as of Oct. 21 of this year, and nearly all coins outside the top 100 effectively lost all their value. That means it is not wise to simply buy a basket of declining cryptocurrencies and hope that time will heal all wounds afterward. Focusing on assets that were growing strongly during the current slump is a better approach.

Neither of those coins needs its price to go up for its fundamental value to increase. And while Bitcoin hasn't done well, it's still getting scarcer over time, regardless of what its price is doing. Each of its halving events cuts by 50% the reward miners receive for each block added to the chains, occurring roughly every four years, and slowing the supply growth rate.

There's no rush to buy anything right now. Don't let the market's fearfulness become yours, and stay focused on the long term in the meantime.

TL;DR: Mortgage rates went up today, but not as sharply as they did late last week.

Yes, mortgage interest rates are higher today, but only by a little.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage rose to 7.27% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is one basis point higher than yesterday and 37 basis points higher than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

On Friday, the Bureau of Labor Statistics released the Producer Price Index for October, which tracks the change in prices that U.S. producers are able to get for their products. This is one way to measure inflation on the market end, rather than the consumer end.

The results were mixed. While prices didn’t rise quite as high as economists anticipated month-over-month (0.3% vs. 0.4%), year-over-year price growth did reach 6.5% — the largest increase in four years. This points to even higher costs for consumers coming in the near future.

Investors are convinced that the Federal Reserve will raise overnight borrowing rates again in December to pull inflation down. And higher overnight borrowing rates — called the federal funds rate, which is what banks pay to fund products like mortgages — usually lead to higher mortgage rates.

» MORE: How the Federal Reserve affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.76% or higher.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

#3045. I Didn’t Expect to Like Xiaomi’s Bizarre Dual-Screen Phone So Much

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Review: Xiaomi's 18 Pro Max is a quirky Android phone that stands out from the crowd with its extra screen on the back. Shame Americans can't have it.

Editor at Large; Lead Photographer, Europe

Editor at Large; Lead Photographer, Europe

Xiaomi teased me with the 17 Pro, its bizarre dual-screen Android phone, last year. But it was sold only in China. Being from the UK, I went back to my regular boring phone with its boring single screen. Big sigh. So imagine my excitement when Xiaomi announced that its new flagship 18 Pro and Pro Max — complete with a second rear screen — would launch internationally, with a rollout including the UK and wider Europe. As with the rest of Xiaomi’s handsets, people in the US are flat out of luck.

That sucks for Americans because this phone is actually damn good. I worried that the rear screen would just be a dumb gimmick — something that tries to separate the phone from competitors but doesn’t actually add anything useful. But I actually like it. Need it? No. But it’s fun and has some genuine uses.

Beyond the screen, though, the 18 Pro Max packs the latest Qualcomm Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor, a fast-charging silicon-carbon battery and a potent camera setup that utilizes the same LOFIC sensor technology that impressed me so much in Xiaomi and Leica’s Leitzphone earlier this year.

The 18 Pro isn’t just smaller (6.4 inches vs. the Pro Max’s 6.9 inches) it misses some of the Max’s top tech as well. The processor is a lesser model, the main camera doesn’t use LOFIC tech and the smaller battery isn’t as capable. Shame.

But the 18 Pro Max is an all-round Android powerhouse, and I’ve really enjoyed getting to grips with it over the past couple of weeks. Here’s what I’ve found and what you need to know about this phone.

The extra display on the back is certainly this phone’s standout feature. It’s basically in the same place as the iPhone 18 Pro’s camera island, but instead of just being a piece of metal, it’s an actual functioning screen. If you’ve ever seen the cover display on a clamshell flip phone like Samsung’s Galaxy Z Flip 8, then it’ll seem quite familiar.

Like the Flip 8, the second display shows incoming notifications, acting as a camera viewfinder and offering a variety of basic built-in functions like calendar reminders. What really hooked me, though, was the ability to create Gen AI apps just by typing in a prompt.

For example, I asked for “a game where you just pop bubbles,” which the “Polish” tool elaborated on with deeper functions and visual styles before generating a finished game that was fully playable on the back screen, complete with a scoring system and, for some reason, a jellyfish mascot. It takes about 5 minutes for the app to be created each time, and its functions are limited. It’s not able to access any app data, so don’t expect to create a new email reader, and anything too technical will result in failure.

I asked it to create a camera overlay that showed exposure settings (shutter speed, ISO and so on) to serve as a light meter for an analog camera. I’m not sure whether the issue was my explanation or a technical limitation, but it took the phone two tries to get something close. It created an interface with dials and exposure information, but it didn’t open the camera to calculate exposure as I’d hoped. As a result, it looked nice but it was functionally redundant.

Another time, I asked it to create an app that showed real-time charging speeds. The resulting app showed current battery level but not charging speed. It did have a baffling “charging milestones completed” button that simply increased by one each time I tapped it. I also had no luck with my “rude word generator,” which just repeatedly came back with “Couldn’t generate.” Frustratingly, each time it fails to create an app, it doesn’t tell you why — like if you’re asking for information it’s unable to access — but just says to try again “in a minute or two,” which rarely resulted in success in my testing time. If I’m asking for something it can’t achieve, it’d be helpful to know that.

Even so, I’m impressed with this app creation tool and, like many of the AI tools that only mildly excite me right now, I can only assume it will improve over time.

One of my favorite uses of the rear screen, though, is for vlogging. Firstly, seeing yourself from the back of the phone means you’re able to accurately film yourself using the best quality camera, rather than limiting yourself to the front-facing camera, which won’t look as good. But there’s also an autocue function where you can input a script and have it overlaid as text, allowing you to read out your words as you present to camera.

It’s a powerful tool for vloggers and other video creators who rely on longer prewritten scripts for their videos. But it’s quite basic: the text simply auto-scrolls at a speed you set in advance. I’d love to see Xiaomi use voice recognition here to automatically progress the text as you read out the words, slowing down or speeding up as you naturally read aloud. This tech already exists, so I don’t think I’m asking for literal magic here.

Tucked into that second display is a 200-megapixel main camera and a 200-megapixel telephoto camera offering 3.2x optical zoom or 6.4x hybrid zoom. There’s also a really tiny 50-megapixel ultrawide camera by itself below the camera island, which makes it feel like an afterthought — something that I’ll come back to later.

The main sensor is physically slightly smaller than the one in Xiaomi’s Leitzphone, but it uses the same LOFIC sensor tech for better dynamic range in a single image. I’ve taken a lot of photos with it so far and I’m really impressed with what I’ve seen. The smaller 18 Pro has an almost identical camera setup but its main sensor doesn’t use LOFIC, which is a shame as it forces you to go for the larger phone if you want the best possible image quality.

Shots are well-exposed, with accurate colors and fine details that manage to look sharp but without the harsh over-sharpened look that’s all too often seen from phone cameras. Images look more natural as a result.

There are a lot of ways to tune your images in-camera — almost too many, in fact. There’s a whole host of built-in color presets, including a Leica-branded high-contrast black-and-white mode that I like, all of which you can customize further by adjusting the tones, colors, grain and white balance. Then there’s the option to shoot using the phone’s default color processing, going with “Leica Vibrant” for more popping colors or “Leica Authentic” for more natural tones. Each of these applies no matter what filter you then apply over the top.

Confused? Yeah, I’m not entirely surprised, there are a lot of variables at play when taking an image with this thing but it didn’t take me long to figure out how to get the look that I wanted. And let’s be honest, there aren’t many photographers who want fewer options in how to take a photo.

Then there’s Essential Moment, which is its own standalone mode where you can select from three distinct styles: a black and white mode, “modern vintage,” or “Iconic CCD.” Each of these is designed to replicate specific looks from cameras of the past, and Xiaomi says it uses AI to analyze the scene to authentically reproduce color tones, vintage lens effects and film grain (though crucially not generative AI to actually alter anything in the scene).

I actually love this, especially the black and white option, which produces monochrome images with beautiful contrast and genuinely authentic-looking film grain. It’s the mode I’d end up using most often, I’m sure, and I’ve taken a bunch of photos with it that I really like.

Oh, and that tiny ultrawide camera, weirdly separated from its friends? It’s not great, with nighttime shots being particularly disappointing here. On the upside, the main camera’s standard focal length is 23mm, which is already pretty wide, so you probably won’t miss the ultrawide much.

While the base 18 Pro uses Qualcomm’s latest Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6, the Pro Max ups the ante with the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6. It’s no surprise that the Pro Max is a seriously powerful bit of kit, returning benchmark scores up there with the powerhouse Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra. Everything ran exceptionally smoothly, from playing demanding 3D games like Genshin Impact to editing photos or navigating the Android 17 interface. I found much the same with the 18 Pro, too — I didn’t see a noticeable difference in performance.

I don’t mind Xiaomi’s software skin, as it’s easy enough for anyone familiar with Android to get to grips with. What I don’t like, though, is the company’s insistence on preloading it with an armada of apps including AliExpress, Netflix, WPS Office, TikTok and others. Together with the variety of Xiaomi apps also on board, the phone feels somewhat cluttered before you’ve even had a chance to add anything of your own. I’ve seen worse examples (Oppo has been bad with this), but it still irks me that the phone ends up feeling almost like it’s ad-supported. And if it is, surely it should be cheaper?

It helps a bit, sure, but it won’t block those creeps entirely. My advice is: if you’ve got information so sensitive that even a glimpse would be career-ending, maybe wait until you’re alone before you put it on screen.

The 7,050-mAh silicon-carbon battery in the larger Pro Max packs a punch, putting in some solid scores on our demanding battery rundown tests. After one hour of YouTube streaming, it dropped to 97%, then to 89% after the third hour. That puts it above the Galaxy S26 Ultra and Google Pixel 11 Pro XL, although still below the current champion, the iPhone 18 Pro Max.

In everyday use, you won’t struggle to get through a full day of mixed use and you can likely be quite demanding with it and still not worry about it conking out mid-afternoon. Take photos, watch videos, listen to music – don’t stress over it; this thing should hold out fine.

The phone supports up to 100-watt wired fast charging, though you’ll need a Xiaomi fast charger to achieve the fastest speeds. I don’t have a Xiaomi charger (and the fastest it sells in the UK is 90W for £25), but I tried it with multiple third-party 100-watt chargers and the maximum I could get was around 65 watts. Even so, it went from 1% to 65% in 30 minutes of charging, which is still pretty quick — on par with the iPhone 18 Pro Max, in fact. Still, it should be able to go faster; you’ll just need to source a charger that will allow it.

With its smaller 6,000-mAh battery the Xiaomi 18 Pro didn’t fare as well on our battery drain tests (it dropped to 93% after an hour of YouTube streaming) but in general use you’ll still comfortably get through most of a day on a single charge.

If you’re in the US, it’s something of a moot point. You can’t buy it. Sorry. Sure, you can probably import it from some third-party resellers, but it’s not officially on sale.

If you’re somewhere where you can buy it, then lucky you — this phone is a blast. It ticks many of the boxes I’d expect from a flagship phone right now (camera quality in particular), and that second rear screen is the cherry on top. I expected it to feel like a pointless gimmick, and maybe it is a bit of a novelty, but it’s fun and I’ve already found it genuinely useful.

I don’t like that there are so many hardware differences between the two phone sizes, as it forces you to have a much bigger model if you want the best performance. I prefer Apple’s approach: With the iPhone 18 Pro, I can have the same exact potent camera setup and processor performance, no matter which size I choose. With Xiaomi’s phones I’m forced to compromise between performance and pocketability. If you want the best camera, then go for the bigger model. Battery life is better, too.

CRWV stock performance has been underwhelming as investors worry about high capital spending, the analyst noted. Chatterjee noted the 25% price hike in July across CoreWeave's product offerings and frequent price increases by rivals like Nebius (NBIS), adding that some peers are charging nearly three times more for short-term compute contracts than what CoreWeave charges on longer-term deals.

"CoreWeave's leverage of the opportunity [is] evident in its recent press release highlighting contracts signed in F3Q at ~$40M/MW," said Chatterjee. JPMorgan said higher pricing is already contributing 5-10 percentage points to contract margins versus earlier deals.

Chatterjee ranks No. 4 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 75% of the time, delivering an average return of 55.3%. See CoreWeave Statistics on TipRanks.

Palo Alto Networks (PANW) is a provider of cybersecurity solutions across network, cloud, security operations, AI and identity. Following a discussion with management, BTIG analyst Gray Powell reiterated a buy rating on PANW and raised his price target to $425 from $404.

After a review of Palo Alto's product-level growth catalysts, Powell sees clear upside to both revenue and next-generation security (NGS) annual recurring revenue (ARR) in fiscal 2027. He expects PANW to deliver pro forma revenue growth of more than 17%, above the consensus estimate of 14.6%, and NGS ARR growth of more than 26% versus the Street's expectation of 24.5%.

Over the past five years, the Palo Alto business mix, has moved to higher-growth product areas and new markets. from what was earlier viewed as a hardware-centric network security company, Powell said. The 5-star analyst estimates that hardware firewalls and attached subscriptions now account for less than 50% of revenue.

Meanwhile, high-growth solutions, including Prisma SASE, software firewalls, Cortex XSIAM, Chronosphere and Idira now represent more than 35% of PANW's revenue. "Investors may not fully realize the growth potential within PANW's platform story," Powell said.

BTIG is optimistic about the prospects of Chronosphere in observability, CyberArk in identity and software firewalls and Prisma AIRS in the network and AI security business.

Powell ranks No. 320 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 61% of the time, delivering an average return of 17.3%. See Palo Alto Networks KPIs on TipRanks.

In a research note on September 30, Rosenblatt analyst Scott Devitt reiterated a buy rating on e-commerce and cloud computing platform Amazon (AMZN), raising his price target to $360 from $335. Fears that agentic commerce poses a major threat to Amazon's advertising business seem "overstated," he said.

Devitt noted that the growing adoption of personal agents and AI shopping assistants has sparked concern about displacement of Amazon's retail media business. But the 5-star analyst remains bullish, given Amazon's ability to adapt to changing consumer behavior, as it's done in the past.

Additionally, Devitt argues that even if an AI agent helps a shopper discover a product, Amazon can still handle the purchase and delivery, keeping much of the transaction value. He highlighted that management believes that existing Amazon shoppers will likely continue to start their shopping journey on the platform because it has better personalization, accurate pricing and inventory information that third-party agents still lack.

Overall, Devitt expects Amazon's retail business to prove a net beneficiary of agentic commerce. Fewer clicks would not hurt the company if the value of each remaining click and overall volumes keep rising, he said. The argument is that even if Amazon loses some sponsored ad revenue over the next few years, it would likely be only a small part of the company's total business and could be offset by growth in other areas.

"Consistent with our AI framework, we continue to view Amazon as one of the most resilient leaders in our coverage, combining owned compute infrastructure with a physical fulfillment moat," said Devitt. His bullish view is supported, Devitt said, by expectations that Amazon Web Services (AWS) will exit the year at a more than 45% growth rate with continued margin improvement.

Devitt ranks No. 765 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 49% of the time, delivering an average return of 12%. See Amazon Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

#3043. Is Nvidia Stock's Trading at 10x Forward Earnings the Bargain of the Century or Dead Money Hiding in Plain Sight?

Nvidia trades at a valuation similar to that of companies with far less impressive growth.

If you weren't sure how valuable Jensen Huang was to Nvidia (NVDA -1.29%), then simply look at the stock over the past month. Nvidia's stock has fallen nearly 30% in the past month (as of the morning of Nov. 16). Huang admitted marital infidelity in a letter to the company on Nov. 8, and his resignation was announced Nov. 12.

This is an enormous move for a stock with a market cap of nearly $3.9 trillion, even after the decline. Huang co-founded Nvidia 33 years ago, and the company now reportedly controls 90% of the general-purpose graphics processing unit (GPU) market, which powers the technology many believe will completely transform the world as we know it.

Nvidia stock currently trades at roughly 10 times its projected fiscal year 2028 earnings (fiscal 2028 ends in January 2029). Is the stock the bargain of the century or dead money hiding in plain sight?

Whatever you think about Huang, who resigned after extramarital affairs came to light, including with one woman who may have been a Chinese spy, there's no denying that Huang was a strong CEO.

He built Nvidia into the juggernaut it is today and has become the voice for the entire AI industry. That said, no person is bigger than a company like Nvidia. Even without Huang, Nvidia still has a dominant product and the team that made it what it is today.

A big reason I think the stock is struggling is that Huang's ouster is not simply about an extramarital affair. It's also about national security, the quality of Nvidia's chip sales, and their end location.

Specifically, Huang's relationship with Alice Huang (no relation) — the controlling shareholder of a Singaporean data center company called MegaSpeed — has raised concerns that Jensen Huang may have been compromised and that Nvidia chips may have entered China illegally.

Former President Joe Biden's administration had only allowed Nvidia to sell older-generation chips to Chinese companies, due to national security concerns. In April 2025, the Trump administration told Nvidia it would need to obtain export licenses to sell chips to China. Since then, Nvidia has said there have been virtually no chip sales to China.

While many details remain unknown, reporting by media outlets, including The Information, has found that a network developed by Alice Huang allegedly helped funnel billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia chips to Chinese companies.

This will raise many questions for investors, and activist short-seller Culper Research estimated in May that a fifth of Nvidia's fiscal year 2026 sales may have illegally ended up in China. (Short-sellers make money when a stock they hold falls in value.)

If this proves true and the Trump administration or Congress can impose even tougher export restrictions, could Nvidia's revenue and earnings be revised downward? Or will it need to spend more for better compliance?

There could also be government investigations that lead to regulatory fines or other punitive measures.

Don't get me wrong, Nvidia stock at 10x fiscal 2028 projected earnings looks incredibly attractive. In Nvidia's fiscal 2027 second quarter, the company grew revenue by 106%; grew earnings by 128%; and posted a 75% gross margin. Companies that do that often see their stocks trade at earnings multiples that are multiples higher.

But one of the big questions at Nvidia is whether the company has been over-earning and whether all of these circular financing agreements it engages in reflect its true financial health.

Unfortunately, none of these questions have an easy answer and will require significant research that may be beyond the reach of the typical retail investor.

On the bullish side, there is still a very good chance Nvidia will continue to perform well and remain the dominant chip player. For all these reasons, I think investors can begin nibbling on Nvidia stock. But I don't think it's time to go all in just yet.

More information about all of this will certainly emerge in the coming weeks and months. Whether it's good or bad for the stock remains the big question mark.

#3041. Grindr launches $120/month subscription with AI chat summaries

After testing a rumored $499/month subscription tier, gay hookup app Grindr is officially launching Edge, an AI-focused plan running for $120 a month in the U.S. or $70 per week.

Edge has three main features: Insights, which shows users compatibility and likelihood to reply; Recommendations, which provides five curated profiles a day; and Reconnect (called A-List in beta), which highlights past connections and generates summaries of your conversations.

Edge includes everything that's in Grindr's Unlimited subscription, as well, which includes features like being able to scroll through unlimited profiles, incognito mode, unsending messages, and expiring photos.

AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections

Tinder — top pick for fast hookups

Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups

Pure — best for anonymous hookups

OkCupid — best app for inclusivity

Edge is powered by Grindr's proprietary AI stack called "gAI." Users can control which sensitive data to provide gAI and whether the app can use this to develop gAI over time. Such data can include preferred position, ethnicity, and user chats.

Grindr states that certain health data won't be used in gAI, like HIV status, last tested date, testing reminders, the "Poz" tribe and tag (which stands for the HIV-positive community), and vaccination status. Grindr recently settled a lawsuit for £26 million after allegedly sharing users' HIV statuses with third parties. (Grindr denied the allegations.) Shortly after, the app acquired a provider of the HIV-prevention medication PrEP, and plans to provide PrEP on the app.

Mashable received an early demo of Edge last week, during which Grindr's chief product officer, AJ Balance, said that Edge is the app's most personalized experience yet.

Balance said that Grindr users are at the forefront of culture and tech, and the Grindr team believes it's their job to leverage new technology. As AI was unfolding and it was clear it was the next paradigm shift, Grindr saw an opportunity to utilize it to add value to its users' lives.

Enthusiasm for Edge was apparently high during beta testing, Balance told Mashable, and beta testers ultimately want more connection with less effort and reduced friction in finding a match. The blog post Balance penned for the release is even called, "More Action, Less Effort."

What about the alleged $499/month price tag for the subscription?

Balance said that the app tested a range of pricing. And while $120 is much less than $499, Grindr CEO George Arison defended the price to BBC News today, saying that, "I think we're a capitalist society, and everything hinges on whether you can afford it or not." Balance told Mashable that 91 percent of its users use the app for free, while the remaining 9 percent are power users who want more convenience and ease to save time.

Edge is now available globally to all Grindr users on iOS and Android.
