#3023. It’s Time To Extend Collective Defense To Consumers

Ravi Dhaval, Fortune 500 advisor & inventor of patent-pending (#19/440,089), quantum-powered AI platform for proactive global cyber defense.

For years, executive security briefings have centered on one fear: machine-speed attacks powered by artificial intelligence (AI). Boards fund automated response, AI red teaming and zero-trust policies to protect the corporate perimeter. Yet most cyber defense remains reactive, built on detection after the fact and limited by classical computing’s difficulty simulating complex attack paths.

That gap is where I focused my published patent application, aiming to close it by simulating attack paths in real time, sharing threat intelligence without exposing raw data, and orchestrating defenses automatically.​

The more unsettling reality sits outside the boardroom. While Fortune 500 companies harden their defenses, everyday people face AI-native attacks aimed at their finances and personal data, with nothing comparable protecting them. Everyday life has become the primary attack surface.

Indirect prompt injection hides instructions in content an AI system later reads and obeys, and OWASP ranks prompt injection the top risk for applications built on large language models. One of the newest delivery methods is the poisoned instruction file. In October 2026, researchers at Forever Security reported finding a malicious AGENTS.md file, disguised as engineering notes, in a customer’s downloads folder, which is the one folder a website can write to without a click. AI coding agents such as OpenAI Codex and Claude Code follow the instruction files in whatever folder they open, so the planted text behaved like a program while slipping past every control built for executables. In testing, it led agents to rewrite their own configuration, opening the door to malware installation and stolen login tokens.

Voice and video impersonation is another growing threat. The FBI warns that criminals use generative AI to clone the voices of loved ones and to produce convincing video for live calls. The FTC notes a scammer needs only a short audio clip, which can often be pulled from content posted online.

The growing list of connected devices in the home adds still more exposure. Thermostats, smart TVs, voice assistants and even light bulbs all exchange data. The FBI cautions that one unsecured IoT device can give an attacker a path into the home router and everything behind it.

This holiday season, many consumers will install shopping agents: AI deal finders and checkout assistants that request access to email, saved cards and sometimes even password managers. OWASP calls this excessive agency, meaning an AI holding more permission than its task requires. A hidden instruction in a fake review or poisoned listing could steer such an agent into leaking credentials or placing fraudulent orders.

Antivirus software and firewalls hunt for malicious signatures and binaries. A natural-language instruction, a cloned voice or an edited settings file is none of those. As the Forever researchers argue, nearly every defense we rely on assumes a human who clicks, approves or runs the code. Once an agent takes the human’s place, that assumption breaks. Asking the public to fight AI attacks with tools from an earlier era invites systemic failure.

Businesses have a system for defending one another, but the public doesn’t. Since Presidential Decision Directive 63 in 1998, Information Sharing and Analysis Centers (ISACs) have let critical-infrastructure sectors pool threat intelligence and defend collectively.

Consumers can report to the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center or the FTC, but those channels exist to support investigations after the fact. None of them pools what one household experiences into protection for the next one in real time.

Public health relies on clean-water infrastructure, not purification tablets in every home. Similarly, internet providers should build behavioral analytics into residential gateways to protect devices that can’t run security software of their own. The attack-path modeling that enterprise platforms are beginning to use, which maps every route an intruder could take and ranks the most damaging, could inform simpler gateway logic that spots and blocks an intruder moving between smart devices.

Consumer AI tools should ship with least-privilege permissions and require explicit human approval before touching credentials or payments. Because no single control reliably stops prompt injection, protections must be layered. Vendors should also disclose which models, plug-ins and data connections their agents can reach.

Corporate defenses are only as strong as the exposed public around them. We built collective defense for pipelines and power grids. It is time to build it for people, and consumer ISACs are where security leaders can start. Leadership will be measured not only by how well we protect balance sheets, but by how effectively we advocate for everyone else’s digital safety.​

#3022. Apple Is Now the World’s Largest Company. Time to Buy the Stock?

Nvidia's fall has opened up Apple's lead.

Nvidia (NVDA -1.29%) was formerly the world's largest company by a fairly wide margin. However, that lead is now gone thanks to the market’s reaction to news of its CEO resigning, and Apple (AAPL +0.39%) is firmly in the lead. As of the time of writing, Apple's market capitalization sits at about $5.2 trillion, while Nvidia's is at $4 trillion.

That's a monster lead, but has Apple reached a ceiling, or is there more room to run? I think there are a few things that investors need to watch out for with Apple, as the future doesn't look very promising.

When you look at the companies that are deeply involved in artificial intelligence (AI), Apple is about the only tech giant that's absent from the list. Nearly every company above a $1 trillion market value is spending big on AI or is a key component provider.

While Apple has integrated some AI feature sets into its products and upgraded its Siri assistant, all of those technologies are using someone else's AI model. Apple realized that just using someone else's product and deploying it in its software was a far more cost-effective option, and that the market has loved that.

Instead of Apple spending hundreds of billions of dollars on an extensive data center network, Apple has kept its spending modest and continued to repurchase shares at an aggressive rate. As of now, this looks like the right choice, as all of the deep AI investments some of Apple's peers are making haven't paid off.

As a result of not going all-in on AI, the stock has become a safe haven for investors who don't want as much exposure to AI. This has caused a lot of investors to buy up the stock, which has inflated its valuation.

Apple is now one of the more expensive stocks on the market, trading at 38 times forward earnings. For reference, the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.39%) trades at some one-time gain on investments is skewing net profits and is trading at about 19 times forward earnings. That's a major mismatch, but is Apple's stock worth the premium from a business standpoint? I don't think so.

While Apple's big tech peers are spending big on AI data centers and haven't completely paid for themselves yet, the reality is that these companies are still growing far faster than Apple. Of the five largest companies in the world, Apple is growing the slowest (Nvidia is excluded because its growth rate was over 100% last quarter).

AAPL Revenue (Quarterly YoY Growth) data by YCharts

While Apple's growth rate is similar to Amazon's, Amazon's business is also shifting to a heavier reliance on cloud computing, which has better margins. When you look at how quickly operating profits are growing (net profits are being skewed by some one-time gain on investments), this argument goes away.

AAPL Operating Income (Quarterly YoY Growth) data by YCharts

The reality is that Apple is growing far slower than its peers yet trades for a substantial premium over them. That is an odd mismatch, and it's something that likely won't last forever. Apple is also facing its own challenges, such as the rising cost of components because the AI build-out is consuming a large amount of production capacity at chip companies.

At the end of the day, Apple is a very dominant company with a very disciplined approach to what it spends money on and how much stock it buys back. This discipline has gotten it to the status of the world's largest company and is unlikely to change anytime soon.

However, the stock has gotten so expensive that buybacks are less effective. This could dampen future returns on the stock, and while Apple may not crash, I think investors are at serious risk of underperformance over the next few years. As a result, I think there are far better stocks to buy now.

#3019. The Stock Market Is Doing Something for Only the Second Time in 155 Years. Here's What History Says Could Come Next.

Should the S&P 500's valuation worry you?

Usually, when something happens in the stock market only a few times over decades, it's either really good or really bad; there's not much in between. In this case, the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.39%) index is doing something that's only happened twice since 1871.

The Shiller price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio is a measuring stick that helps put the S&P 500's valuation in perspective. It compares current prices to the index's average inflation-adjusted profits over the past 10 years. The S&P 500 didn't exist in 1871, but economists have pulled historical data to show what it would've been.

Right now, the Shiller P/E ratio is 40.7, which is, to put it lightly, very high. The only other time the ratio has hovered above 40 was during the dot-com bubble. Those aren't exactly encouraging words, but will the results be different this time around?

The dot-com bubble -- which began in the late 1990s before bursting in 2000 -- was a case of investors getting a little too excited about internet start-ups as the internet became more mainstream. Companies with nothing more than a functioning website and charming founders were going public at wild valuations. Many had no meaningful revenue, let alone profitability.

At its peak, in November 1999, the Shiller P/E ratio reached 44.2.

Today, the index's high valuation comes from the ongoing artificial intelligence boom, which has driven many tech valuations to unprecedented levels. At the time of writing, nine of the world's 10 most valuable public companies are tech companies, with Meta Platforms being the least valuable at $1.6 trillion.

The flood of money pouring into mega-cap tech stocks is the reason the index has nearly doubled since the start of 2023, but it's also what has pushed the S&P 500's valuations to levels we haven't seen since the dot-com bubble. One major difference this time, though, is that the companies driving this surge are real businesses making real billions.

There's no way to know how the market will move in the short term, but we know one thing from the stock market's history: Bear markets and crashes are inevitable parts of its cycle. This isn't to say one of those is imminent (again, we can't predict the market), just that they will happen.

The good news is that regardless of what happens, the S&P 500 has solidified itself as one of the best investments you can make for the long haul. Since the present-day S&P 500 was introduced in 1957, it has experienced 12 bear markets and bounced back from each. During the dot-com crash, the S&P 500 plunged by 49%, yet it's up 880% as of Nov. 12.

Instead of trying to guess what will happen, focus on business as usual and trust the long-term vision, even if the S&P 500 pulls back (which it eventually will).

#3018. AI Outlook For 2027: Top Four Trends To Watch

Alessio Alionço is the founder and CEO of Pipefy, a global leader in AI-driven business process automation solutions.

​In 2026, we were captivated by what AI could do. Every new model promised to be smarter, to be faster and to fix the workflows that never quite worked.

In 2027, the honest answer will often be that it’s not the AI but, rather, the process. A more powerful model merged into a fractured process is just a faster way to compound a multisystem pile-up. The work ahead is less glamorous, but we’ll need to focus on structuring inputs, fixing processes, strengthening guardrails and orchestration.​

In the year ahead, instead of pinning hopes on the capabilities of new AI models, it’ll be time to focus on work that enables you to scale your results or else risk getting stuck in a loop of pilot projects that never pay off.​

I’ll be watching four AI trends closely. Leaders who treat these trends as mere technology topics will miss the business consequences. Here’s what they mean for the business:​​

Governance decides which processes AI’s allowed to touch. An April 2026 Deloitte survey of IT and business leaders found that only 21% of respondents reported having a mature governance model for agentic AI.

For everyone else, the ceiling isn’t the technology. Companies without execution-level controls can run pilots, but they can’t put AI into regulated, high-value processes, which is where the real returns are. Controls aren’t the brake on scale. They’re the license for it.

Having AI agents that aren’t connected is as helpful as having four wheels but no car. Organizations will need to shift from a more-is-better mindset to connecting agents to how work actually flows.

An April 2026 Harvard Business Review Analytic Services report found that among surveyed organizations using or exploring AI, 39% said most AI-enabled workflows still relied on stand-alone tools, while only 12% said AI was embedded directly in the flow of work. Stand-alone tools create activity, while orchestrated processes create throughput.

Business leaders need to identify where AI can change the economics of the business. Financial evidence, not the impressiveness of the demo, will fund projects.

An October 2025 Forrester report found that fewer than one-third of decision makers could tie the value of AI to their organization’s financial growth. That leaves most AI portfolios exposed when budgets are reviewed. Internal teams and vendors alike will be measured on outcomes they can attribute to a process.​ The demo gets the meeting, but the P&L gets the budget.

As AI usage scales, cost scales with it. In McKinsey’s 2026 State of AI survey, one in five responding organizations said AI operating costs, including tokens, already constrained their use. Without unit economics, AI spending grows faster than the value it creates, and nobody notices until the invoice arrives.​

Finance is already stepping in. A September 2026 Deloitte report found that 54% of surveyed finance leaders were leading enterprise AI and technology capital allocation. The companies that scale will manage AI the way they manage any other operating input: by the unit.​

To find the clearest sign that AI has entered a new phase, look at where AI now sits in the budget. For the last few years, AI was funded as innovation: pilots, labs and experiments with loose expectations.

Today, it’s increasingly funded as operations, approved by finance and measured against the same standards as any other investment. AI has graduated from capability to accountability. The first phase proved what AI can do. The next one will be judged on the impact it has inside the business: in which process, under which rules, at what cost, and with what result. That shifts the center of gravity of the AI program and the entire organization.

The real advantage goes to the companies that can make AI dependable, measurable, governed and orchestrated. The first phase was about intelligence. This next one is about execution.​

#3016. Jim Cramer says Costco's hefty special dividend signals ‘more gains ahead’

Costco is rewarding shareholders with a $30-per-share special dividend, and CNBC's Jim Cramer says history suggests that investors should stick around despite the catalyst moving into the rearview mirror.

The warehouse retailer announced its sixth special dividend last week, alongside a $4 billion share repurchase program. Shareholders of record as of Nov. 24 will receive the payout on Dec. 4. The company also pays a regular quarterly dividend of $1.47 that yields just 0.5% annually.

"With all due respect to the buyback program, which represents less than 1% of Costco's $490 billion market cap, it's the special dividend that I'm excited about," the "Mad Money" host said. "The sporadic special dividend is one of the unique privileges of owning Costco shares."

Costco issued its first special dividend in 2012 and has announced five more since then, with payouts arriving roughly every three years over the past decade. Together, those six payments have totaled $74 per share, on top of the company's regular quarterly dividend.

To be sure, given Costco's track record of these periodic extra payouts, some investors may view last week's announcement as a "buy the rumor, sell the news" situation. However, Cramer said in each of the past three instances — 2023, 2020 and 2017 — Costco shares have outperformed the S&P 500 over the next year.

"That's a very good verdict for those who wonder what to do with the stock now that the good news is out," Cramer said. "It says hold on, don't sell. More gains ahead."

There's also compelling math suggesting that investors should look to reinvest those dividends back into Costco's stock.

Cramer looked at investor returns over the past 15 years. A $1,000 investment in Costco's stock in November 2011 would have grown to approximately $13,321 through Friday, reflecting a 1,232% gain. But reinvesting all dividends into additional shares would have increased that investment's value to roughly $18,411, representing a 1,741% total return.

That's more than $5,000 in additional gains from reinvesting dividends rather than collecting the cash. Special dividends played an outsized role, accounting for roughly 64% of the $116 per share Costco paid in total dividends over that period. "That's an incredible case made for reinvesting of dividends," Cramer said.

"The sporadic special dividends have boosted this stock's total shareholder return meaningfully over the past decade-and-a-half, and they help keep you invested in the stock when it has its occasional lulls," he said.

Beyond boosting returns, the prospect of another special dividend gives investors an incentive to hold Costco through periods of weakness. That patience paid off this year, when shares retreated from nearly $1,100 in May into the high $800s before rebounding sharply this fall. The stock is now up 30% for the year.

"Sometimes I think that the stock's too expensive and it might be a good time to take profits," he said. "But then I remind myself that there's a good chance of a special dividend right around the corner, and it's so much easier to stick it out."

#3015. Disney Increases Dividend By 33%. Here’s What’s Driving the Shift.

Here’s how much of Disney’s cash the new dividend will consume.

Disney (DIS +2.27%) paid shareholders $1.50 per share in dividends during its 2026 fiscal year. For fiscal 2027, it just set the dividend at $2.00, a 33% raise. That's a hefty hike for a company that's also spending heavily on content and new experiences across its parks and resorts, while also repurchasing a boatload of its shares.

Here's a look at what's driving the shift toward returning more capital to shareholders.

Disney declared a $2.00-per-share dividend for fiscal 2027, to be paid in two installments (January and July). That's a 33% increase from the $1.50 it paid in its 2026 fiscal year. At its new rate, Disney's dividend yield will rise to around 1.7% based on its recent share price. That makes Disney a more attractive dividend stock, as the S&P 500 yields around 1.1%.

The raise is a continuation of Disney's dividend rebuild following the pandemic-driven pause in payments. The entertainment, experiences, and sports giant suspended its dividend in 2020 to preserve its financial strength and fund its streaming investments. It reinstated its semi-annual dividend in late 2023 at $0.30 per share, and has steadily raised its payment each year.

Disney is coming off a strong fiscal year. Its revenue rose 8% to $102.3 billion, while its total segment operating income increased 12% to $19.7 billion. Earnings per share were up 18% after adjustments to $7.02 per share. Meanwhile, cash flow was strong at $19.3 billion (up 6%), while its free cash flow rose 5% to $10.6 billion.

The company's entertainment segment was the biggest growth driver, with revenue rising 10% to $46.6 billion and operating income rising 16% to $5.4 billion. Experiences had a record year, delivering 9% revenue growth to $39.6 billion and 12% operating income growth to $11.2 billion. That helped offset slower growth in sports (5% revenue growth and 7% operating income growth).

Disney expects to deliver double-digit growth in its adjusted earnings per share for fiscal 2027. That suggests it will earn at least $7.72 per share this year. With its new payout set at $2.00 per share, Disney's dividend payout ratio is around 26% of its earnings.

However, the dividend is only part of the company's capital allocation strategy. The company plans to invest $9 billion to continue to drive growth across its experiences this year. Despite that heavy capital spending, Disney expects to generate around $11 billion in free cash flow this fiscal year. That's still plenty to cover the 33% increase in its dividend payment. Disney's dividend cost the company about $2.6 billion last year, up from the $1.8 billion paid out in fiscal 2025. The raise implies Disney will pay out around $3.5 billion in dividends during its 2027 fiscal year, depending on the impact of share repurchases on its outstanding shares.

However, Disney also plans to repurchase another $9 billion of its shares this year. Add that to the dividend, and total cash returns to shareholders will be around $12.5 billion, which exceeds its anticipated free cash flow by about $1.5 billion. That means Disney will utilize its balance sheet to help fund its 2027 capital allocation strategy.

With $6.7 billion of cash on its balance sheet (against $44.5 billion of debt), it has ample capacity to fund the shortfall. The company also outspent its cash flow on capital spending and cash returns to shareholders in fiscal 2026. It's part of Disney's strategic shift to use its strong A-rated balance sheet to return more cash to shareholders even as it invests heavily in new experiences across its parks and resorts.

Disney is coming off a strong year and expects to deliver double-digit earnings-per-share growth again this fiscal year. That's supporting its shift to pay out more of its cash as dividends. While the company's total capital spending and capital return plans will again exceed its anticipated free cash flow this year, it can easily cover the shortfall with its fortress balance sheet. That puts its newly raised dividend on a rock-solid foundation. Meanwhile, if this year doesn't go as planned, Disney could simply reduce its share repurchases to preserve more financial flexibility.

#3007. Turning Clinical Knowledge Into Consistent Healthcare Operations

Arpan Saxena is the COO/CIO at basys.ai (based out of Harvard University), a leading healthcare AI solutions company.

​Most health plans and provider groups already have the clinical knowledge they need to run well. The problem is where it lives. Some of it sits in medical policies and guidelines. The rest sits in reviewer notes, email threads and the heads of a few experienced nurses and physicians. When that knowledge is scattered, operations pay for it.

I see this often in prior authorization, utilization management, chart review and coding. Two reviewers look at the same case and reach different answers. A policy update takes months to show up in daily work. A new hire takes a year to make calls a senior reviewer makes in minutes. The root cause is usually fragmented knowledge, not the people doing the work.

Here is a framework clinical and operations leaders can use to put that knowledge to work.​

“Stable” means different things in different service lines. In musculoskeletal care, it may mean a patient has completed conservative therapy and still shows functional decline. In surgery, it may mean the patient is fit for the procedure and the risks are documented. In diabetes, it may mean glucose control has held over several months.

So the first question is always context: Which service, which patient population, which decision and which policy applies? Get this wrong and good knowledge gets applied in the wrong place. Context also tells you which clinicians should shape the logic. The experts for spine surgery are not the experts for continuous glucose monitors.​

1. Identify: Where does clinical judgment matter? Start with workflows where a clinician’s decision changes the outcome or the cost, such as prior authorization, utilization management, chart review and coding. Not every step needs a clinician. Some do.

2. Codify: What knowledge drives the decision? Write down what reviewers actually use. That usually means guidelines, medical policies, coverage criteria and evidence, plus the informal rules experienced staff apply.

3. Standardize: What can become repeatable? Some decisions follow the same clinical logic every time. Those can be applied consistently across reviewers and shifts. Others carry real ambiguity and should stay with a clinician.

4. Embed: Where should knowledge appear in the workflow? Knowledge helps most at the moment of decision, inside the tool the reviewer already uses. A guideline in a shared drive does little for a nurse working a queue of 40 cases.

5. Supervise: Where must clinicians remain in control? Define checkpoints where a clinician reviews, approves or overrides. Place them where errors are most likely, most costly or hardest to reverse.

6. Learn: What should improve over time? Every override, appeal and escalation is feedback. Feed it back into the knowledge base so the gray areas get smaller.​

Clinicians think differently, and that is often a strength. Two physicians can weigh the same evidence and land in different places for defensible reasons. The problem is variability that no one can see or explain.

This is where AI can help. It can define the gray area: cases where documentation is incomplete, criteria conflict or the pattern differs from similar past decisions. Instead of deciding those cases, it can nudge the reviewer to take a second look or route the case for a double-check. Clear cases move faster, and unclear ones get more attention.

Used this way, AI enables clinicians. Their expertise reaches more decisions with more consistency, and they spend their time where judgment is actually needed.​

Clinical teams are not uniform. In most organizations I work with, roles fall into three groups:

• Clinicians Who Execute: Reviewers and coders making case-level decisions

• Clinicians Who Own Policy: Medical directors and committees who define criteria and approve changes

• Clinicians Who Oversee Quality: Those who audit decisions, handle appeals and track outcomes

Each group needs different knowledge at different points. A framework that treats them as one audience will frustrate all three. When you map a workflow, assign each checkpoint to the role that should own it.​

Too many checkpoints slow work down and train people to click through. Too few let errors pass. Place them where the stakes justify the time: high-cost services, likely denials, cases with weak documentation and actions that are hard to undo.​

When AI is part of a decision, everyone should know who is accountable for it. Each recommendation should show what knowledge it drew on and which clinician approved, changed or rejected it. That record supports appeals and audits. It also shows clinicians that their judgment is recorded and respected.

In a recent World Economic Forum piece, Dr. John Halamka of Mayo Clinic Platform, Amber Nigam and I described this as a human-in-command approach: AI earns authority step by step, oversight matches the risk and clinicians stay accountable for outcomes. The framework above is how that idea shows up in daily operations.​

Pick one workflow where inconsistency is costing you, such as a high-volume prior authorization category. Run it through the six questions. Map the roles and checkpoints. Then measure what changes: turnaround time, reviewer agreement, overturn rates and appeal outcomes.

Healthcare does not lack clinical knowledge. It lacks a consistent way to use it. Organizations that build one will run faster and make better decisions, with clinicians firmly in command.

#3005. NIU Technologies: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Lower-tier store productivity, not store count, is the bet NIU is making to fund over 1,000 new retail locations in 2027.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 16, 2026, NIU Technologies (NIU -5.68%) announced total sales volume grew 15.4% year over year to 534,457 units, even as quarterly revenue rose just 1.2% to RMB 1.71 billion. Short-term margin pressure from clearing aged international inventory and domestic regulatory shifts created a gap between unit growth and revenue growth. Understanding how the company is navigating these operational transitions helps clarify its path toward multiyear margin expansion. Three key takeaways from management explain where the business stands today and where it's headed next.

Domestic demand for electric bicycles softened ahead of new national standards, but electric motorcycle sales expanded rapidly in tier-2 and tier-3 cities. Strategic product launches targeting commercial delivery riders and high-mileage commuters enabled NIU Technologies to capture market share and raise its average selling price.

International sales volume surged 226% to 47,100 units, but profitability suffered due to heavy discounting on old micro-mobility stock. Clearing this aged inventory removes a structural margin drag, establishing cleaner unit economics for international operations moving forward.

Rather than aggressively expanding store count while demand in top-tier cities remained soft, the company focused on driving per-store productivity in tier-2 and tier-3 markets. Stronger dealer-unit economics in lower-tier regions provide a sustainable foundation for adding over 1,000 retail locations in 2027.

Retail productivity gains and product refreshes are driving momentum in underpenetrated markets. Management is targeting product mix optimization, research and development cost efficiency, and inventory normalization to expand gross margins sequentially into 2027.

Electric motorcycle momentum in lower-tier cities offers a secondary growth engine alongside an eventual recovery in core urban markets. As global channel inventories normalize, the company remains well positioned to capture rising demand for electric two-wheelers.

#3002. FitLife Brands (FTLF) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Irwin revenue nearly doubled while restructuring savings take hold.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

FitLife Brands, Inc. (FTLF -0.73%) reported year-over-year revenue growth driven by the integration of the Irwin brand and expansion in digital sales channels. Management completed a restructuring program involving headcount reductions and facility consolidation to lower the company's annual cost structure. The company increased working capital to fund strategic forward purchases of key commodities, aiming to protect margins against rising global costs for protein and fish oil. Performance in the online segment reached record levels for specific brands, offsetting declines in the specialty retail channel and legacy wholesale business. Management indicated that the business has maintained relatively stable revenue and adjusted EBITDA levels over the preceding four quarters.

Operator: Greetings. Welcome to the FitLife Brands Q3 Earnings Call. [Operator Instructions] Please note, this conference is being recorded. I will now turn the conference over to your host, Dayton Judd. You may begin.

Dayton Judd: Good afternoon. I'd like to welcome everyone to FitLife's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. We appreciate you taking the time to join us this afternoon. Joining me on the call is FitLife's President, Ryan Hansen; and FitLife's CFO, Jakob York. For the third quarter of 2026, total revenue was $25.6 million, an increase of 9% from the third quarter of 2025. Growth came from a full quarter of Irwin, partially offset by a year-over-year revenue decline for Legacy FitLife. Online revenue was $11.8 million, an increase of 15% year-over-year and represented 46% of total revenue. Gross margin was 37.7%, up from 37.2% a year ago.

Excluding the $0.4 million of inventory step-up amortization in the prior year quarter, the gross margin during the third quarter last year was 38.9%. Gross margin improved sequentially from 37.0% in the second quarter. Contribution, which we define as gross profit less advertising and marketing expense, grew 10% to $8.1 million or 31.5% of revenue. Net income was $1.6 million, up 71% from $0.9 million a year ago. Diluted earnings per share was $0.16 compared to $0.09 last year, and basic earnings per share was $0.17 compared to $0.10 last year. Adjusted EBITDA was $3.3 million compared to $3.8 million a year ago.

For the trailing 12 months, the company generated $103.4 million of revenue and $13.7 million of adjusted EBITDA. Although some brands and channels continue to be challenged, others are growing. Sequentially, for each of the past 4 quarters, revenue for the combined business has been relatively stable between $25.3 million and $26.5 million, and adjusted EBITDA has also been consistently between $3.3 million and $3.7 million. During the third quarter, we completed a restructuring initiative to improve efficiency and lower our cost structure. We recorded $0.3 million of restructuring expense, primarily severance, and we expect the initiative to reduce annual operating expense by approximately $1.2 million with savings beginning in the fourth quarter of 2026. Turning to brand level performance.

I'll start with Legacy FitLife, which includes MRC and MusclePharm. Legacy FitLife revenue was $12.6 million, and it has been stable throughout the year, growing 1.5% sequentially in the third quarter of 2026 compared to the second quarter of 2026. Year-over-year, wholesale revenue for Legacy FitLife was down 34%, primarily due to reduced sales to certain retail partners, mainly GNC. However, wholesale revenue for Legacy FitLife has increased sequentially from Q1 to Q2 and from Q2 to Q3, largely offsetting the declines in online revenue driven by MRC. Online revenue for Legacy FitLife was $8.2 million or 65% of total revenue.

Gross margin for Legacy FitLife was 41.6%, up from 39.3% a year ago and similar to the second quarter's 41.7% gross margin. Contribution from Legacy FitLife was $4.2 million or 33.6% of revenue, up from 31.5% during the third quarter of 2025. Sequentially, the Legacy FitLife business has been remarkably stable over the last 3 quarters. Total revenue has ranged between $12.4 million and $12.6 million, with sequential growth in wholesale revenue, largely offsetting the sequential declines in online revenue driven by MRC. Gross margin has ranged between 41.2% and 41.7% and contribution has ranged between $4.2 million and $4.3 million.

The MusclePharm brand is doing well with online revenue during the quarter reaching an all-time high and wholesale revenue reaching its second highest quarter since we have owned the brand. All of this at significantly higher gross margin. Moving on now to Irwin. Irwin generated $13.0 million of revenue, a 91% increase from the partial period last year. Online revenue rose 5% sequentially to $3.6 million and now represents 28% of Irwin's revenue, up from approximately 5% a year ago. Irwin's annual revenue run rate on Amazon exceeded $12 million at the end of the third quarter. Wholesale revenue for Irwin during the quarter was $9.4 million.

With that backdrop, though, we are building a stronger supply chain and new product pipeline as well as a more efficient cost base. On a consolidated basis, online revenue continues to grow with Irwin and MusclePharm delivering all-time highs during the quarter. And we believe that the cost actions we have taken will favorably impact SG&A and cost of goods sold. These cost actions include the $1.2 million expected savings from the restructuring I previously mentioned as well as additional non-headcount-related savings. We ended the quarter with $39.3 million of debt, consisting of $34.5 million on our term loan and $4.8 million on our revolving line of credit.

Our net debt increased slightly from $37.0 million at the end of the second quarter to $38.6 million at the end of the third quarter. Given our general trend of reducing indebtedness each quarter, I want to comment on reasons for the increase. In short, working capital increased $3.5 million sequentially from $9.6 million at the end of the second quarter to $13.1 million at the end of the third quarter. More specifically, inventory increased $1.7 million, receivables increased $1.1 million and prepaids increased $0.7 million, while payables only increased $0.3 million.

A large part of the increase in working capital reflects deliberate decisions we made to lock in commodity pricing through forward purchases of whey protein and fish oil, 2 commodities facing sharp cost increases due to supply shortages. With those payments made, we have locked in fixed price fish oil for the majority of our needs over the next 12 months, and we expect working capital to normalize over time. Over time, we also expect these forward purchases will convert to cash at higher margins than if we had purchased on the spot market. Our weighted average cost of debt is approximately 6.7%, and we intend to continue deploying excess free cash flow toward debt reduction.

So that concludes my opening commentary, and we can now go ahead and open it up for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] The first question comes from Ryan Meyers with Lake Street.

Luke Fingerson: Luke Fingerson on for Ryan Meyers. You expect $1.2 million of annual OpEx savings beginning in Q4. Should we expect this $300,000 benefit immediately? Or does that ramp over a couple of quarters?

Dayton Judd: Luke, it will be -- that will be the number for Q4. So the actions were actually taken. I'm not going to remember exactly when, but call it mid-August. So it wasn't kind of done at the end of the quarter. We should see kind of the full impact of that. In terms of cash, right, so there's a $0.3 million charge that hits during Q3 in terms of cash out the door, about 1/3 of that was paid out before the end of the third quarter with the remainder being paid in the fourth quarter. So P&L-wise, the full impact and cash-wise, you'll see some of that trailing into the fourth quarter.

Luke Fingerson: Got it. And then on the MRC, it continues to drive most of the legacy online weakness. Are you seeing any evidence that the rate of decline is moderating?

Dayton Judd: Yes, kind of, but not really. Let me maybe qualify that with some numbers. So we've been seeing kind of strong double-digit declines, about 20% year-over-year for about somewhere between a little bit more than 1.5 years now. The decline started in February of last year, not at the double-digit rates and then accelerated. I mean in recent -- the last 3 quarters or so, it's still declining. But I would say if you look at the sequential rates, perhaps not as bad. I mean just to put a finer point on it, in Q1, MRC online revenue was about $5.1 million. In Q2, it was about $4.9 million. In Q3, it was about $4.5.

So the other thing that's happening is Prime Day, right? So Dr. Tobias and the other MRC brands are primarily Amazon-based brands. Prime Day was in Q2 this year instead of Q3, which was last year. So some sales that would have been in Q3 may be pulled into Q2. So kind of seeing so far sequentially about $0.5 million decline so far year-to-date. So I guess some moderation, but still declining, answers your question.

Operator: Your next question is coming from Sean McGowan with ROTH Capital.

Sean McGowan: Is that a promotion for Ryan?

Dayton Judd: Yes, Ryan Hansen is the President. So I think we announced that earlier this year. I believe it was in May.

Sean McGowan: Okay. So I missed that, but belated congratulations. Following up on the previous questions, can you help us with where on the income statement we would see the benefit of those restructuring savings? Is it all in G&A?

Dayton Judd: It's all in G&A. I referenced kind of in the opening, there's -- we've done more than that, right? So that $1.2 million represents personnel-related savings. There's other things that we have done. We kind of renegotiated our lease or renewed our lease is a better way to say that in Los Angeles, where the Irwin office is based at, I would just say, very substantial savings. We didn't need as much space. So the space we have is a lot smaller and the rate is substantially lower. So we'll save like 50% on our occupancy in L.A., right? You kind of work that out. It's in the 6 figures over the course of the year.

There's other initiatives we've done on both the SG&A front and the cost of goods front. But yes, the only one we kind of quantified, the $1.2 million was all personnel related, and that's all flowing through SG&A.

Sean McGowan: Okay. And then given that last year you had that step-up account or I should say, keeping in mind that last year you had the step-up accounting issue. Can you talk about some of the components of gross margin trend? I would have thought you'd be getting a bit more benefit by now from the shift to online.

Dayton Judd: Yes. So online is still higher margin. The one difference for Irwin, and I think I may have talked about this on a previous call, but I -- if not, I'm happy to kind of address it right now. There's 2 reasons why Irwin's online margins are not as high as the rest of the business. One is Irwin has -- a lot of Irwin's products are lower dollar price. And we include the Amazon referral fee, which is 15% in our cost of goods. And we also include the Amazon FBA, Fulfillment by Amazon shipping charge in our cost of goods.

And when you have a lower dollar price item, the Fulfillment by Amazon as a percent of the revenue tends to be higher. So that's one reason our margins won't be as high as the rest of the business. If you look at Legacy FitLife, the margins there, you can see they're quite a bit higher. And that's one of the reasons why. Another challenge that we have with margins is that most of the Irwin products are in glass bottles. And you can't sell glass bottles on Amazon unless each bottle is wrapped in bubble wrap. And then you've got to do labeling or stickering on the outside of the bubble wrap so they can scan it.

So right now, right, our volumes keep going up significantly on Amazon. But for every single item that we ship into Amazon that's in the glass bottle, our 3PLs have to open the box, take each bottle out, wrap it in bubble wrap, sticker it, put it in a different box because they're now bigger and they can't fit in the same box and then ship it into Amazon. We're probably paying more than $1 a unit right now just on Amazon prep. So one way we can address that is we're not going to abandon glass bottles.

There's some -- the value in that in particularly the health food channel, which is where we also sell a lot of product. But for certain high-volume SKUs, we're going to start packing them out in both glass for the brick-and-mortar channel, but then plastic for the Amazon channel. I think our first SKUs with that pack-out will be probably late this year, early next year. And then we'll start saving kind of $1 a unit, and we'll start to see kind of higher margins on the online side for Irwin as well.

Another thing we're doing, and you can go look at our listings and see this is, if one kind of a single product is $19.99 on Amazon, we'll create a 2-pack version, right, where we're actually packaging 2 bottles together. And instead of charging $40, maybe we'll charge $37 or $36 or something like that, but we pick up quite a bit of savings on the FBA front. So to ship 1 bottle, Amazon might charge us $3.50, but to ship 2 bottles packaged together, they charge us $3.80 total or something like that. So that's another way we can -- we're doing -- making some changes to try and improve our online margins.

To be clear, though, we -- online is still more profitable than brick-and-mortar or than wholesale, I should say. But the margins aren't as attractive as the rest of our business until we kind of make some of these changes.

Sean McGowan: So if we look then at the Legacy business, are you seeing the level of margin improvement that you would expect to get given the shift in -- actually, that online business was down, wasn't it?

Dayton Judd: Yes. So online is declining -- well, largely primarily driven by MRC. But you can see kind of gross margins in that business are fairly consistent.

Sean McGowan: Yes. Okay. One more question, and I'll jump back in the queue. Is Irwin's shift to online, is there evidence -- any evidence that, that might be hurting the wholesale business?

Dayton Judd: So there's no evidence that we can quantify. But unequivocally, right, I don't think we can argue that it isn't. So there are declines in wholesale. We see that more in the health food channel. So I commented in the press release as well as in the introduction to the call today. Specialty retail, just as a channel, and by specialty retail, I mean kind of small box specialty retail, not large grocery stores or Walmart or anything like that, but the smaller mom-and-pop type stores are really challenged in the current environment. You all know we sell a lot through GNC and in particular, the GNC franchise network, and we've kind of talked about the declines we're seeing there.

We're seeing similar declines in the HFS side of Irwin, but not so much in the mass market side. So are some of those people that are -- now that more of our products are available on Amazon and there's a lot more sales happening on Amazon, are some of those people migrating from the brick-and-mortar stores? Absolutely, right? I don't think we can argue at all that they're not. But how much of that -- what the impact is of that, we can't quantify, right? We don't know who it was that was buying in the HFS channel, and we don't know who it is that's buying in the Amazon channel.

But certainly, some people are choosing to buy online.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] The next question comes from Igor Novgorodtsev with Lares Capital.

Igor Novgorodtsev: Dayton, it's nice to be again a shareholder of FitLife after a long track. So I have a few questions. Legacy GNC, specifically the stores, what's the situation there? Is it still representing a significant amount of your sales? And is the decline the result of diminishing store count of GNC franchisees? Or are they just buying less or some combination of the 2?

Dayton Judd: Yes. So first of all, welcome back to being a shareholder. It is a combination of the 2. So it's probably not my business to kind of give their numbers, but there's been a double-digit decline in the number of doors, and I'm talking here specifically franchise locations. So it's a -- when the stores close, right, we lose all of those sales. Maybe some of it transfers to other stores that are close by. But then even in remaining stores, we are seeing in our numbers, meaningful same-store declines. So you add those 2 up, it's kind of -- it's a 20% plus decline.

In terms of the impact on the business overall, GNC at this point is probably close to -- I'm going to guess, I don't have the numbers in front of me, but maybe about $10 million of our revenue, so they are maybe about a 10% customer. There are some things we're doing to address that. We have a handful of brands that have historically been exclusive to GNC. They're going to largely remain exclusive to GNC, but in the face of declines, there's some things that we can do both internationally as well as maybe in independent or in geographic markets where there is no large presence of GNC franchisees.

So we can start to take those brands to stores, locations that don't compete with GNC. So hopefully, that kind of frames the current situation, but call it about $10 million of revenue on an LTM basis, and it's been declining, again, double digits. I don't have the exact number in front of me, but depending on the quarter, maybe 15% to 25%.

Igor Novgorodtsev: Okay. The other question I have is Amazon changed the algorithm, which I believe I discussed with you previously quite in detail. And I understand that you have a team behind your Amazon presence. How much progress have you made so far to address the issues of the changed algorithm, which wasn't favorable to you? And how much is left to do? And kind of where are you at, at this point?

Dayton Judd: Yes. So Amazon is an always changing black box is maybe one way to describe it. I think that we're seeing good momentum on most of the brands, except the MRC brands. And again, I gave some numbers earlier in the call that perhaps shows a reduction in the decline of the MRC brands. I commented in the prepared remarks, like not all of our brands are declining, and our online revenue is growing sequentially. I think Q3 was a very small downtick compared to Q2.

But when you take into account, again, Prime Day shifting from Q3 into Q2 and you kind of normalize for that, right, even though MRC is declining, right, the other brands are growing enough to offset that, right, and then some. So we're seeing some progress. What I've commented before is we see a very strong correlation, very, very high correlation between the percent sales that a brand is getting on Amazon and its performance on Amazon. And that's somewhat counterintuitive. But the more beholden we are or the brand is to Amazon, the less off Amazon presence it has, the worse it does.

And that's kind of MRC definitionally, right, something like 99% of our revenue historically, again, came from Amazon. So are we selling more off Amazon? A bit. We've shifted quite a lot of the advertising dollars for the MRC brands off of Amazon and more kind of DTC. So I think Google, Meta. We've been doing a lot on TikTok. So we've shifted the advertising dollars to try and build awareness off Amazon. But looking at some of the other brands, I commented MusclePharm is -- every month for the past couple of few months has been a new all-time high for MusclePharm.

So when the brand has had stronger off Amazon presence and awareness, it is doing better on Amazon. So our Amazon declines are really an MRC issue. And then we have one other brand or -- it's really not a brand, it's a product that had a really big run last year that -- and it's not doing as well this year, right? So it's a product that got really hot and now is falling somewhat out of favor at least compared to last year. So if I take those out, like everything else is fine.

So that -- so in terms of your specific question, how are we doing with the algorithm changes, I think we're doing pretty well with Dr. Tobias and MRC in particular, the place where we're still seeing the biggest declines, but perhaps not as significant as they have been.

Igor Novgorodtsev: Okay. My other question, which you alluded to is the ingredients and other costs basically going into your gross margin. Have they spiked mostly because of the situation with diesel and oil? Or this is just an ongoing situation, which is specific to other things? In other words, would you think that if the prices of oil come down for one reason or another or diesel, your prices will significantly come down? Or it's really ingredient by ingredient and those are specific problems to your ingredients?

Dayton Judd: Yes. So there's 2 ingredients that have been a challenge. And when I say been a challenge, I actually feel like we've been on top of it. And because of the purchases we've been making over the last, gosh, I think we started forward buying protein last year. You actually -- we don't expect to see these in our cost of goods, right, because we've been -- we're expending the cash sooner to lock in the lower prices. I don't think it really has anything to do with the cost of oil.

I would say the bigger issue with the cost of oil is gas prices being high is affecting the consumer along with a whole lot of other things affecting the consumer, and that's affecting kind of where they spend their money and how they spend their money. The issues with these 2 ingredients, so whey protein is just -- protein has become more and more popular, partially driven by the GLP-1 trends that have been going on and doctors tell people as they lose weight, as they take the GLP-1, they need to supplement with protein.

You see it any time you walk into the convenience store or a grocery store, right, protein's in everything now from candy bars to -- it's in your Starbucks coffee, it's in your potato chips, right? People are putting protein in everything. The net result of that is whey, which has been our primary protein that we have used has gone from about $2.50 a pound a couple of years ago to it peaked around $15 a pound. It's now back down to between $9 and $10. So what we did is we started forward buying the whey last year. We bought a bunch at about $5 a pound, and we bought a bunch at $7.17 a pound.

And that is -- and we're about to finish using that up. So because of that, right, our margins have not been affected perhaps maybe as much as other people have. The other thing is we have not had to be as aggressive in raising our prices. We have raised price, but certainly not as much as a lot of other people. And that, I think, is one big reason why the MusclePharm brand is doing well right now, right? I think we're stealing share because we have a bit of a cost advantage because we locked in the pricing. So we're about to finish production with the last of our whey that we bought at $7.17.

If we were to buy right now in the spot market, it's between $9 and $10. So we'll probably -- once we start dipping into the $9 and $10 whey or buying on the spot market, our costs will go up a bit, and we'll probably raise price again. The other big area, though, and this is a new one is fish oil. And I'm not a fisherman. I can't explain all of the details, but there are fishing seasons when -- and this is a global phenomenon. This has nothing to do with the U.S. In fact, most of the fish oil that is consumed in the U.S. comes from outside the U.S.

There's fishing seasons down around South America, Peru, in particular, and when the catch is not strong or the fish are too small, they have to throw them back and Peru actually, I think, canceled the last fishing season. What I would encourage you all to do is just go to Google, go to AI and just ask what's going on with the fish oil market, and it will explain it to you better than I can. To kind of give very specific numbers, in the third quarter, we paid $1.4 million was the final payment we made for the protein that we had locked in.

And again, that will be consumed over the next couple of months probably or sold in the next couple of few months and converted to cash. On the fish oil side, most of that is still in prepaid, but we made a payment of a few hundred thousand. I can't remember the exact number in Q3 and then another payment very early in Q4. And both of those payments combined, again, I'm going to guess it's $600,000 to $800,000. With that, we've kind of locked in our cost on fish oil for what we think probably until Q4 of '27. So it's a cash outflow now.

But when it flows through the P&L over the next year, right, it will be a favorable cost. We hope to be able to perhaps gain some share on the fish oil side as well like we're seeing in MusclePharm. So long answer, but hopefully, that addressed your question.

Igor Novgorodtsev: Okay. No, no, no, this is very detailed. And I'll just take privilege to ask the last question. So you alluded that certain categories are doing better and certain categories are doing worse, and it has to do basically with consumer being squeezed by higher prices. So which categories are doing better, which ones are doing worse?

Dayton Judd: Yes. I think the way I would say it is everything is doing worse than it was a year ago, is probably the way I would say it. So like again, MusclePharm is doing great right now. But the consumer headwinds that -- look, we've been pretty open. And when we see something, we talk about it. I think it was the third quarter call last year when we first started talking about seeing these kind of consumer headwinds and you kind of see it in the numbers. So where our biggest challenges are, like if I -- there's 2 areas -- 2 problems, right? And we've talked about this, I think, somewhat extensively. Number one is MRC on Amazon.

And number two is the specialty retail channel, right? And so that includes GNC and that includes health food stores for the Irwin brands. If you ignore those, and we can't completely ignore them and pretend they're not there. But if you isolate those from the rest of the business, I don't really see anything in the rest of the business where I am concerned, right? It's generally flat, maybe down a little bit or up a little bit or growing. And so -- in fact, I commented in our remarks, if you take it the last 4 quarters, right, the business is relatively stable, right?

Revenue has been within about $1 million or a little bit more than $1 million, right, in each quarter over the last 4 quarters, right? EBITDA has been within a couple of hundred -- between $3.3 million and $3.7 million. So these challenges, whether it's GNC or the health food stores for Irwin or MRC, right, are being offset by strength in other areas. So I guess I want to make it clear to people like this is not the sky is falling and everything is going down, right? We're dealing with MRC issues, and we're dealing with specialty retail issues, that channel, which, by the way, I don't think is specific to our brands.

GNC is not -- it's not like our brands are down at GNC and everyone else is killing it, right? Or our brands are struggling in HFS and everyone else is killing it, particularly in the smaller independent HFS stores. So hopefully, that answers your question, but those are -- GNC, specialty retail are our problem areas. Everything else, I'm not losing any sleep over.

Operator: We have a follow-up question coming from Sean McGowan with ROTH Capital.

Sean McGowan: You addressed a couple of the other follow-ups I had, but I do have a couple left. Can you be more specific about how the margins at MusclePharm are trending? I think that going back a year or so ago, that was an issue and it sounds like things are going better on the revenue side. Can you talk a little bit more about the margins there?

Dayton Judd: Sure. So -- and back when we used to break out the numbers for MusclePharm, we used to generate, call it, 30% margins. And then we -- when we -- shortly after we bought the brand and we had built some inventory, we wanted to grow the brand. And so we said, hey, we're going to be promotional. We're going to try and build distribution, et cetera, et cetera. And margins went from like 30% down to like 20%. And then I think 1 quarter, maybe even 2 quarters, a little bit below 20%. Then we had the spike in protein prices.

And we basically told there's a number of protein companies that sell protein internationally that are very price aggressive and really just -- I'd call them bottom feeders, but that maybe makes it sound bad, right? It's just their business model. When prices of protein went up, we're just like, sorry, we're not going to sell to you guys anymore, right? Or certainly not at those prices. So part of what we've seen is a shift away from the low-margin international business. And look, we have raised prices wholesale to everyone. So some of those people may continue to buy, but certainly not in the volumes that they used to buy before.

So no, margins are several hundred basis points higher than they were when we last broke them out, which was when they were around, call it, 20-ish percent. So we're not up to 30% yet, but we're north of 25%. I'll just kind of maybe leave it at that. So -- and again, I think we're helped by the fact that we locked in our protein prices. Again we have raised our price both at wholesale and at retail, but not to the extent that other people have. So we've benefited from our forward purchasing there.

Sean McGowan: And then finally, this is more generally speaking, we're now slightly more than halfway through the fourth quarter. You commented a little bit on some things continuing. But more generally, do you think that all the trends that you've seen in the third quarter continued into the fourth?

Dayton Judd: Yes. So online continues to be very strong. MusclePharm October revenue, I think, is probably quite a bit higher. I'll look at it here online while we're talking quite a bit higher than it was, I believe, in September. Yes, I would say, generally, the trends have continued. Revenue -- if I look at shipments, revenue for October is roughly similar to what we've seen throughout the year. We see fluctuations primarily on the wholesale side. We had a lot of product that was in transit at the end of October that will show up in November revenue, but the basic trends are the same. So nothing new to report in that regard.

But here, I'll tell you like some MusclePharm online, at least directionally. Yes, I mean, like October revenue was probably several percent -- let's see, yes, call it 10 -- October revenue for MusclePharm Online was 10% higher than September revenue. Now we also had fall Prime Days or they don't call it Prime Day, but their October Prime essentially for Amazon happens in October. So October is generally a strong month for online across all of the brands, not just MusclePharm.

Sean McGowan: Okay. And MRC is still trending as it was?

Dayton Judd: Yes. MRC, nothing different than the kind of previous trends that I called out. I will say, again, I don't know -- I don't have a number for Q4. I'm not giving guidance. I'd just remind everyone, Q4 is generally the weakest quarter just seasonally in the supplement business and then Q1 and Q2 are generally stronger. We didn't unfortunately experience that earlier this year, the Q1 and Q2 part, but we're hoping that things get -- that pattern resumes starting next year.

Operator: Okay. We currently have no further questions in the queue. This concludes the Q&A portion of the call. I'd like to turn the floor back to management for any closing remarks.

Dayton Judd: Well, thank you all for participating in the call. If you have any other questions, either now or in the coming months, please feel free to reach out. And we look forward to talking to you on our next call. Thank you.

Operator: This concludes today's conference, and you may disconnect your lines at this time. Thank you for your participation.

#3000. What A Successful AI Pilot Doesn't Tell You

Rahul Saluja is a technology and business leader focused on AI-driven enterprise transformation and operating-model innovation.

A successful AI pilot can leave leaders confident about the technology and unclear about the work still required to make it useful.

We encountered that gap during an AI initiative. The use case was strong, and the early results were promising. We kept the problem narrow, involved the business early and put something tangible in front of users. Those choices helped us learn from actual use instead of spending months discussing AI strategy.

The difficulty came when we tried to move beyond the controlled pilot environment. The biggest friction was data: inconsistencies in how information was captured, accessed and governed. The pilot had demonstrated potential, but moving into everyday operations exposed conditions it hadn’t resolved.

The lesson was more specific than “we needed better data.” We needed to treat data readiness as part of the AI initiative rather than as a prerequisite someone else would solve. I would bring that work forward much earlier now.

A pilot necessarily has boundaries. Narrowing the problem and controlling inputs can help a team establish whether an idea deserves further investment. The next step is to examine how those conditions differ from the intended operating environment.

For the workflow being tested, I would ask: How was the pilot’s information prepared? How will that same information be captured during normal operations? Who will need access? What governance decisions remain unresolved?

These questions help explain what the result actually demonstrates. A promising output is evidence about the inputs and conditions tested. It doesn’t establish that the business can consistently provide those inputs under different conditions.

That distinction should shape the next stage of work. Each material difference between the pilot and the operating environment needs to become an explicit part of the plan.

There’s a danger in responding to every data gap with a much larger enterprise transformation program. An initiative can become dependent on solving problems far beyond the workflow it was intended to improve.

I would apply the same discipline to data readiness that helped the pilot: Keep the scope specific. Start with the information the chosen workflow depends on. Establish what must be consistent, who must be able to access it and how its use must be governed. Then identify which gaps prevent the next stage of deployment.

This makes readiness something a team can investigate and act on. “Improve data quality” is difficult to assign or complete. Identifying an inconsistency in information that a particular workflow requires creates a clearer problem to resolve.

The objective is sufficient readiness for the intended use, with the remaining limitations understood.

Recognizing a data problem doesn’t resolve it. A useful plan also needs to establish who has the authority to act.

For each material gap, I would want three things made explicit: the decision required, the person accountable for resolving it and the evidence that will show it’s been addressed. Some gaps may require changes to how information is captured. Others may involve access or governance. Treating them all as technical cleanup can obscure the business decisions involved.

This is where early business involvement needs to continue beyond demonstrating the use case. The people who understand the workflow must remain involved as the team determines what needs to change. Those decisions belong in the initiative’s scope, resourcing and rollout plan. Leaving them outside the plan makes progress dependent on work for which nobody has taken responsibility.

I would still move quickly to put something tangible in front of users. Our early results helped establish that the idea was worth pursuing. What I would change is the conversation at the end of that stage.

Alongside reviewing performance, I would ask the team to explain what had to be true for the pilot to work, which conditions would differ in everyday operations and who owned closing each consequential gap. A team doesn’t need every answer before it can learn, but it does need to distinguish what it’s demonstrated from what it’s still assuming.

For leaders, that distinction makes a successful pilot more useful. It provides both evidence of potential and a clearer account of the work required to realize it.

Before approving the next stage, ask: Does the plan include the work needed to make the pilot’s conditions repeatable? If that work sits outside the initiative, part of the AI business case is still unowned.

#2998. Data center policy dominated the midterms. The 'Virginia of Europe' is the latest battleground

Spain's government is seeking to tighten restrictions on one of Europe's fastest-growing data center booms, as the country's Socialist prime minister prepares to fight an election. Investors like Amazon, Microsoft and Blackstone-backed QTS are on tenterhooks.

The measure, which doesn't need parliamentary approval, could be approved by Pedro Sánchez's cabinet by next week, and is widely expected to pass ahead of the Nov. 29 elections.

It could potentially cost one of Europe's fastest-growing tech regions billions of dollars in investment.

The government first introduced the decree in August, partly in response to concerns over energy demand and prices. After fierce opposition, it put forward a revised version on Oct. 26, but the proposal still includes strict renewable-energy requirements.

"These requirements could pose insurmountable barriers and act as an effective moratorium," S&P said in an October report. The proposed rules would require 80% of electricity used by data centers to come from renewable sources matched hour by hour, with projects potentially losing grid access if they fail to comply.

Projects already in development or awaiting grid connections would also be subject to the rules, with a five-year transition period to comply.

Data center build-out has quickly become a prominent political issue around the world. In the U.S. midterm elections, CBS exit polls found data centers were a major influence for more than half of voters.

In Spain, concerns over the water and energy demands of data centers are increasingly part of the election debate as the country faces mounting pressure to expand its electricity grid to meet the demand.

CBRE estimates that while developers have announced 10.5 GW of data center capacity across Spain and Portugal, only about 4.5 GW is currently considered realistically deliverable because of grid, permitting and infrastructure constraints.

Alberto Nadal, the opposition center-right Popular Party's deputy secretary for the economy, has said a conservative government would repeal the decree. Recent polling shows the Popular Party leading, with several seat projections putting the PP and far-right Vox together above a parliamentary majority.

Aragón, a landlocked region in the country's northeast, governed by the Popular Party, has emerged as one of Europe's fastest-growing digital infrastructure hubs and is at the center of opposition to the draft rules.

The region has attracted investors with fast-track permits, abundant renewable energy and land, and international cable connections. Aragón president, Jorge Azcón, wants to turn it into the "Virginia of Europe," referring to the U.S. state with the world's highest density of data center sites.

Aragón is set to receive more than 60 billion euros ($66 billion) in data center and digital infrastructure investment over the next decade.

But concerns are growing among residents over noise, water use and pressure on the electricity grid.

Pilar Alegría, leader of the Socialist Party in Aragón, told a Nov. 15 rally that the election would be decisive for the region's future and for protecting its natural resources.

She highlighted the Ebro River, which runs through Aragón, and raised concerns about the resources used by data centers in a region vulnerable to drought.

Popular Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, speaking the same day, sought to reassure investors.

"It would be a mistake to squander that advantage through poor planning or regulation that creates uncertainty for investors," Feijóo said.

Eva Valle, Aragón's economy minister, has also called for the decree to be scrapped.

"It is necessary to halt the approval of this decree, which abounds in harmful conditions placed on the sector," she said at an AWS-organized event on Oct. 27, accusing the government of pursuing "a political agenda."

Amazon Web Services and Microsoft have said their investment plans in Aragón remain unchanged, while urging Spain to provide long-term legal certainty and regulatory predictability.

Google has already put a multibillion-euro data center project on hold pending greater regulatory certainty, according to a report in Spanish newspaper El Mundo, which cited anonymous sources. Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNBC.

SpainDC, which represents the data-center industry in the country, said the decree would give the group's members the most restrictive data center framework in the European Union and could put 80% to 90% of investment at risk.

"We are going to use all the institutional, regulatory and legal avenues at our disposal" to challenge the decree, said SpainDC president Emilio Díaz.

#2997. Prediction: This Will Be Broadcom’s Stock Price by the End of 2028

Broadcom has underperformed the semiconductor sector over the past year, but that could change as its growth accelerates.

The past year has been a forgettable one for Broadcom (AVGO +1.67%) investors, as the stock has significantly underperformed the broader semiconductor sector, posting paltry gains of 1%.

The PHLX Semiconductor Sector index, meanwhile, has shot up by 48% over the past year despite experiencing volatility in recent months. However, a closer look at Broadcom's financial performance makes it clear that the market has been unnecessarily harsh on the stock.

In fact, I won't be surprised to see Broadcom stock stepping on the gas and delivering terrific gains to investors over the next couple of years. Let's look at the reasons why.

Broadcom designs application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) and networking components. These chips are in terrific demand from hyperscalers and AI companies, which explains why Broadcom has built a solid client base that includes Anthropic, OpenAI, Alphabet's Google, and Meta Platforms.

In all, Broadcom has six customers for its custom AI processors and networking chips, and they are poised to ramp up the deployment of its products. This explains why the company is on track to deliver significant acceleration in AI revenue over the next couple of fiscal years.

Broadcom's AI semiconductor revenue will nearly triple in fiscal 2026 (which ended earlier this month) to $58 billion. Even better, the company expects its AI revenue to double in each of the next two fiscal years, reaching $115 billion in fiscal 2027 and $230 billion in fiscal 2028. However, Broadcom's AI revenue growth could exceed expectations.

That's because the demand for optical networking components is poised to jump exponentially between 2026 and 2028. Goldman Sachs estimates that the optical component space could generate $154 billion in revenue in 2028, up from just $15 billion this year. Broadcom designs optical digital signal processors (DSPs), electro-absorption modulated (EML) lasers, and other components to enable optical networking in data centers.

What's more, Broadcom management noted on the September earnings call that the demand for its AI solutions exceeds its outlook. The company is focused on securing additional supply to meet growing demand, which I think gives it the potential to exceed its forecasts over the next couple of years.

Broadcom's underperformance this year and its exceptional growth explain why the stock can be bought at an incredibly cheap 18 times forward earnings. That's lower than the tech-laden Nasdaq-100 index's forward earnings multiple of almost 21.

Analysts are projecting a 71% increase in Broadcom's earnings per share (EPS) in fiscal 2026 to $11.67. Looking ahead, Broadcom's earnings are poised for a big lift-off over the next couple of fiscal years.

AVGO EPS Estimates for Current Fiscal Year data by YCharts

It is worth noting that the fiscal 2028 EPS estimate is almost in line with Broadcom's guidance. Assuming Broadcom trades at even 25 times earnings after two years, a slight premium to the Nasdaq-100 due to its terrific growth, its stock price could reach $763 (based on the EPS estimate seen in the chart above).

That implies potential gains of 124%, suggesting investors can buy a top AI stock at an attractive valuation right now.

#2996. Top Wall Street analysts prefer these 3 dividend stocks for stable income

Global stock markets remain volatile amid persistent geopolitical tensions and concerns about the sustainability of AI trade. Given this backdrop, investors seeking steady income can add dividend-paying stocks to their portfolios.

Tracking recommendations from top Wall Street analysts can help investors pick attractive stocks, as these experts assess a company's ability to pay dividends consistently.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Integrated oil and gas giant Chevron (CVX) is a dividend king. The company has increased its dividend for 39 consecutive years. At a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share (annualized dividend of $7.12 per share), CVX offers a yield of 3.14%. Chevron will announce its third-quarter results on October 30.

In an earnings preview note on U.S. oil majors, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on Chevron with a price target of $241. The analyst is focused on the company's international growth prospects across Latin America, the Middle East, West Africa, and the Eastern Mediterranean.

Specifically, Mehta highlighted management's commentary on solid execution in Venezuela, with gross production expected to more than double to nearly 600 kbd (kilo barrels per day) by 2031 via three joint ventures. He also noted a recent oil and gas condensate discovery in offshore Angola and is awaiting commercial updates on the West Qurna 2 and Nasiriyah projects in Iraq.

Furthermore, Mehta expects CVX to report improved productivity and capital efficiency across domestic shale assets. He expects the improvement mainly in the Permian Basin, where Chevron projects advanced chemical treatments to drive about a 10% recovery uplift in new wells and bring down capital spend per barrel by about 25% year-over-year.
