Just given the acceleration that you saw last quarter versus this one, can you talk about the pace of adoption that you're expecting from here? And how are you thinking about how much utilization NTAP will actually drive in the fourth quarter? And anything you can say at this point around whether you're seeing a noticeable change in utilization or the pace of hospital adoption since that October 1 effective NTAP went into place?

Gregory Demopulos: Yes. Thanks. First, I mean, as we have said previously, we won't really be guiding to fourth quarter results other than, I think, to underscore what I said in the opening comments, which is that the momentum of growth has continued in Q4. So, we are seeing continued growth in Q4. With respect to the impact of NTAP, it's interesting that NTAP, obviously important to us, obviously, important to you as well. But it is interesting to us how physicians and frankly, institutions aren't widely aware of the NTAP award for YARTEMLEA.

And this is one of our current areas of focus, which is to make sure that, that understanding of YARTEMLEA receipt of NTAP and the importance to the inpatient facilities and specifically Medicare patients, how that is important to those facilities as well. Bill, do you have any other comment you want to add on that about NTAP?

William Woodman: Yes. I have experience with NTAP with other companies and other drugs, and it is a learning process that you have to teach people on how to take advantage of that situation. We have a booth coming up here at ASH that will highlight the NTAP changes and what is available to these accounts. It's interesting to note that the largest growth in allogeneic transplant is patients over 65.

And actually, at a recent meeting, actually a couple of days ago, they talked about the silver tsunami they're expecting to see as these treatments for AML and in particular, get better and better, they can get more and more patients to transplant, and they expect to transplant more and more patients over 65. So, NTAP is going to do nothing but help us as we move into that growth. And we're looking forward to educating as many people as we can to take advantage of this program.

Gregory Demopulos: So, what we see is Medicare now representing about 30% of allogeneic transplant. We would expect, as Bill just said, that number to grow. I think it's also important to recognize that while we're talking about a Medicare segment of the population, the allogeneic transplant population only, once again, that institutions, transplant centers start using the drug for their Medicare patients. I expect that they will see the response, and that just causes continued expansion throughout each of those centers, transplant patients and TMA patients more broadly.

Olivia Brayer: Okay. Very helpful. And then if I could ask a follow-up on gross to net. Where do you ultimately expect that to shake out as you shift patients to the outpatient setting moving forward?

Gregory Demopulos: Yes, that's a great question. I don't think that we have we have shared a target number there, but I think that we are approaching it more quickly than we had anticipated it and meaning anticipated approaching where we think that cap will be. And I think that is reflective of the shift, obviously, given that this increase in gross to net is, as I said, almost exclusively due to 340B. This is a very encouraging signal to us of transfer from inpatient to outpatient. And again, for us, as you know, but just to make sure everybody understands, the 340B discount has no impact on our ASP.

This is a government-mandated discount, not one that the company is taking independently. So, it has no impact on our ASP, which overall then really just exemplifies, I think, the expansion from inpatient to outpatient, which, as I think we pointed out, benefits not only the patients, but the centers as well. So, I think that overall, Olivia, I would think -- and again, I'm giving you a very soft number here, but somewhere in the high teens would be what we would think we might be approaching at some point.

But to jump from 11.5% to 14% from the prior quarter to this quarter, we see as sort of a resounding acknowledgment, recognition and of the importance of the drug and moving it into the outpatient setting. It also underscores, I think, the safety of the drug, certainly, the perceived safety of the drug by the physicians that they're willing to move this out of the inpatient setting where there is, as you know, very regular constant monitoring and into the outpatient setting. I think it speaks really strongly for the potential of YARTEMLEA and the safety of YARTEMLEA from -- as well clearly of its efficacy. Did that help?

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Serge Belanger with Needham.

Serge Belanger: Can you guys hear me now?

Serge Belanger: Sorry, technically challenged. Anyway, I guess a couple of questions on YARTEMLEA to start off with. Can you maybe talk about the volume of vials in the inpatient setting versus the outpatient setting that you're currently seeing? And then secondly, just curious, what is the average price you estimate for -- on a per patient basis? Because I think in the past, you've talked about some patients being treated on a weekly basis and some others on a twice weekly basis. So, just curious where that has settled and what kind of revenues you're seeing per patient on YARTEMLEA?

Gregory Demopulos: Understood the question. We haven't shared the vial split between in and outpatient. And so we won't today other than to say that the outpatient use has meaningfully increased. With respect to utilization per course, it's interesting. I think we're seeing a shift. And again, we don't have great access because of HIPAA and all of the confidentiality components around HIPAA. We don't have really great visibility into patient level data, patient level information. But what I think we are seeing is an increase in the use of twice weekly early on, which as we think about it and probably as you think about it, that probably ties to the increased outpatient use that we're seeing as well.

So, hit them hard early and then move them to the outpatient setting where you can treat them on an outpatient basis. The average use for our study and for our EAP were in the 8 to 10 vial per course range. Having said that, I think we've noted before, we had some patients, primarily pediatric patients who had remained on the drug for a very long time, beyond a year. And when we went to run that down to see why these patients had been kept on the drug for such a lengthy time. The question was, gee, are you not seeing the response that you are hoping to see with the drug? The answer was quite the opposite.

It's no. Drug is working great. This is why we have the patient on and we're keeping the patient on because we are concerned always about relapse. So, obviously, the fact that we were running this through the expanded access program where we were providing drug for free, I would expect, had a very large impact on their ability to use it for that extensive amount of time. But I think it does underscore that when you -- when one does, and this is what we hear from experts, so I am only relaying what I'm hearing.

But when we hear that the benefit risk balance in the use of YARTEMLEA is so heavily weighted toward the benefit that they are -- that a number of physicians are reticent to take their patients off YARTEMLEA simply because they want to keep them covered, protected in the event of a relapse. So, I know I'm not answering your question specifically on what are the numbers. I can tell you that we don't have those tightly because those are -- those are really patient-level data that we just don't access. But I'm trying to give you some color, Serge, as to what we're hearing and what we're seeing. Does that help?

Serge Belanger: Yes. And maybe just one last one. It looks like you have reimbursement access more or less buttoned up here with the NTAP, the J-code and some clarity with the 340B coverage. Just curious if you'll be in a position to provide guidance for 2027.

Gregory Demopulos: We will begin providing guidance at some point in 2027, I expect. We just want to get a sense of how the overall sales are looking. We're very pleased with what we're seeing. But what we don't want to do is get out ahead of ourselves and guide when we really don't have the data to back up that. It is one thing when estimates are provided by analysts like yourself and others. It's another thing when we provide those estimates and then there's not -- those are skewed a little differently.

I'll ask Bill about his comments just on the utilization of the drug as well to see, Bill, if you have any other thoughts for Serge on utilization and vials per course?

William Woodman: Yes. I think you can see -- I think the biggest thing you can see is that shift to the outpatient is the increase in our 340B discount. Whenever you launch an acute disease, generally, you get the sickest of the sick first. And the great thing about YARTEMLEA is it works. So, they're treating the sickest sick on the inpatient side. They get more comfortable with it. Those patients leave the ICU, they go home, they get treated in their outpatient center. And you can see that shift as we go from quarter-to-quarter, and it's going to get nothing but better from there.

We have many, many examples of people walking out of ICUs that they didn't expect to happen. So, the good news is the drug is working. That shift over time, as Greg alluded to, will probably increase as people get more and more comfortable with it. We've had situations where people have gone home to their -- just their regular community-based hospital and continue to receive treatment and that hospital is not a transplant center and have had no problem infusing, billing for, getting paid for the drug. So, all these things are good signs to see that we're going to treat more and more patients in the outpatient side.

And as people get really comfortable with it, they'll treat on the outpatient side before they come in, and you'll get a more consistent basis over time as you treat those patients before they get into trouble. Right now, we're really treating the patients who are already in trouble. We want to move that to the outpatient side.

Gregory Demopulos: So, once -- thanks, Bill. So, once we have a better sense of all of those factors that Bill just touched on, we'll be more comfortable providing guidance. Until then, really, we're still sifting through data as you are. All I can say is the data that we see, all of the data that we see are highly encouraging for the potential of YARTEMLEA in TA-TMA.

William Woodman: Yes. From a marketing perspective, we grew in every metric that we measure. We can't be happier. The momentum is easy to see and feel, especially at recent medical meetings. We're built for the long-term sustained growth, and we're going to ensure to invest in ways that this education occurs and people are more ready to treat these patients as quickly as possible.

Gregory Demopulos: And I think that's underscored by just the focus that we went through in the prepared comments about the number of education positions, educator positions that we've added. We've added 10 positions in the last 6 weeks. And this is not driven by a concern that we're not educating enough. It's driven by the customer requests and customer need for the education. So, it's not -- we're not trying to fix a problem by adding these educators we're addressing a need that's being voiced by the transplant physicians, pharmacists, nurses, the end users or the end-use administrators of the drug. And I think that's an important distinction.

Operator: Your final question comes from the line of Steve Brozak with WBB.

Stephen Brozak: Actually, I do have two. Just to reiterate, you are not just cash flow breakeven, you actually are cash flow positive right now. And I guess you can repeat anything you've got because the only question becomes on the treatment of the derivative. When do you expect that, by the way, to clear up? And I've got a really significant question...

Gregory Demopulos: Well, I'll start with the last question first. As soon as we get rid of the convert overhang, which we've taken a large part of that away through the repurchase of the converts. But however, we eliminate the remainder of that convert, that derivative will disappear with it. With respect to your question about cash flow positive, yes, we're $13.3 million cash flow positive from operations this quarter. Frankly, we were also cash flow positive last quarter in our first full quarter of the launch, which we think is pretty remarkable. We don't frankly expect that.

I know we've said we won't guide for Q4, but I think it's pretty clear that we don't expect that's going to change in Q4. So, this is where we stand. And this is how we're able to continue funding all of the other things that we're doing with the company. That and what we expect will be the revenues coming from the Novo transaction. All of this, I think, puts us in a very strong financial position across the company. David, any other comments on that or color you want to add?

David Borges: No, I would echo what you said. I mean, we've seen a nice path from $4.1 million of cash from ops in Q2 to over $13 million this quarter and see that trend continuing going forward, as you said.

Gregory Demopulos: So, -- and as we move really to what we expect will be standard of care, at some point, that threshold is reached and the use of the drug just, I think, will increase even more so. But that, again, is my personal view.

Stephen Brozak: Okay. That brings me to a perfect segue here. 30 years ago, I worked on a private transaction and a public offering for a company called Alexion. And just about 20 years ago...

Gregory Demopulos: I've never heard of them.

Stephen Brozak: Good. Just keep to that. And they came up with a product, eculizumab, a complement product, obviously. And how would you -- I'm sure you've looked at what they did and how they grew their revenue. How would you compare your approach with what they did because obviously, it's a good historical mark. I'm not saying it's identical, but it's a good historical mark. And I'll jump back in the queue with that open question. How is that?

Gregory Demopulos: Yes. I mean, look, I understand the question. I understand, I think, the relevance of it and the curiosity about it. Remember that these were very different products, right? When -- when Soliris or eculizumab was launched, that initial indication was for PNH, paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, which is a chronic disease. What we are treating is TA-TMA, which is an acute disease. So, duration of therapy, obviously limited. One is we're treating until we cure the patient, which is to the best of our knowledge, relatively quickly, and eculizumab was used chronically, so treating effectively for that patient's life. The pricing, we have looked at that. Obviously, we looked at that as we were determining where to price YARTEMLEA.

And the course of therapy for a year, pretty similar, ours probably less, as you might imagine, for an acute or episodic treatment versus chronic. So, there are real differences there, Steve. But having said that, I think as you may have anticipated, certainly, we've looked at that. I -- the eculizumab numbers aren't readily available for U.S. They sort of need to be implied from the worldwide sales. But for third quarter of their sales versus third quarter of our sales, our sales U.S. only, we exceed their third quarter worldwide sales, at least I think that's my understanding, Bill. Is that correct?

Gregory Demopulos: And then when you look at the first 3 quarters of sales, again, implied in the U.S. based on subsequent splits, we're -- in the U.S., we're doing about 60% better in net revenues than they did in their third quarter. So, we're pleased with how we're stacking up. That does not, in any way, predict, guide what we're going to do in the future. But obviously, we're happy with where we stand. And I think, yes, your question was an interesting one. Of course, we look at these things. We don't only look at eculizumab. We look really at all complement inhibitors. That includes pegcetacoplan or EMPAVALI, that includes even ravu, and it also includes defibrotide.

So, we have a pretty good set of metrics against which to assess ourselves and YARTEMLEA's growth and uptake. And I think we're quite pleased with it, particularly given what I said about chronic versus episodic use. But, I don't know, I'm guessing that answered your question, but if not, do you...

Stephen Brozak: No, no, it does. They say history doesn't repeat itself, but it does rhyme. So, you've answered it.

Operator: There are no further questions at this time. I will now turn the call back to Dr. Demopulos for closing remarks.

Gregory Demopulos: Thank you, operator, and thanks, everyone, for your time. YARTEMLEA's approval really turned years of scientific work into a treatment for patients who urgently needed one. Its adoption is now helping fund, as we discussed, the next chapter of that work, extending its reach and advancing therapies for other serious diseases. We're excited about YARTEMLEA's expanding potential and confident in our science and our team's ability to develop new medicines that improve patients' lives and build lasting value for our shareholders. So, thank you again all for joining this afternoon and for your continued support. We look forward to speaking with you again. Thank you.

Operator: This concludes today's call. Thank you for attending. You may now disconnect.

#2978. Gold Falls Below $4,000: Is Now the Time to Invest in This Gold-Backed ETF?

Investors have been bearish on gold of late, but that could change in the not-too-distant future.

The price of gold has been falling sharply over the past several months. The days of it being well over $5,000 per ounce are long gone. On Tuesday, it was trading below even the $4,000 mark, as a rise in interest rates has led to investors seeking assets with high yields.

As a result of the decline, SPDR Gold Shares (GLD +0.46%), which is backed by physical gold, is down 11% this year and has declined more than 30% from its 52-week high. In the past five years, however, it has doubled in value. Could now be an opportune time to invest in this fund while its valuation is lower?

While gold is not typically known for being a great investment, the SPDR Gold Shares fund has surprisingly outperformed the broader market over the past five years. It's up around 104% during that time frame, while the S&P 500, which tracks the top stocks on U.S. markets, has generated total returns (which include dividend payments) of around 70%.

Many investors see gold as a way to diversify their portfolios and even hedge against market uncertainty. Late last year, it rose significantly in value as investors grew concerned about high valuations in the market. While valuations remain high today, interest rates have also been climbing, making gold less attractive to hold. The concern is also that in the near term, rates may rise even higher given that inflation isn't at the Fed's target level of 2%.

Right now, the outlook doesn't look all that enticing for buying the SPDR Gold Shares fund. Interest rates are on the rise and could continue climbing next year.

However, I'm optimistic that this won't be a repeat of 2022, when inflation was wildly out of control due to high post-pandemic spending. This time around, it's more to do with higher commodity prices and the war in Iran. With Democrats having control of Congress next year, there could be more of a push to end the war and to help alleviate inflation. Should that happen, that may lessen the need for higher interest rates.

The economic picture can change quickly. While the expectation right now is that interest rates will continue to rise next year, I believe those concerns may be a bit overblown. If the war in Iran ends, that could drastically change that outlook. Meanwhile, with many stocks still looking overpriced, gold could remain in high demand as investors seek safe-haven assets to hold, which is why I believe investing in the SPDR Gold Shares fund may prove to be a good move right now.

#2977. Berkshire Hathaway raised its stake in Delta in the third quarter. It also trimmed a key bank holding

Berkshire Hathaway made several moves in the stock market during the third quarter, adding to key positions and trimming others.

The Omaha-based conglomerate, now led by CEO Greg Abel, increased its Delta Air Lines stake by 12%, scooping up 7.13 million shares. The position was worth $5.37 billion at the end of the third quarter.

Abel succeeded legendary investor Warren Buffett, 96, at the start of this year. Buffett continues to control roughly 13% of Berkshire common stock, Reuters said Monday, after the former CEO donated $5.5 billion to nonprofit foundations.

Berkshire boosted its stake in Delta as the Atlanta-based carrier's shares tumbled 11% in the third quarter, hurt by rising jet fuel prices due to the U.S.-Iran war that pressured the entire airline industry. That marked the stock's worst quarterly performance since the first quarter of 2025, when it plunged 28%. Delta last month also cut its full-year earnings forecast, citing a surge in fuel costs.

To be sure, buying that dip has been a winning investment thus far. Delta is up 3.8% so far in the fourth quarter, while the S&P 500 has dropped 3.1%. Shares are also up nearly 15% over the past month.

Berkshire also trimmed its holding in Bank of America by nearly 6%, selling more than $1.6 billion worth of stock.

BofA was under pressure in the third quarter, falling more than 4%, as interest rates surged alongside stubbornly high inflation and expectations of tighter Federal Reserve monetary policy. At one point in September the 30-year Treasury bond yield surged above 5.6% to its highest level since 2002.

Despite the share sale, Bank of America remains a top Berkshire Hathaway holding, with the conglomerate's stake valued at $24.8 billion at the end of the third quarter.

Berkshire also initiated a position in Bending Spoons and nearly doubled its stake in homebuilder Lennar in the latest quarter.

#2971. Prediction: This Is What Nvidia's Stock Will Be Worth by the End of 2026

Investors shouldn't assume the worst is over for the chip stock.

On Monday, Nvidia (NVDA -1.29%) shares fell below $160. Since the beginning of the year, the stock has lost 16% of its value, and that climbs to 31% when looking at just the past six months.

The business is facing considerable uncertainty with Jensen Huang recently resigning as president and CEO of the company. Question marks about who leads the company moving forward could weigh on the stock. But there are also broader macroeconomic issues that investors shouldn't overlook either, which were already troubling before this recent fallout.

Regardless of who is leading Nvidia's stock as of the end of the year, I believe it'll continue to fall in value, simply because the appetite for tech and artificial intelligence (AI) stocks isn't what it was even a few months ago. Investors are becoming more concerned with high tech spending, especially with interest rates on the rise and expected to continue rising in the near future. That alone might have a much larger impact on Nvidia's stock than who is running the business, at least in the near term, anyway.

A slowdown in customer spending would be much more problematic for Nvidia, as it could prompt adjustments to analyst forecasts and, in turn, make the stock's valuation relative to expected earnings look far different and more expensive.

The truth is, Nvidia's stock already wasn't doing all that well this year even before the controversy surrounding Huang came out. Now, however, bearish investors have even more of a reason to sell the AI stock.

If there is a big rate hike next month, as some analysts believe, it could rattle the markets, especially tech, where expectations of continued high spending are necessary to justify high valuations. Huang is also expected to testify before Congress this month, which may lead to more questions and raise new issues regarding the business and its practices.

There are simply too many headwinds at this stage; it appears much more likely that Nvidia's stock will decline further than rally. And Nvidia's stock has been highly volatile. Thus, I think going on another 20% drop or so, down to $125, may not be unreasonable by the end of the year.

The good news for investors is that, in the long run, it may still be worth investing in the business given its dominance in the chip market. And if its share price comes down even further, as I believe it will, it'll simply be an even better buy at that point.

U.S. Vice President JD Vance said Monday he will make a decision next year about whether to run for president in 2028.

"We'll figure it out sometime next year," he told Fox News host Laura Ingraham in an interview that aired Monday evening.

"I'm not an expert in this but my understanding with a presidential campaign is there's a lot of infrastructure that you have to set up, fundraising, all that stuff and so you can't declare a month before the Iowa caucus that you're going to run for president," he said. "So, you know, I haven't made a decision."

Vance has yet to openly declare any ambition to succeed President Donald Trump when his current term ends, but speculation that the vice president has his sights set on the White House has been mounting for some time. In the wake of the GOP's crushing defeat in the U.S. midterm election on Nov. 3, anonymous sources involved in campaigns told Reuters Vance was among the high-profile Republicans who had begun early preparations for a 2028 run.

Candidates typically announce their intentions to run in the election in the spring of 2027, with parties holding nominating conventions to formally select their presidential candidates between July and September.

Polymarket currently slates Vance as the frontrunner to win the Republican presidential nomination for the 2028 election, with the prediction market giving him a 37% chance of becoming the nominee. Kalshi currently gives a 73% chance that Vance will run for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination. Let's take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country."

In his interview with Fox News on Monday, Vance said the Republicans got "shellacked" in the midterms.

"We have to take messages from that, but the message that we have to take is that the American people want prosperity, they want freedom, they want sovereignty within their own country and they want us to do more of the good things that we've done," he said.

He added that lawmakers needed to double down on "economic nationalism" and bring "prosperity to the homeland" to deal with "economic pain" in the United States.

#2965. PicS (PICS) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Rising delinquencies test a quarter of strong credit and efficiency gains.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

PicS N.V. (PICS -30.85%) management reported that the business model reached all nine guided targets for the third quarter while improving operational efficiency through accelerated AI adoption. The company is transitioning its credit strategy toward lower-risk products, including private payroll loans and secured lending, which now constitute a significant majority of the total revenue base. Strategic consolidation of the Kev acquisition has added insurance underwriting capabilities to the existing distribution ecosystem, creating a new growth engine. Furthermore, management announced an accounting refinement to its write-off policy for unsecured loans to align with industry benchmarks and provide clearer asset quality transparency as the portfolio seasons.

Operator: Good evening, everyone, and welcome to PicPay's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. Joining the call today are Eduardo Chedid, Chief Executive Officer; Andre Cazotto, Chief Financial and Investor Relations Officer; and Danilo Caffaro, Vice President of Consumer Banking. Please note that this presentation may contain forward-looking statements and non-IFRS financial measures. Please refer to the disclaimer on the screen and to the earnings materials available on the Investor Relations section of PicPay's website for additional information. This call is being recorded, and a replay will be available on the company's website shortly after the conclusion of the call. At this time, I would like to turn the call over to Eduardo Chedid, Chief Executive Officer of PicPay.

Eduardo Simoes: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for joining us. This was a quarter where the model did what we said it would do. We grew credit by 88% year-over-year. We beat every single line of the guidance we gave in August, and we did it while becoming more efficient, not less. I will walk you through the headline numbers and the operating highlights. Danilo Caffaro, who leads our Consumer business will then take you through our credit portfolio expansion, and Andre Cazotto will close with asset quality in detail, the financials and capital. Let me start with execution against guidance. Three months ago, we gave you guidance on 9 metrics on a peak stand-alone basis.

We met or exceeded all of 9. Net interest income came in at BRL 2.17 billion, about 3.5% above what we guided. Quarterly cost of risk was 3.8% at the low end of the range we had indicated. And adjusted earnings before taxes reached BRL 388 million, 2.5% above guidance. The message is simple. We are growing fast, and we are growing in a way we can forecast. That is the discipline we want you to expect from us every quarter. Now where is that growth coming from? Three places: First, consumer credit. The credit portfolio reached BRL 35 billion, 88% above a year ago and up BRL 3 billion in the quarter alone.

We are taking share where we choose to compete. In private payroll loans, our market share went from 2.4% a year ago to 7.3% today with roughly BRL 3.5 billion originated this quarter. In cards, our share of TPV rose from 1.3% to 1.8%, mostly by extending credit limits to mature cohorts we already know well. Second, small and medium businesses. Business banking is gaining real traction. New business accounts are running at 126,000 per month, 48% above the first half of the year. Supply chain finance origination hit BRL 1.4 billion, up 37% quarter-on-quarter, and we launched a free online store for merchants, a new front door into the ecosystem. Third, insurance: our insurance distribution keeps growing.

Active policies in the PicPay base rose 39% year-over-year to 11 million. And with the Kev acquisition now completed and integration underway, we have added the underwriting side of that business. To give you a sense of scale, Kev wrote BRL 939 million of premiums this quarter, 62% more than a year ago. It is early two months of consolidation only. But this is a genuinely new engine, and you will see its contribution build from here. On the operating side, the ecosystem keeps compounding. We have now 72 million accounts and 46.4 million quarterly active clients, up 10% year-over-year. That's an activation rate of 64%.

Cash in the money our clients bring to PicPay, reached BRL 141 billion, up 13% year-over-year. Total payment volume reached BRL 175 billion in this quarter, up 24% year-over-year. More clients, more activity per client and more of their money coming into the ecosystem. That is the base everything else is built on. Total revenue and financial income reached BRL 4.7 billion this quarter, 73% above last year on top of a 94% growth the year before. As important as the total is the mix. Today, 73% of our revenue comes from sources with lower or no credit risk. Fees and services, floats and secure and partially secured credits, such as FGTS and payroll loans.

Only 27% comes from unsecured credit. 73% with lower or no credit risk. That is what resilience looks like in a model that is also growing credit at 88%. And that revenue growth is translating into profit, and it's doing so with operating leverage. Gross profit reached BRL 1.3 billion, up 38% year-over-year and 5% in the quarter. Adjusted earnings before taxes reached BRL 388 million, up 131% year-over-year and 33% quarter-on-quarter. Notice the gap between those two sequential numbers. Gross profit grew 5% in the quarter. Earnings before taxes grew 33%.

That difference is operating expenses growing much more slowly than the business, which brings me to the slide, I think, matters most for how you should think about PicPay. Here's our unit economics over 5 quarters. Average revenue per active client reached BRL 103 this quarter, 58% higher year-over-year. Over the same period, cost to serve per active client rose 20% to BRL 21.40. So revenue per client is growing almost 3x faster than the cost of serving that client. Today, we generate BRL 4.8 of revenue for every real we spent serving a client. And that ratio has widened every single quarter on this chart.

You see the same thing in the efficiency ratio from 53.8% a year ago to 42.4% today, five consecutive quarters of improvement. This is Kev doing what Kev is supposed to do. With that, let me hand over to Danilo Caffaro, our Executive Vice President of Consumer Banking, who will give you more detail on the growth of our credit portfolio. Danilo, over to you.

Danilo Caffaro: Thank you, Eduardo, and good evening, everyone. This quarter is above all a story of consistent execution. The credit strategy we have been sharing with you over the last quarters remains the same, and it keeps delivering. We continue to grow fast, and we continue to grow in the right places. Lower-risk products and clients, we already know well. Let me start with the big picture. Our total credit portfolio reached BRL 35 billion, up 10% quarter-over-quarter and 88% year-over-year. We added more than BRL 3 billion in a single quarter. Total loan origination was BRL 5.9 billion, 2.5x what we originated a year ago and in line with last quarter. That stability is a choice.

We are allocating origination to products with better risk-adjusted returns, mainly private payroll, while keeping unsecured personal loans disciplined. On cards, PicPay card TPV reached BRL 21.4 billion, up 10% in the quarter and 44% year-over-year. We keep gaining share. We now hold 1.76% of the market's card TPV, up from 1.3% a year ago. Now where is this growth coming from? This bridge makes it very clear. Of the BRL 3.1 billion we added this quarter, 93% came from two sources: Secured and partially secured loans and mature credit cards. Private payroll alone added BRL 1.9 billion. Cards for clients who have been with us for more than 12 months added another BRL 1.5 billion. That is our playbook.

We extend more credit once clients have shown us how they behave, mostly through limit increases for mature cohorts. Meanwhile, FGTS and public payroll were roughly flat and unsecured personal loans declined slightly by design. As a result, about 54% of our book is secured or partially secured, a mix we are keeping stable as we scale. Let me spend a moment on private payroll because it is the clearest example of what our platform can do. A year ago, this portfolio was BRL 1.5 billion. Today, it is BRL 9 billion. That is up 25% in the quarter and more than 6x year-over-year.

We originated around BRL 3.5 billion in the quarter alone, and our market share went from 2.4% a year ago to 7.3% in September, and this growth is profitable. The product runs at a marginal ROE above 80%. Payroll clients generate 8.6x the revenue of our average client and 67% of these contracts come with an insurance policy. On risk, we are well diversified across more than 370,000 employers with no meaningful concentration in any single company or sector. First payment defaults averaged around 7.8% in the second quarter, and we monitor every cohort closely month by month. We have now issued 5 million contracts since launch.

Every one of them helps us know the client better and serve them across other products. That is the flywheel we are building. To sum up, consistent execution, a credit book that keeps growing quickly, mostly through secured products and clients we know with disciplined underwriting and strong returns. With that, I will hand it over to Andre Cazotto, who will cover our financial results, asset quality and capital.

Andre Cazotto: Thank you, Danilo. Moving to the next slide. Let me walk you through the evolution of our delinquent metrics and explain the dynamics behind these curves. On the left, early NPL, which are loans between 15 and 90 days past due, it rose to 9.2% from 7.5% in the second quarter. Two things explain this movement. First, portfolio aging, which added 127 basis points, reflecting the natural aging of our portfolio, particularly in private payroll loans. And second, the Desenrola program, which added 118 basis points. The Desenrola effect comes from clients who renegotiated their debt under the program in the second quarter but did not keep up with their new installments.

Because the renegotiated contracts move out of the 90 days plus bucket, these clients now show up again in early NPL. Excluding the Desenrola effect, early NPL would have been 8% in the quarter, and we expect it to come back to 7.9% by the end of the year. This shows the stability of this metric over the last 18 months, which has remained in a range between 7.5% and 8.5% since the third quarter of 2025. NPL over 90 days reached 10.7%, up from 9.8% in the second quarter. The increase in NPL over 90 days is primarily a function of portfolio aging, which added 307 basis points.

As our vintages mature, a larger share of the book naturally migrates into larger stages of delinquency. This is a mechanical expected dynamic for a portfolio that has grown as fast as ours, no sign of deterioration. We expect NPL over 90 days to reach 12.7% by the end of the year. These NPL metrics reflect our current 360-day write-off policy. And in a few slides, I will walk you through the new write-off policy we will implement starting next quarter. Stage 3 formation came in at 4.6% in the third quarter compared to 3.6% in the second quarter. As we explained last quarter, the second quarter figure benefited from the Desenrola renegotiated program.

And excluding that effect, stage 3 formation would have been around 4%. The third quarter level, therefore, reflects the normalization of this one-off benefit, combined with the natural aging of the portfolio and our deliberate strategy of intentional risk taken in private payroll loans, the increase in our Stage 2 portfolio was also partially driven by a higher portion of customers enrolling in the Desenrola program, who had already exceeded our 360-day write-off threshold. As these customers entered the renegotiated program, their previously writing off exposures were restated in our balance sheet, contributing to both Stage 3 formation and the overall Stage 3 outstanding balance.

Importantly, this effect reflects the reactivation of previously written off exposures through renegotiations, rather than a deterioration in the underlying credit quality of our performing portfolio. Now moving to the next slide on coverage. Stage 3 closed the quarter at 71.9% versus 74.1% in the second quarter. The reduction in stage 3 coverage is primarily related to the Desenrola program. Loans renegotiated under the program benefit from an FGO guarantee, the operations guarantee fund covering 50% of the outstanding exposure. This increases expected recovery and lowers the LGD of those loans. So they carry lower provisioning needs and mechanically reduce the overall stage 3 coverage ratio. It's a mix effect not changing provisioning standards or in risk appetite.

Excluding this effect, stage 3 coverage would be 76.4% in the quarter. Moving to financial margin. Net interest income reached BRL 2.2 billion, up 9% quarter-over-quarter and 70% year-over-year. To deep dive into our margin dynamics, we are now also showing our net interest margin with clients which measures the margin generated by the financial products we offer to our clients, excluding the effect of our treasury and cash position. Net interest margin with clients remained stable at 27.3% in the third quarter compared to 27.4% in the previous quarter. Our consolidated net interest margin came in at 18.8% compared to 19.4% in the second quarter.

This movement mainly reflects a larger share of cash in our balance sheet following the market funding transactions we completed during the quarter, including the promissory notes and debt security issuances. These resources earning a lower yield than our credit portfolio, so they temporarily dilute the consolidated margin. As this liquidity is deployed into credit, we expect this effect to normalize. Margin of credit products reached BRL 2.3 billion, growing 9% sequentially and 81% year-over-year.

As a reminder, this metric captures the full economic contribution of our credit operations, including revenues from products directly tied to credit origination such as credit card interchange and credit insurance, while excluding cash remuneration and derivative revenues, providing a more complete view of the true margin generated by our lending activity. Net interest margin from credit products came in at 27.2% compared to 27.8% in the quarter. Equally important, margin from credit products after losses crossed the BRL 1 billion mark for the first time, up 11% quarter-over-quarter and 60% year-over-year. The net interest margin after losses remained broadly stable at 12%.

Moving to the next slide, provisioning continues to scale with the portfolio, while cost of risk remains under control. Credit loss allowance expenses reached BRL 1.3 billion in the quarter, up 8% quarter-over-quarter. Quarterly cost of risk came in at 3.8%, down from 3.9% in the second quarter and below the low end of the 3.9% to 4.1% guidance range we provided at the beginning of the quarter. Total portfolio coverage reached 14.9%, an increase of 100 basis points from 13.9% in the previous quarter and the highest level in the series. Moving to funding on the next slide. Our total funding base grew 15% quarter-over-quarter reaching BRL 43.7 billion in the third quarter, up year-over-year.

At the same time, our cost of funding improved to 95.5% of CDI from 96.2% in the second quarter. An important driver of this improvement is the strong growth in consumer deposits. As we become the primary financial relationship for more of our clients, a larger share of their income and day-to-day balances stays with PicPay. This gives us a growing base of granular stable and lower cost funding supports a structurally more efficient funding cost over time. During the quarter, we also continued to execute our funding diversification strategy, raising approximately through the promissory notes and debt security issuances we completed in July and August.

These transactions were fully swapped into local currency, so we have no FX exposure from them. They add to our creditor fund structures, consumer deposits and third-party platforms. Together, these sources further strengthened our balance sheet and enhanced our capacity to sustain the rapid growth of our credit portfolio in a disciplined and cost-efficient manner. Moving to profitability. Adjusted net income reached BRL 271 million in the third quarter, up 157% year-over-year with an annualized adjusted ROE of 18.5%. The 4% sequential decline is fully explained by the tax effect we anticipated in our last call. In the second quarter, we recognized a tax benefit under Brazil's Lei do Bem, which supports investments in research, development and technological innovation.

This is a recurring benefit for the year but it was recognized only in the second quarter, which positively impacted our results and adjusted ROE in that period. In the third quarter, our effective tax rate normalized in line with what we had guided. At the pretax level, adjusted earnings before taxes grew 33% quarter-over-quarter, which better reflects the underlying momentum of our business. Moving to the next slide. I would like to talk about Kev, which includes its insurance and brokerage businesses and adds new growth streams to the group. Written premiums reached BRL 939 million in the third quarter, up 14% quarter-over-quarter and 62% year-over-year.

Since the closing of the acquisition in August, Kev generated BRL 56.3 million in gross profit, BRL 6.4 million in earnings before taxes and BRL 4.5 million in net income for August and September. It's important to note that this is the first time we are reporting Kev's results under IFRS and these figures still reflect accounting adjustments related to the conversion of Kev's financial statements to this methodology. They are not directly comparable to Kev's historical results under local accounting standards. In addition, Kev's contribution to our consolidated results is affected by the elimination of intercompany transactions between Kev and PicPay, which I will explain in more details on the next slide.

On the next slide, present our consolidated results by entity. PicPay stand-alone generated BRL 367 million in earnings before taxes and Kev added BRL 6 million. On a consolidated basis, earnings before taxes reached BRL 290 million, and adjusted net income reached BRL 223 million. The difference comes from consolidation, elimination adjustments of BRL 83 million at the pretax level or BRL 52 million at the net income level related to intercompany transactions. On a stand-alone basis, PicPay recognizes its credit insurance commissions upfront. At the moment, the loan is originated, while Kev recognizes the related costs and revenues on a deferred basis over the lifetime of the contract.

On consolidation, we eliminate PicPay's upfront revenue, but only the portion of Kev's cost that has already been amortized, which creates a negative effect in the period. It's important to highlight that this is a timing effect, not an economic loss, with no cash impact. The amount eliminated today will be recognized in our consolidated results over the lifetime of the contracts. As the book of contract matures, the amortization of earlier policies will increasingly offset the elimination of new upfront commissions. And this effect will normalize over time.

In addition, now that we manage our insurance operation as a single business from distribution at PicPay to underwriting at Kev, we are evaluating adjustments to the commission structure between the two companies, which could further reduce this effect. On capital side, we closed the quarter with a total capital ratio of 15% and a common equity Tier 1 ratio of 13%. And both including the excess capital held at our holding company in the Netherlands. The sequential reduction mainly reflects the closing of the Kev acquisition in August, which had 180 basis points impact on our capital ratio. Moving to the next slide.

Starting the fourth quarter of 2026, we will refine our write-off policy exclusively for our unsecured personal loans portfolio, reducing the write-off period from 360 to 120 days past due. This change is strictly limited to this portfolio with all other credit products, maintaining their existing 360-day write-off policy. The primary rationale behind this change is to ensure that our reported asset quality metrics, particularly NPL over 90 days better reflect the underlying performance of our credit portfolio by mitigating the impact of portfolio aging on reported indicators. This is particularly relevant for a fast-growing credit platform like PicPay where portfolio growth and aging dynamics can significantly influence reported asset quality trends.

This refinement also brings a write-off policy closer to industry practices, including Nubank, which we consider a relevant benchmark given the similarities in customer profiles and unsecured lending products. Importantly, this is not a response to credit deterioration or changes in market conditions. Our credit portfolio remains healthy with underlying asset quality trends performing in line with our expectations. The change does not affect our underwriting standards, risk appetite, collection strategy or recovery efforts. It's also purely an accounting effect with no impact on our cash position. We will continue pursuing recoveries on written-off loans through our existing collection process. Turning to the financial implications.

We expect the implementation of the new policy in the fourth quarter '26 to result in a onetime negative impact of approximately BRL 325 million on our quarterly earnings. In terms of the asset quality metrics, considering the 120-day write-off policy for unsecured personal loans and the 360-day policy maintaining for all other products, we expect our consolidated NPL over 90 days ratio to reach approximately 6.8% in the fourth quarter of 2026, reflecting the mechanical reduction in older delinquent exposures following the policy change. Looking at the breakdown, NPL over 90 days for our unsecured personal loans portfolio stabilizes earlier and at a slightly lower level than the consolidated ratio.

As the portfolio continues to grow and age, we expect our consolidated NPL over 90 days ratio to progressively normalize at around 9% from the second quarter of 2027 onwards, a level where we expect it to stabilize. This trajectory is mainly driven by the aging of our private payroll loans portfolio, which maintains the 360-day policy. From a capital perspective, we expected an associated of approximately 150 basis points on our regulatory capital ratio. Importantly, this impact is already incorporated into our capital planning and does not change our expectations for credit portfolio growth or capital requirements in 2027.

Looking ahead, even after absorbing the impact of the write-off policy change in the fourth quarter, we expect to close the year with a total capital ratio between 13% and 13.5%. And a common equity Tier 1 ratio between 11% and 11.5%. These levels are comfortably above the regulatory minimum of 8.5%, which already includes the conservation buffer and give us the flexibility to continue our growth trajectory in 2027. In addition, with our adjusted ROE nearing 20% and expect it to keep growing over time we have a tremendous capacity to generate capital organically to support our growth. With that, I will now hand the call back to Eduardo Chedid, who will present our guidance and his final remarks.

Eduardo Simoes: Thank you, Andre, and thank you, Danilo. Let me close with our guidance for the fourth quarter and the full year, and then a final few remarks. As in previous quarters, our guidance is for PicPay on a stand-alone basis, excluding Kev so that it is directly comparable with what we gave you in August. For the fourth quarter, under our current write-off policy, we expect the credit portfolio to reach BRL 37.1 billion, managerial revenues of approximately BRL 4.2 billion, net interest income of BRL 2.25 billion and gross profit of BRL 1.33 billion. Quarterly cost of risk should remain between 3.7% and 3.9%.

On that basis, adjusted earnings before taxes should be around BRL 466 million and adjusted net income, around BRL 334 million. As Andre explained, in the fourth quarter, we will also move our unsecured personal loan book to 120-day write-off. We are therefore showing you the full year on both basis, the current policy and the new one, so that you can see exactly what changes and what does not. What does not change revenues and net interest income. Under either policy, we expect managerial revenues of roughly BRL 15.2 billion for the year and net interest income of BRL 8.1 billion. What changes is the time of provisions.

And here, I want to pause on the first column for a moment. Under the current policy, we expect full year adjusted net income of approximately BRL 1.06 billion, and IFRS net income of approximately BRL 1 billion. For a company that reported its first full year of profit in 2023, crossing BRL 1 billion of net income in a single year is a milestone. It reflects what this business is now capable of generating and that earning power does not change with the accounting policy. Under the new policy, the same year shows approximately BRL 733 million of adjusted net income.

The difference being the onetime charge of approximately BRL 325 million recognized in the fourth quarter that Andre described. The credit portfolio closes the year at BRL 34.6 billion as loans passed 120 days are removed from the balance sheet. Beyond 2026, as Andre noted, we expect NPL over 90 days to stabilize at around 9% in the second half of 2027. Before we open for questions, let me put two items from this call in context. The first is Kev. We are very pleased with this acquisition and more confident in it today than when we signed. The reason is simple. Insurance is one of the most natural products to distribute inside an ecosystem like ours.

We already have 11 million active policies in the PicPay base, growing 39% a year. Kev brings the underwriting, the product capability and a solid pipeline of other distribution partners. It wrote BRL 939 million in premiums this quarter, up 62%. Putting distribution and underwriting in under one roof is what makes this a new engine for the group. As Andre explained, in these first months, the elimination of intercompany commissions reduces our consolidated results. That is a timing effect with no cash impact. as the book of contracts matures, the amortization of earlier policies increasingly offset the elimination of new ones, and we expect this effect to reverse over the course of 2027. The second is the write-off policy.

We're moving our unsecured personal loan book to 120 day write-off because a portfolio that has grown as fast as ours carries aging effects that make our reported NPL harder to read than it should be. The new policy reduces that distortion and it puts our asset quality metrics on the same basis as Nubank's, which we see as the relevant benchmark for this product. I want to be clear that this has nothing to do with any deterioration in asset quality. Cost of risk is at the low end of our range. Underlying trends are in line with our expectations, and we remain confident in our ability to keep expanding the credit portfolio in 2027.

With that in context, here's what I think this quarter tells you about PicPay. It tells you the model scales. Revenue per client up 58% and cost to serve up 20%. Efficiency ratio down 11 points in a year with AI adoption across operations becoming an increasingly important lever. It also tells you the model is diversified. 73% of our revenues comes from sources with lower or no credit risk, which is what allows us to grow credit with discipline. And it tells you the model is predictable, 9 guidance metrics, 9 beats. A full year outlook, we are confident enough to give you under the two accounting policies at once.

And on the underlying basis, our first year with more than BRL 1 billion of net income. Growth with discipline is what we set out to build. This quarter is what that looks like in practice. A larger ecosystem, a more efficient company and a credit business growing in a way we can forecast and explain. Thank you for your time and for your trust. Andre, Danilo and I are now happy to take your questions. Operator, please open the line.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from the line of Gustavo Schroden from Citi.

Gustavo Schroden: Congrats on the solid growth. Now let me explore this move from 360-day to 120-day write-off policy. So my first question here is why now? I think it is important you explain us why are you changing the debt at this moment? And also, we should expect some improvement in reported NPLs numbers as we show it that should go down to around 6%, if I'm not wrong, considering your slides. But it is stabilizing in 2027 onwards. So what are the key assumptions behind that stabilization?

So more specifically, if we look through both the accounting change and the increased contribution from payroll and other secured loans, does management believe the unsecured portfolio has already reached this steady-state loss profile? Or should we still expect further normalization in underlying credit performance over the next few quarters?

Andre Cazotto: Thanks, Gustavo. It's Andre here. Thanks for your question. So starting with the first part of the question, why now? It's because now we have history to support this change. We have a much more mature origination business here at PicPay. So we have more history, we have more data, and we have a book that continues to scale and season for us to see how our portfolio actually is performing over its full time and how well our indicators really represent the quality of the assets.

So at the end of the day, I think that our main goal with this change is to make sure that our reported asset quality metrics, especially the overnight days are reflecting the real underlying performance of our portfolio and not just how old it's getting, right? Because for a fast-growing credit platform like us, it's really important. If you take a look at the older policy under 136 days, the NPLs over 90 days continues to carry balances, there are almost a year past due. So the metric keeps going up as the book is aging, right? Even when the credit is performing in line with our expectations.

So under 360 days, you can see that the line just keeps climbing, right? So the change to 120 days significantly reduces these aging effect on our reported metrics. In terms of the level that we are achieving, first of all, we're going to see that metric going to 6.8% in Q4 and should stabilize at around 9% from the second quarter 2027 onwards. Very important to break down here because the unsecured book will stabilize even earlier at slight lower level than we have in the consolidated number that is 9%. So what is basically driving the consolidated ratio to around 9% is the aging of the private payroll loan, which stays at 360 days policy.

Gustavo Schroden: I see. I see. If I may be still on that, you presented that you were expecting a BRL 325 million one-off impact in the fourth quarter and also an impact in 150 basis points on capital. Could you explain us from or the nature of this impact where this impact is coming from?

Andre Cazotto: All right. So just to be precise here, Gustavo, BRL 325 million is the impact on the net income after taxes in the fourth quarter. So it's a onetime effect. There is no cash effect. It's just an accounting effect here. So basically, the loans that were already largely provisioned and the BRL 325 million is essentially the remaining portfolio. So what we are doing, we're bringing forward the recognition of the losses that under the 360-day policy would be gone through our P&L over the coming quarters anyway. In terms of the capital effect, it's exactly what we said. We're expecting around 150 basis impact because the accounting losses reduces the equity, but that's already in our capital plan.

We still expect to close the year with a total capital ratio between 13% to 13.5%.

Gustavo Schroden: Okay. So just to summarize, you are changing because now you have more data and you have, let's say, a relevant book to change? Are you still comfortable with asset quality metrics to keep growing at the same pace, right?

Andre Cazotto: Correct, Gustavo. And there's also a second point here that is the comparability, right? Because this change in the write-off policy is bringing us much closer to Nubank. That is our main benchmark given that we have a very similar client and product profile. So it becomes much easier to put it side by side.

Andre Cazotto: Thanks for your question. Basically, the calculation that reaches 11% to 11.5% in common equity Tier 1 is including the excess capital at the holding in the Netherlands that we can bring down to the operating entity at any time. So just to summarize what happened in the quarter, so we closed the quarter at 15% total capital ratio and 13% common equity Tier 1. The Kev acquisition took about 180 basis points. So we finalized it, let's say, the third quarter with the total capital ratio, including the excess capital that we have in the Netherlands around 13% -- sorry, 15%, and the common equity Tier 1 ratio around 13%.

So considering now that the write-off change should bring like 150 basis points impact in our total capital we're expecting to finalize the year considering the excess capital that we have in the Netherlands, around 13% to 13.5% and the common Tier 1 between 11% to 11.5%. So we feel comfortable with this level. Our plan for 2027 growth. It's basically funded with the capital that we had plus organic generation as we are -- adjusted ROEs are near to 20% and growing. We also have, let's say, other to optimize capital, if it makes sense. For example, you saw in previous quarters that we had portfolio securitization like we did a few times with our FGTS-backed loans.

So it could be another optimization, not necessarily a need.

Mario Pierry: Okay. So basically, then you're saying that this excess capital is going to be moved to the...

Mario Pierry: And just to be clear, this capital is invested is it in dollars today? Or what currency is it?

Andre Cazotto: Yes. Yes. It's in dollars.

Eduardo Simoes: Basically, the -- remember that the proceeds of the IPO, so in U.S. dollars that we can bring back to Brazil.

Mario Pierry: Okay. All right. And then my second question is related to Kev, right? Like as you show like a net income of like about $4 million -- BRL 4 million. And then a negative contribution of BRL 52 million for the consolidated, right? So my question is this BRL 5 million on a stand-alone seems a little bit lower than what we were thinking originally. Is this solely because we're talking about IFRS rather than they are GAAP.

Andre Cazotto: That's right, Mario. It's accounting of the business. So remember that we said that we were expecting Kev to contribute in a stand-alone basis between BRL 80 million to BRL 100 million, right? So those numbers that we shared before were under the IFRS 4. That's the framework that SUSEP, the Brazilian insurance regulator works with. And it's how Kev has always reported their IFRS numbers. But now that Kev is fully consolidated into our international, let's say, financial statements, we have to move to the IFRS 17, that is the current IFRS standard for insurance contracts. And basically what our auditors are requiring for the consolidation.

So just to share some additional color for Q4 on Kev contribution in a stand-alone basis under the IFRS 17. We expect Kev's stand-alone net income for the fourth quarter to be between BRL 35 million to BRL 45 million, before the consolidation adjustments. And the biggest difference that we have between the IFRS 4 and the IFRS 17 is that basically under the IFRS 4, a good part of the, let's say, revenue recognition of the policies shows up early. And on the IFRS 17, we can say that the profit on each contract, it's basically gradually released over the life of the coverage.

So these are the main changes between both methodologies, but it's just an accounting not a business. If you take a look at the total profit over the life of the contracts will not change, and there is no impact on cash or the economics of the business. But just to reiterate, considering these IFRS 17, we believe that Kev on a standalone basis and before the consolidation adjustments should contribute to something around BRL 35 million and BRL 45 million.

Mario Pierry: Okay, clear. And then on the guidance that you gave for the fourth quarter, on Page 28, right, the IFRS net income of BRL 327 million. This is excluding Kev.

Mario Pierry: Should we assume another negative impact of around BRL 50 million?

Andre Cazotto: Early to say it's going to be exactly the same BRL 50 million, but should have some negative contribution. And basically, what happens here, Mario. First of all, we're expecting to normalize that by 2027 onwards. So it's a timing effect. It's not a cash or economic loss. So what happens is that PicPay books the credit insurance commission upfront when the law is originated, and Kev basically recognized all the related cost and revenues over the lifetime of the contract. So when we consolidate both entities, we basically eliminated the PicPay full upfront revenue, but only a very small part of the Kev cost that has already been amortized. So that's what drives a negative effect.

But of course, that has come back into the results over the life of the contracts. So like I said, we're expecting that to normalize. There is a natural, let's say, maturation of the book of contracts over time. So once the amortization of the older policies, we believe that could start offsetting the elimination of new commissions, but also now that we are handling the business -- the insurance business as a single, let's say, business model from distribution on PicPay and the underwriting with that, we can also look and evaluate changes in the commission structure between the two companies. So also that could help us to reduce this negative effect faster.

So we believe that by beginning of 2027, you should expect that to normalize.

Operator: Our next question comes from Dan Dolev from Mizuho Group.

Dan Dolev: Eduardo, really nice results. Congrats. I wanted to ask you a little bit more on the AI efficiencies and the return that you've seen on those really impressive to see that and just wanted to know like how the efficiency gain results and the AI developments are helping PicPay and what else can be done in 2027 on that front?

Eduardo Simoes: Hi, Dan. This is Eduardo. There are many -- I'd say in many dimensions, we can see that happening on a day-to-day basis. And if you look at, let's say, code being shipped. We have a gain of, let's say, same developers are actually shipping around 60% more codes than before. And we also have around 30% of more people actually coding because of that, which in the end of the day, it accounts for more than 100% of productivity gains on coding itself.

Another thing that is quite important is that right now, every third-party contract, especially software contracts that we have and is due in the next months, we go through an analysis, which is can we actually do it ourselves or we want to keep buying. And either of those decisions, they come with a reduction of costs. So we've had some really, let's say, important third-party software that we've been replacing. And you can see already that in the numbers, and you will see it even more in the coming months. So there are plenty of new things happening on the let's say, productivity and cost avoidance part.

Another one is basically -- you know that we've migrated most of our customer service into AI, and it's been going on for quite a while. Basically, we're doing the same thing that we used to do by actually spending 3% of the previous cost, and we've avoided hiring an additional 3,000 customer service representatives in the last two years. And all that also in terms of token consumption, it basically went through the roof. But at the same time, we had a 98%, let's say, cost reduction on the token unit cost per token. So it means that we've been managing really well the cost of using AI as well as gaining all the productivity from it.

And besides that, basically, if you look at the let's say, the top of line and more revenues coming from that. Lots of new initiatives also with our clients. Our PicPay AI assistant, for example, and we're on the second version of it, and it includes many things that we believe that we are basically ahead of most of the -- of our peers. It's multitask. So now you can basically have a, let's say, a complex instruction like, "Hey, I need to pay all of my bills, they're due this week. I still need to keep BRL 5,000 in my wallet balance.

Please let me know which investments should withdraw money from." And then it will perform all of those tasks at once and allow you with one single command to withdraw money from the, let's say, the investments with worst yields pay for your bills as well as end up with a BRL 5,000 balance for the remaining of the month. So this is quite a different set of skills we're introducing on the small and medium businesses. For example, we've launched already an agent for marketing that basically can set up a new campaign for the small and medium businesses.

And actually, it will shoot that campaign for our more than 72 million clients and geo located as well as directly to the, let's say, the most relevant profile of customers. So many things also on the, let's say, customer side of the business. So basically, I'd say those are just a few examples of how it's basically contributing. So the top line as well as to the bottom line of the company.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our next question comes from Matthew Inglis from RBC.

Matthew Inglis: So on the private payroll loans, you have over 80% marginal return on equity with strong revenue per active compared to the broader consumer base or customer base. And you grew market share by, call it, 100 basis points quarter-over-quarter. But as more competitors enter the space, are you seeing or expecting any changes to pricing or underwriting behavior. How sustainable do you think these returns are as that portfolio matures?

Eduardo Simoes: Here. Yes, we've been seeing in the past months new competitors such as actually the Nubank and other players. But that is not a significant change in terms of pricing pressure, I would say. Again, the way we do it, we price the risk. And in our perspective, we do use the, let's say, the centralized distribution platform from the market, but also the majority of the origination comes from our own platform, our own app where there is less pressure.

Matthew Inglis: Understood. And then on the SMB side, you've seen strong merchant account adds. How is the monetization of the newer cohorts progressing, particularly as it relates to acquiring lending and even advertising? And then kind of holistically, when do you -- when does this business maybe become a bigger contributor to the total business?

Eduardo Simoes: We look at it as a -- the overall business, we look at it as a, let's say, horizon 2, which means that it's still not contributing to the bottom line, but it's picking up really well in terms of growth. So first phase, you can already see, which is more clients coming, 126,000 on average per month now. And if you look at the first half of the year, around 85,000, more usage of products. So it means that we're getting more activation as they actually get more of our products, but still cross-selling and the third wave would be credit products coming on also so that it becomes a contributor to the overall results.

I mean I'd say that if you consider the -- let's say, the early stage in which we are, we're pretty happy with the first, let's say, phase, which is attracting more and more clients and getting them to use the product so that we can start to push and cross-sell more products. It's more or less the same playbook we use on the consumer banking now being used on the small to medium businesses.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] The question-and-answer session is over. We would like to hand the floor back to Mr. Eduardo Chedid for the company's final remarks.

Eduardo Simoes: Thank you again for joining us. We keep trying to give you the best guidance we can, and delivery on those that we gave you. We did that last quarter. We remain focused on doing that from -- for the next quarter. And we'll be here for additional questions on the next interactions we have with you all. With that, we'll finalize here, and thank you again.

Operator: PicPay's conference is now closed. We thank you for your participation and wish you a nice day.

#2964. AI Is Creating A More Dynamic Future For Airline Revenue Management

The airline industry has always used technology and data to help teams make decisions that improve the customer experience or increase revenue. Today, airlines have an opportunity to automate and improve many of those decisions.

AI can help them respond more dynamically to demand, manage inventory more effectively and determine the best action to take for a particular flight or customer.

This shift is especially important after a customer has already purchased a ticket. The post-booking period has traditionally received less attention than initial pricing and sales, but it may represent one of the industry’s largest opportunities to improve both profitability and customer satisfaction.

When airlines sell all their inventory on a flight, there is very little they can do to accept additional last-minute, high-yield demand.

When a flight is full, airlines may be unable to accommodate business travelers and other passengers who really need to get on that specific flight. Those customers may then purchase tickets from a competitor, even though some passengers already booked on the original flight might have been willing to travel at another time.

A sold-out flight does not always represent the best revenue or customer outcome. The airline may still be turning away high-value demand while carrying passengers with more flexible schedules.

AI can help airlines move toward managing their inventory much more dynamically. Rather than treating a booking as final, airlines can continue evaluating demand, capacity and customer needs as departure approaches.

Post-booking optimization focuses on what happens after the customer has purchased a ticket.

Historically, customers could keep their itinerary, cancel without a refund or receive a credit. Airlines had limited ability to create better alternatives as demand changed.

AI-informed systems provide an efficient way to recapture that opportunity. Once the airline understands where that opportunity may exist, it can identify customers who could be interested in moving to another flight in exchange for an incentive, such as a travel voucher.

That voluntary change frees inventory for passengers who need the peak flight, allowing the airline to capture incremental demand while offering flexible customers more options.

The goal is not simply to move people from one flight to another. It is to optimize revenues and load factors at the same time while giving customers more flexibility.

Making this model work requires airlines to understand two things.

The first is which flights are likely to sell out and overflow high-yield demand. Predictive models can anticipate where that opportunity will appear.

The second is the willingness to change and the flexibility of individual customers. Using different features associated with each booking, AI can help estimate which passengers may be open to moving and what the right offer for each customer might be.

This allows the airline to maximize both conversion and revenue per transaction. Rather than sending the same incentive to everyone, the airline can make a more relevant offer based on the context of the booking and the customer’s likely preferences.

AI-driven optimization should give passengers a clear, voluntary choice and something valuable in exchange for changing their itinerary.

When done correctly, post-booking optimization can create what I see as a win-win-win situation.

The first winner is the customer who needs to purchase a ticket on a particular flight. By creating available inventory, the airline can allow that passenger to get onto the flight they really need instead of losing them to a competitor.

The second winner is the flexible customer, who voluntarily switches flights in exchange for an incentive they consider worthwhile.

The third winner is the airline. It can improve customer satisfaction while also generating a revenue uplift and making better use of its available capacity.

The incremental profit can be significant, and implementation may require relatively few resources. Airlines can introduce targeted capabilities and begin seeing results within months.

Post-booking optimization is part of a broader opportunity for AI across the customer journey.

Conversational AI, including large language models, can help airlines improve customer satisfaction and become more efficient. Unlike a traditional call center, an AI-supported system is not limited by the number of agents available to have conversations with customers.

However, the greatest opportunity is not simply creating a conversational user experience. Airlines should connect that experience to an intelligence or context layer that can determine the best offer or decision for each customer.

A call center employee may be working with a limited amount of information. An intelligent system can consider millions of data points and a much broader context before recommending an action.

The result is a more efficient and intelligent interaction that identifies the best decision and most relevant offer at that moment in the journey.

For decades, airlines have often lagged behind online travel agencies and other retailers in their retailing capabilities. AI creates an opportunity to accelerate the process of closing that gap.

By building or accessing the right knowledge, intelligence and context layers, airlines can orchestrate decisions in real time across the customer journey. They can become much better retailers while improving both the customer experience and profitability.

Every relevant technology change creates winners and losers. The speed at which companies embrace new technologies often helps define which category they enter.

We saw this with the internet and online sales, which transformed airline retailing and contributed to the rise of low-cost carriers. AI may create a similar dividing line over the next several years.

The airlines that succeed will not necessarily be the ones that deploy AI everywhere at once. They will be the ones that identify the decisions where intelligence can create real value and move quickly enough to capture the opportunity. Post-booking optimization is one of those decisions, and it illustrates how the industry can become more dynamic, flexible and profitable.​​
