#2962. Iran escalates threats as third U.S. carrier arrives in Middle East, tanker struck in Hormuz

Iran has ratcheted up threats against U.S. forces and commercial shipping as a third American aircraft carrier arrived in the Gulf, stoking fears of renewed escalation in the nine-month conflict.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy warned shipping companies against using the U.S.-backed southern route through the Strait of Hormuz, describing it as fully closed and a "minefield of fire," according to regional media outlets citing a statement from the force.

Brig. Gen. Mohammad Akrami-Nia, a spokesperson for the Iranian Army, said the Strait of Hormuz would not reopen until "the enemy accepts Iran's conditions."

Separately, CNN reported Monday that new U.S. intelligence indicated Iran was developing plans that could target senior Trump administration officials with a so-called dirty bomb, or a chemical weapon in Washington, D.C. CNBC cannot immediately verify the report.

The intelligence was characterized as an effort by Iran to develop options rather than evidence of an imminent attack, CNN reported. U.S. officials have held several meetings over the past week to consider how to respond to the potential threat.

The heightened security concerns come after Iranian threats prompted Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to relocate to military housing last week.

"We remain vigilant, monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland," a White House spokesperson said in a statement to CNBC.

Oil prices inched lower in Asian trading Tuesday, with international benchmark Brent crude futures dropping 0.7% to $91.8 a barrel and U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures falling 0.7% to $85.1 a barrel.

On Tuesday, the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations said a tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile in the Strait of Hormuz and subsequently caught fire. The agency did not say who was responsible and urged vessels to transit with caution and report suspicious activity.

Separately, the Iranian navy said four oil tankers had struck mines and caught fire in the eastern Strait of Hormuz over the previous 24 hours.

The escalation in Tehran's rhetoric came as the USS Theodore Roosevelt arrived in the Gulf region on Sunday, joining the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington. That added to U.S. firepower near Iran even as President Donald Trump said the war was winding down.

Trump has sent mixed signals regarding the conflict in recent weeks, alternating between declaring it could soon end and warning of renewed large-scale strikes if efforts to reach a deal fail.

After meeting Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani last week, Trump said the war with Iran could end "fairly soon," adding that it "militarily is effectively over."

Tehran said Sunday that it launched six drones at a U.S. air-defense radar at Bahrain's Riffa air base, the second attack Iran claimed against the kingdom in three days. Bahrain's military said it intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned the attacks in a call Monday with Bahraini Foreign Minister Abdullatif bin Rashid Al Zayani and reaffirmed Washington's commitment to the security of Bahrain and other Gulf partners.

The conflict began in late February when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran, prompting Tehran to retaliate with strikes on Israel and Gulf states hosting American military bases. Indirect talks between Washington and Tehran through Qatar have since appeared to run into a stalemate as warring powers disagreed over terms to reach a lasting peace deal.

Washington appears unwilling to accept several of Iran's demands to end the war, including lifting the U.S. naval blockade on its southern ports and lifting sanctions, while stressing that Iran cannot possess a nuclear weapon.

Iran is likely to continue escalating attacks on tankers and container ships, along with occasional strikes on U.S. military targets, in an effort to pressure Washington into offering concessions, said Ian Bremmer, president and founder of Eurasia Group. In response, Washington will likely expand its blockade on Iran's maritime and inland trade routes, he said.

"The presumption is that eventually Iran can't handle the economic pressure and will accept better terms," Bremmer said, calling that view a "misread of the Iranian leadership and their capacity to resist."

Over the coming year, Iran is likely to intensify efforts to disrupt shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, Bremmer said.

#2960. PowerCompute: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Its hardware refresh and HPC tests will determine whether margins hold once capital returns to miners.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 13, 2026, PowerCompute (PWCM +3.12%) announced that it mined 36% more Bitcoin year over year. For long-term investors, lower mining costs and reduced debt levels dictate whether the company can compound capital over time. Three things management said stand out.

PowerCompute cut its energy cost to mine one Bitcoin from about $58,000 to $35,000 through energy sales and site curtailment, which means shutting down miners during peak-price periods. This operational flexibility allowed mining margins to exceed 50% despite lower average cryptocurrency prices.

Management reduced secured debt from $19.4 million to $1.25 million, thereby reducing annual interest expense to $138,000. Settling loan facilities also removed all pledges on the company's 63.8 Bitcoins and restored full control over its digital asset reserve.

The company is testing high-performance computing, or HPC, by listing GPU capacity at its Oklahoma site on Vast.ai. While HPC requires dedicated hardware, management sees it as a way to maximize returns on its 26 megawatts of power capacity.

Mining output is expanding as updated hardware replaces older machines across existing facilities. Owned power infrastructure and low utility rates protect margins, allowing management to focus on capital allocation.

Execution hinges on completing hardware refreshes and maintaining strict cost discipline. Management is focused on directing its power capacity toward the workloads that deliver the highest long-term returns.

#2959. Anthropic IPO: For hundreds of billions of dollars flowing into AI startups, a big debut is a must

Artificial intelligence has propelled big gains in venture capital funds this year, and a flood of money — over $350 billion — into AI startups. Venture funds were up close to 18% through the first half of 2026, with 86% of U.S.-based VC investor money going into AI companies. With Anthropic set to make its public market debut this week at a reported valuation of $1.4 trillion, the market's reception to the deal and early trading in its shares may set the tone for the next leg in the private market AI boom.

It has been a period of increased volatility for tech stocks and the public market AI trade. In addition to concerns about balance sheet strength and valuation, midterm elections showed widespread public opposition to data centers, and the CEO scandal rocking Nvidia, the "central bank" of AI financing, has compounded risks in the sector.

But on the private side of tech investing, firms are closely watching how investors react to Anthropic's IPO. "I think that will end up guiding further intentions for the VC space," said Mike McLelland, managing director of investments within private markets at Cleveland, Ohio-based Clearstead. "Once you have a couple of good exits, it gives people a little more confidence in the realization story."

Read more: Everything you need to know about the Anthropic IPO

Anthropic is getting some deep-pocketed support for the deal. Altimeter Capital is aiming to invest $5 billion, according to its founder and CEO Brad Gerstner, who noted that was five times as much as he has ever invested in an IPO. "I think this is a cornerstone compounder for a long time," Gerstner told CNBC's "Halftime Report" on Monday. "It's where the trade is going."

Chip giants Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, Nvidia, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and Micron are all investing, as are Google and Microsoft.

The direction of the IPO market is important given that companies have been staying private longer than they did in the past and strategic exits have been relatively muted, McLelland said. A notable exception is Google's $32 billion acquisition of cloud security firm Wiz. That 2025 deal was Google's largest ever, overtaking its $12.5 billion purchase of Motorola in 2012.

VC gains have been concentrated in a small number of large funds that hold the biggest AI-linked companies. MSCI reports that the 10 largest holdings make up 22% of the value of its venture index.

That concentration comes amid improved performance.

Venture capital funds returned 17.8% in the first six months of 2026, according to Opto Investments, using proprietary and MSCI Private Capital Solutions data. Venture fund portfolio data is reported by fund general partners on a delayed basis. The six-month gains would equate to a full year return as high as 38% if the pace is maintained. It comes on the heels of a recent period of underperformance for the asset class, with a 6.19% return over five years, according to Juan Mier, lead analyst of fund strategies at PitchBook. Venture's 10-year average return is 13% annually, according to PitchBook. For the year ended March 2026, venture capital delivered a nearly 22% return, driven in large part by AI valuations, Mier said.

It is not just the largest AI companies that are venture-backed and tied to the IPO performance of the giants. Thousands of smaller companies that supply AI giants with infrastructure, component manufacturing, and data services, for example, have also seen their valuations rise quickly, said Jake Miller, co-founder of New York-based Opto Investments, which helps investment advisors design private investment programs.

Notably, AI captured $355.9 billion, or 86% of U.S. venture dollars in the first half of 2026, according to Clearstead analysis of PitchBook data. Globally, AI deal value reached $521.4 billion over the trailing twelve months. That's more than double the prior year, even as AI deal count fell 21.6% from the previous quarter.

Mier said venture capital returns are expected to moderate in the third quarter as valuations in the AI space in public markets have adjusted, and that flows to private markets eventually. "That may moderate returns for the second half of the year," he said. Anthropic's deal, reported to be on target for a $1.4 trillion valuation, is well below the $2 trillion deal value originally floated by bankers.

But amid the AI proliferation, industry participants expect VC to continue piquing investors' interest in the coming years. "It's been a great place to be, and it's going to be a great place to be given the momentum of venture companies," said Jeff Masom, head of U.S. distribution and global wealth management for private markets at Franklin Templeton, which manages several private markets investments.

That said, some investors are getting more discerning. "We see those opportunities among early-stage — Seed, Series A and Series B — companies rather than trying to get in on a later-stage company at a higher price," said Opto Investments' Miller. He's looking for opportunities to buy stakes in lower-valuation companies that could climb 10 times to 20 times from their current value through an IPO or acquisition.

Private infrastructure, meanwhile, returned 4.2% over the first six months of the year, a pace of about 8.5% a year, according to Opto Investments and MSCI data. "That is close to infrastructure's 10-year average of just under 10% a year," said Miller, but good enough to be the second-best among major private fund categories through the first half of 2026, ahead of private credit (2.6%) and buyout funds (1.4%). Private credit has been hit hard by fears about lending to software companies that could be rendered uncompetitive by AI, while private equity funds have struggled to sell portfolio companies at a profit this year, with a huge backlog of portfolio holdings.

But the AI boom has also benefited investors in infrastructure funds, given the needs for power, data centers, and fiber, areas where activity has been the strongest. "It's what's been driving most of those returns in the last 18 months or so," said Uday Karri, a member of MSCI's Private Capital Research team.

A recent MSCI report on private infrastructure showed that the index returned 11.9% over the 12 months through June 2026, compared with 7.7% for the median asset. Returns are based on MSCI's asset-level index, which measures underlying asset performance before fund fees, according to a spokesperson.

There's been tremendous growth in the past few quarters within infrastructure, and there continue to be opportunities for investors in the asset class, especially in AI-ready and liquid-cooled data centers, he said. Of course, midterm elections could slow new data center development through tighter permitting and regulation. In Texas, for example, Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned on a statewide moratorium on new data center permits. Shortly after her election, the new governor stressed in an interview with CNN that the key is creating state laws that protect Texas communities, not banning data centers.

With more political pressure related to data center construction, the infrastructure sector may benefit from expected opportunities outside the AI infrastructure build-out over the next several years. "Power, grid connections, water, cooling, fiber, and permitting are likely to shape where capacity can be delivered. Shifting trade routes, geopolitical disruption, and more frequent extreme weather are supporting investment in ports, railways, intermodal terminals, cold-storage networks, and other strategic transport infrastructure," according to a report from BlackRock's Preqin division.

Legislation is also advancing that could raise project costs for the biggest data centers, but potentially have more positive impacts on broader infrastructure projects. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), a sweeping bill on energy infrastructure, is "the most comprehensive permitting bill to date," according to The Bipartisan Policy Center. If passed, it is expected to increase the speed of project permitting and reduce delays.

Here too, investors need to be discerning. "For investors, the key point is that asset selection can matter more than regional allocation. Larger portfolios can spread this dispersion across many assets and are more likely to track the index. Smaller portfolios hold fewer assets, so their results may differ materially from the index in either direction," MSCI wrote.

Private credit did perform better over the trailing 12 months ending in March, 8.3%, while real estate debt and core-plus strategies returned 7.2% and 5.1%, respectively, according to data from Preqin.

"The broader takeaway is that private markets are not moving in lockstep," Pei Yin, director at Preqin Private Markets Research, said in an email. "Venture capital has shown stronger return momentum, infrastructure continues to benefit from long-term investment themes, while private credit and selected real estate strategies have offered more income-oriented sources of return."

#2958. Robinhood shares fall as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses

Robinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.

Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.

Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity.

Robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly important sources of transaction revenue, while the company has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.

Transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million.

Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.

Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.

Net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.

—With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney

#2957. Why Nike Stock Popped Today

Nike has a plan for profit -- and investors love it.

Nike (NKE +2.43%) stock is hopping Tuesday morning, up 2.2% through 10:10 a.m. ET after the shoes and sportswear icon laid out a new five-year strategy -- and a plan to fix a stock that has underperformed the S&P 500 by 50 percentage points over the past year!

Nike calls its plan "Full Stride Ahead," and the goal is to make a giant leap in profitability -- turning around a business that earned just $2.08 per share over the past year, and delivering profits of $3 or even $3.50 per share by 2031.

How will Nike do that? As just described at its 2026 Investor Day, the plan is to invest in athlete endorsements and in bringing new products to market faster, and to cut costs to improve profits.

Nike will focus on five categories of footwear: Running, training, soccer, basketball, and outdoor. Nike expects to get more than 90% of its money from these markets in 2031. Working off a base of $42.8 billion in expected 2027 revenue, the company hopes to add $5 billion in incremental revenue by fiscal 2031. Of this, shoes will contribute an extra $4 billion, and sportswear the remaining $1 billion.

If all goes as planned, that would yield $47.8 billion in 2031 revenue.

That's the good news -- now here's the bad: According to data from S&P Global Market Intelligence, Wall Street analysts expect Nike to generate nearly $51 billion in 2031 revenue. So Nike's plan for a "turnaround" actually appears to fall short of what Wall Street hoped for, sales-wise.

On the plus side, however, Nike was only expected to earn $2.95 per share in 2031. From that perspective, Nike's promise to earn $3, or even $3.50 in 2031, represents more profit than Wall Street was betting on.

I think this, in a nutshell, is the reason Nike stock is up today -- and why, if Nike can deliver, Nike stock might keep on racing ahead.

#2956. Roth 401(k) matches are 'surging,' report finds. What workers should know

Many more workers can now or will soon be able to accept a 401(k) match as a Roth contribution — giving them a new avenue to build a bucket of tax-free savings for retirement.

Historically, workers could only accept 401(k) match money from an employer as pretax, meaning they had to defer income taxes on those funds until they withdrew them in retirement.

Until a recent rule change, workers generally couldn't elect to receive a match as a Roth contribution. With Roth savings, investors don't get an up-front tax break — they pay income tax on the funds now but can take out the contributions and growth tax-free in retirement.

A law known as Secure 2.0, which former President Joe Biden signed into law in 2022, gave employers the option to add a Roth match as a feature of their 401(k) plans. If a plan offers a Roth match, it's not automatic; workers must opt in.

The number of employers that now let workers accept a 401(k) match or other employer contribution as Roth savings has "surged," according to a new report from the Plan Sponsor Council of America, a trade group representing employers.

About 42% of surveyed businesses that sponsored a 401(k) plan in 2025 have added or will add an option to accept employer contributions as Roth savings, according to an annual PSCA report published Nov. 10. That's more than double the share — about 20% — that did so in 2024, the report found.

Another 11% are still considering the option, according to the report.

The PSCA report is based on data from 753 employers that sponsor 401(k) plans of various sizes.

"My guess is we will continue to see [the share] increase," said Hattie Greenan, the group's research director. "Roth is becoming mainstream," she said.

But just because employees have the Roth match option available to them doesn't mean it will be their best option.

There are pros and cons to pretax and Roth savings, and the right choice can vary from person to person, financial advisors said.

"[Roth] is not a bad idea if you're not so worried about your taxes today," said Philip Chao, a certified financial planner and chief investment officer at Experiential Wealth, based in Cabin John, Maryland. "It's personal preference."

While there are ample benefits to saving at least some money as Roth funds in a 401(k), most investors opt against it.

In fact, while almost all 401(k) plans already allow workers to save part of their paychecks as a Roth contribution, only a quarter of workers actually do so, according to the PSCA report.

"The list of cons may be short for Roth 401(k)s, but missing tax deferral is a big one," according to a May article written by Fidelity, a retirement plan administrator. "When faced with a choice of paying more tax now or later, most people choose to pay later, hence the low participation rates for Roth 401(k)s."

Tax deferral has long been a "key driver" of retirement savings, Fidelity said.

Saving on a pretax basis effectively increases a worker's take-home pay. It also reduces their adjusted gross income today, and may therefore positively impact the calculation of eligibility for child tax credits, financial aid for college or federal aid, according to Fidelity.

A Fidelity example shows the financial benefit of an up-front tax break: Let's say a saver with a $75,000 annual income in the 22% federal income tax bracket makes a $400 monthly 401(k) contribution. Making the full contribution as Roth would reduce their paycheck by $400. Making the contribution into a traditional — i.e., pretax — 401(k) would reduce their paycheck by just $312.

For those who can stomach the up-front tax hit, Roth provides for powerful tax-planning opportunities in future years, according to financial advisors.

"Roth gives you a lot more flexibility at retirement," Chao said. "But you have to be OK with paying years of tax on it first. It's never something for nothing. There's always a trade-off."

For example, the government doesn't require investors to withdraw a minimum amount from Roth accounts in retirement, as it does with pretax savings. These annual "required minimum distributions," or RMDs, generally start at age 73 for traditional 401(k)s and IRAs, among other accounts.

Additionally, withdrawing money from Roth accounts in retirement can help limit taxes on Social Security benefits and reduce Medicare premiums, which are based on taxable income. Roth withdrawals don't count as taxable income.

Retirees can also make strategic withdrawals from Roth accounts in certain years to avoid jumping into a higher federal or state income tax bracket, advisors said.

"Once you pay the taxes [on a Roth contribution], the government is out of your hair," Chao said. "There's no amount you must draw out. It's your money; it's all tax-free when you take it out."

For example, many investors must wait until at least age 59 1/2 to withdraw funds tax-free from a Roth 401(k) account. Additionally, due to a so-called five-year rule, investors must have had Roth 401(k) funds for at least five years to make a tax-free withdrawal.

Because Roth employer matching contributions are included in the saver's income, investors should ensure they have enough tax withheld from their paycheck to cover the income tax, according to Fidelity.

The ultimate goal for savers choosing whether to make Roth or pretax contributions is to pay income taxes when their tax rate is lowest, advisors said.

For example, Roth savings can work well for younger savers over the long term if they anticipate their incomes — and tax rates — will grow over time, said Andrew Bachman, director of tax and retirement income on Fidelity's financial solutions team.

Similar logic applies to people who plan to move from a low-tax to a high-tax state in retirement, such as from Texas to California, he said.

While it's impossible to know future tax rates, investors can hedge by splitting contributions between both types of accounts, advisors said.

Similar to contributions, workers may be able to split a 401(k) match between pretax and Roth savings. However, workers will be constrained by what their employer does and doesn't allow, Chao said.

#2955. Contango (CTGO) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Exploration spending and diesel costs weighed on third-quarter results.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Contango Silver & Gold Inc. (CTGO +2.94%) reported a net loss for the third quarter as it increased exploration activity and transitioned mining operations at its Manh Choh joint venture. Management reported that high exploration expenditures across three major projects drove the loss while production results were affected by seasonal rains and mill maintenance. The company is focusing on debt repayment and the elimination of gold hedge contracts by mid-2027 while advancing resources at its Kitsault Valley and Lucky Shot properties. Management indicated that future growth will rely on high-grade deposits and a direct shipping ore model to minimize capital requirements for new production facilities.

Romeo Maione: I'll start with a couple of just brief housekeeping notes. I want to welcome everybody to today's event. [Operator Instructions] But I'll now formally announce as we've got gotten started. I've got with me today as CEO, Rick Van Nieuwenhuyse of Contango Silver and Gold and the company's CFO, Michael Clark. Gentlemen, how are you today?

Rick Van Nieuwenhuyse: Well, I have to say, hanging in there is a good term probably.

Romeo Maione: And let's get right into that actually because I want to deal with it pretty much upfront. I don't want that sitting around in the comments. Stock obviously fell close to 10% on Friday, on 2x normal volume. It is down a bit today as well. One thing I noticed the release mentioned that $75 million at the market program under the company's shelf. And I saw some of the most well-traveled AI summaries of the release are telling people Contango is doing a financing. So let me just ask you in plain terms, what is the shelf and is Contango doing a financing right now?

Rick Van Nieuwenhuyse: Yes. I'll have Mike jump in here in a while to explain in more detail what the shelf is, but let me make it very, very clear. We are not doing a $75 million financing. What we have as a shelf at an ATM and at the market transaction that allows you to issue shares. It doesn't guarantee that you issue shares, it doesn't obligate to issue shares. So shelf is something you put in place to -- when you want to go raise money -- when you want to go raise money, the shelf is there to have them be free trading at the outcome. The ATM does not obligate you to issue shares.

Having a shelf is what normal companies do. They last for 3 years. They get renewed. This is part of that standard process. So AI is a great thing and can do a lot of things, but it also does get stuff wrong sometimes. But if that's -- if that's the news that's out there, that's just categorically wrong. We are not doing a $75 million financing. You want to have an ATM available to use opportunistically if you see an opportunity to acquire something or to do something and you don't want to use your normal cash. That's what that is. It's a flexible instrument. It's a great instrument, but it doesn't obligate you to do a financing.

And again, I'll probably repeat this 10 times we are not doing a $75 million financing. We don't need it. We've got debt to pay off. That's probably the most important thing that's due in 2 tranches in March and in June. Then we're hedged free and debt free. That has always been our objective from the beginning when we had to put the hedges in place to build Manh Choh. Look Manh Choh is still putting out a lot of cash. And we always said this year was the slow year in terms of cash flow and in terms of production in the mine plan. We had a 5-year mine plan.

2026 was always the year that we're going to see the lowest production and the highest cost. Now the cost has certainly been exacerbated to the upside because of diesel price mainly. But we're still making positive cash flow. We're paying -- continuing to pay down debt and continue to operate the company in a prudent manner. And part of that prudent manner is having a shelf in place that gives us flexibility.

Romeo Maione: Great. I hope the AI summaries of this event pick up no $75 million financing, certainly. But I'll ask just generally, Rick, I know I've used unlike AI -- what do you think generally of people using AI summaries of news releases because obviously, they got it wrong in this case.

Rick Van Nieuwenhuyse: Yes. I mean, look, I use it as well. I use it to take a look at -- I see an interesting press release on our company and I'll often use AI as a deeper dive. I've also -- we've also been at conferences where people have used AI and then have a series of questions that they want to ask based on AI summaries. And some of those -- some of the questions are based on information that's accurate and -- but some are not. And the advice I give people using AI to investigate anything, whether it's a mining company or anything, is ask specific questions.

And the more information you can input the better AI is going to do in terms of output. If you just ask AI, a, is Contango a good mining company or a good investment for gold or whatever. The more general you are with your questions in AI, the worse the outcome. It is grabbing information from everywhere and making a summary of it. And who knows, I have no idea how it decides what an answer is to a more general question. When you give it more specifics, it frames it better and getting the dialogue with it. I just ask the simple question. Question the questions -- question the answers. That's how I use it.

Romeo Maione: No, it's generally very good AI advice, I think, because if you use a general question, it takes everywhere on the Internet, and I don't know if people know this with the Internet, you can't just make stuff up. That is something that happens on equipment. Mike, I'm going to get you in here because I know the quarter showed a loss on paper, and most of that is exploration spending, which under U.S. accounting runs straight through the income statement. Can you explain how that works and what the number really reflects for the folks in the room?

J. Clark: Yes. Romeo. Yes, when I -- when you look at kind of how companies treat exploration, in Canada, you have the option to capitalize or expense. And then in the states, you are forced to expense. So many companies in Canada will just capitalize those to the balance sheet, which is a fair classification from my opinion, because you're basically building value similar to buying trucks and all those things. And it's not really -- it doesn't really demonstrate how the company is performing, especially if you have some of your projects in production, some in exploration. So from our perspective, we don't have an option.

So when I look at the quarter, we had a loss of $23 million, but you spent $27 million in exploration. So if you kind of add those losses back, we actually had income during the quarter on a very low quarter of production from the Peak Gold JV. So it wasn't -- expensing those exploration expenditures isn't the greatest way to view the company, especially since all those expenditures are optional. And our $27 million is more or less equally spent across 3 of our projects of JT, Kitsault Valley and Lucky Shot.

Romeo Maione: Great. No, I appreciate that extra context. And Mike, I'll stay on you. I want to talk about the credit facility because I know there's still about $44 million of principal due on the credit facility by the end of June against $56.6 million in cash at quarter end. And as I understand, the $16 million distribution expected this quarter. Can you walk us through just the plan for how the debt gets repaid from here?

J. Clark: Yes. Well, that $56 million was the cash at the end of September. We hadn't actually even received our distribution for Q3 for Campaign 3 until after the quarter. So there's another $6 million you'd add to that. So we expect about $22 million to -- somewhere around $22 million to $24 million in distributions during this quarter.

So with that and then with the expected cash flow that we're going to receive in '27 from a much larger year of production, there's more than enough cash there to pay back the debt in March, which is around 15 and about 30 in June as well as continuing to advance our other 3 projects, while also what I expect to happen is we'll continue to advance those projects while also growing the cash over the year. So we ended the year in a much, much higher cash position in '27.

Romeo Maione: Okay. Great. Rick, one thing I want to note that just got kind of, I'll say, buried, but I think it certainly didn't get picked up as much. In September, the Federal Court in Alaska ruled in your favor on the challenge to the Johnson Tract Section 404 permit. So what does that ruling take off the table as you head towards starting that tunnel on that project in '27?

Rick Van Nieuwenhuyse: Yes. So the ruling was the Center for Bio diversity and others were challenging the 404 permit that was issued by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. And I think there were 3 different specific challenges and the courts ruled that they lost on all 3 challenges. So it's a positive outcome for us from a litigation standpoint. And we have -- there's a lot of talk right now about permitting reform. There's a bill before the Senate and the House to approve. And hopefully, they will approve it because it's not only permitting reform, but it's litigation reform. And so the new law will put up some sideboards so these nuisance lawsuits just don't come along.

But yes, the short answer is ruled in our favor 100% on all 3 issues. And so it had to do with building the road to connect the camp to the proposed portal site, which, of course, is now completed. The roads -- our contractors did a fantastic job. And -- in fact, they did such an efficient job that we ended up getting a little more work done, a little more construction work around camp and around the portal site. We actually got those completed as well. And those were works that were actually planned for next year. So yes, bottom line, the lawsuits basically has gone away -- been dismissed, I think, is the legal term.

So we're free to start building a tunnel next year. And now that doesn't say there won't be more lawsuits. That's just part of the American landscape, the right to s., .

Romeo Maione: It's a wonderful -- country. It's one of its most fun elements. But I know, Rick, the fourth campaign is getting underway. It's the biggest of the year, as I understand it, 13,000 to 15,000 ounces. Mill grade was flat in Q3 and even with moving to the south pit. So when is that high-grade ore that we've been talking about actually going to show up at the mill?

Rick Van Nieuwenhuyse: Yes, it's a 2027 event, and that's why we always -- this year was because of that transition between the North pit and the south pit, a lot of the equipment is moving waste material, getting the pit, the North pit or finalizing the development of the North pit and then transitioning and pre-stripping the south main pit. So the main pit has more tonnes and the better grade. It is also more sulfide. It wasn't the north pit -- main pit is not as oxidized as the North pit was. There's a lot more oxidation in the North pit. So that means more total sulfur and more copper because there is copper associated with the sulfide ore.

And so that means higher consumables. We'll see that reflected in the cost next year as well. And then also, it is overall high grade -- higher grade. So you're going to see that grade profile increase through the year. And I think we'll probably talk about costs more later, but -- that's the basic ingredient is next year is going to be a nice solid year. We don't have guidance -- official guidance yet from Kinross. I think we had -- we put our initial guidance on 2027 as 70,000 to 75,000 ounce -- 75,000 to 80,000 something like that.

I think it's going to be lower than that just based on the whole mine plan has sort of shifted out another -- into the next -- into the following year. So that's because we found -- fundamentally because we found more ore in the North pit than was in the original mine plan. So that tended to shift things down a ways. If that makes sense. So -- but yes, next year is going to be a good year and with very strong cash flows.

Romeo Maione: I appreciate that. And like Rick foreshadowed very well, we are going to talk about costs for a second. And people in the Q&A are mentioning the AISC because it looks like cash costs are running about $2,700 an ounce this year. And in May, you guided 2027 to $1,200 to $1,300 on 75,000 to 80,000 ounces. So it's always going to be the kind of hot year. But without front-running the December guidance, which I obviously wouldn't want you to do, what are the moving parts that are bringing cost per ounce down that far? Like why can the market rely on that reduction?

J. Clark: Yes. Well, yes, there's a few components to it. And the way I kind of view it is you had -- we guided to, let's say, $2,000 cash cost in 2026, and we're going to end up at about $2,700 there's the cost increases for -- inflationary increases for diesel, which is a main component of our trucking. So that makes up a big chunk. Then you kind of have the increased consumables over where we have before. So that makes up a large chunk. And then I just look at the project overall is kind of fixed cost driven in a way. Obviously, there's some more variable costs in there.

But if you have the smaller amount of production produced, your AISC per unit is higher. And so that's what we've seen in 2026. The costs went up, so that makes up kind of for half the increase and then you kind of see your production where we're not at the low end of our guidance. And so you're seeing your costs kind of creep up as a result of that. So what you're going to see in '27 is you're going to see -- we're not focusing on pre-stripping and doing all these other activities. We're just focusing on our mining and processing more tonnes at higher grade from the South pit.

And so you're going to have -- your production is not going to double from what we're in '26, but you're going to have it be significantly higher from 2026. And then your cost should stay relatively -- your total cost overall should be relatively flat. But when you put those together, our costs should come down considerably from where they are in 2026. And we'll find that information out. We'll get the formal guidance in the next month or so. But we -- we're going to be more giving a range when we get that guidance.

And I would expect you're going to see a modest increase from where we guided last year on where '27 production costs would be. But I'd be guessing right now, but I'd say those cash costs are going to be somewhere between $1,600 and $2,000 on the high end, but I don't think they'll get that high. Rick will probably swat me for saying that. But...

Romeo Maione: I do. I'll get Rick in on cash costs, too, because I do want to ask why cash costs and AISC continued to be high in Q3? Because I know you initially guided they would be kind of coming down in the second half of the year.

Rick Van Nieuwenhuyse: Yes. I'll jump in on this one because it is kind of just timing and math. So because you're reporting quarterly costs, we moved 300,000 tonnes, and this is the -- we here is the joint venture, moved 300,000 tonnes of ore. So you mine it, you paid for mining it and then you paid for transporting it, but then you only process 200,000 tonnes because of the heavy rains in September. So that's why it's sort of on the ultra-high side, if you will, or higher than -- much higher than expected. Now we'll get the benefit of that in Q4, but we're also now seeing the costs over -- again, due to diesel that have gone up.

In the first half of this year, we were using diesel that we purchased last year, so at the lower cost. And now we're using all the diesel we're using is at the higher cost. So it's -- mining is not an easy business and it's certainly not an easy business to explain -- you definitely have to dive into some of the details. But that is -- those are -- that's basically the answer. So I think we're expecting this year just to be a high cost year. And I think the $2,700 is probably not a bad number now with 3 quarters behind us and the last quarter to go.

Next year, I feel comfortable with Mike's range sort of in the most broad range, and we'll -- in December, we'll have our joint venture meeting, approve the budget and part of that will be what we expect for cash and all-in sustaining costs. We'll certainly communicate that to the market right after that meeting.

Romeo Maione: Great. No, I appreciate it. I do see all the questions coming in. I just got a couple more that I wanted to run through before we get into those. I do want to talk about Kitsault for a second because, Rick, I know you drilled 56,000 meters there, about 40% more than planned on the same budget. The trade-off, as I understand, is that the initial assessment now lands in late 2027 after an updated resource in the first half. Why is that the right order? Walk us through your thinking just for the investors in the room.

Rick Van Nieuwenhuyse: Yes. Maybe I'll just start by saying I have to say we're pretty delighted that we executed our plan flawlessly this year. I'm really proud of the team. The teams and the contractors did a great job spending roughly $25 million on each project. We spent $75 million derisking every project. And in particular, at Kitsault, we got 56,000 meters of drilling when we had planned to do 40,000 meters of drilling. So that's 40% more drill holes, 40% more information on what will go into an MRE, Mineral Resource Estimate planned for the end of Q1. So by the end of March is what we're planning.

So that adds on to the 160 million ounces of silver equivalent that we put out in September. That's it. And so to answer your question specifically about why the initial assessment will be in the fall. We want to use all the drilling that we did this year. We -- in addition to just analyzing the core, we also did a bunch of geotech and a bunch of hydrology -- hydrologic information and metallurgy. And so all of that, we want all that information to be included in coming up with initial assessment, which, of course, is the U.S. terminology for PEA, Preliminary Economic Assessment in Canada, same thing. So that will be in -- by Q4.

I don't -- we don't have a time line on it because we're still obviously working with just getting all the information now. I don't expect we'll have all the assays finalized and QA/QC until January as I mentioned in our previous conversations, previous webinars, we were -- it took us longer to get the MRE out this year because it was in an older database and it just -- we underestimated the length of time it was going to take to get the thing done. But it is a good MRE now. We have -- it's in a modern database. So it will be much easier to update this time. So it will be done by March.

There'll be a significant increase in tonnage in total silver, gold and base metals. What I really like about Kitsault is, it is a true silver deposit. It's not a zinc deposit masking as...

Romeo Maione: A lot of those going around, yes.

Rick Van Nieuwenhuyse: There's a lot of those around with the silver equivalent. Most of our equivalent, silver equivalent is gold. So that's a true precious metal deposit. About 10% comes from the base metals, copper, lead and zinc.

Romeo Maione: Great. I got one last question for you, Rick, and I'll get into those audience questions. And I'll start with Rick, but Mike, if you want to jump in on this one, too, feel free. I know Q3 is peak field season with drills turning on 3 projects at once. With Kitsault and Johnson Tract wrapped for the year, as I understand it, and only Lucky Shot still drilling, what does the spending profile look through the rest of the winter?

Rick Van Nieuwenhuyse: Yes. Well, obviously, we take the gas, the foot off the accelerator here in the last quarter of the year. Kitsault is pretty much shut down. There's a bunch of work going on. The assay is going on, metallurgy is going on, some of the geotechnical reports and hydrology reports are -- the information is still being gathered there. But -- and Johnson Tract is pretty much on care and maintenance right now. So costs are very low. Lucky Shot is still full steam ahead. Second rig, I think, is turning now at Lucky Shot underground, and that will be the case through probably March time frame. And then we'll finalize the assays there.

That will probably take another 6 weeks or so and finalize updating the model. We'll put the MRE out in by the end of Q2. So Kitsault MRE in Q1, Lucky Shot MRE in Q2 and then work on the feasibility study for the direct mine plan there. And the feasibility study for Lucky Shot, I'll just remind everybody, I call it feasibility light because it's just the mine plan, the transportation plan and a tolling arrangement. Fort Knox is the obvious destination for it, but we are looking at a couple of different options, other options that we'll do an internal study before we make a final decision on whether it's Fort Knox or not.

So a lot of -- this year was a lot of data gathering, and we wanted to get it done. We had -- we wanted to get it done on time. The cash flows from our Manh Choh operation are largely responsible for financing all that. And so we want to stay on track with that. I'll repeat again, we are not doing a $75 million financing. So if the shorts on the stock are based on that, I'd unwind it if I were you.

Romeo Maione: No chance I guess. That's a good segue, I think, into the audience questions because there's a number of stuff that I think we've already tackled a little bit, but worth reiterating. J. Clark: No. You shouldn't expect dilution. These costs are -- this is just based for '26, and we expect to see the costs come down significantly next year. Guidance to come in a month's time. But yes, there's no plans to raise equity and there's no need to.

Gold is money. That's what JPMorgan said in 1912, 1 year before the Fed was created, by the way. Rick Van Nieuwenhuyse: That's a great point, and it's probably something we just need to emphasize that's why our whole DSO model is focused on high grade. #2954. Ukraine damages Putin’s prized Crimea bridge as Zelenskyy lauds ‘unprecedented operation’

Ukraine has damaged the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to the occupied Crimean Peninsula, delivering a symbolic blow to President Vladimir Putin as Kyiv reels from strikes on its own infrastructure.

Sergey Aksyonov, the Russia-installed governor of Crimea, confirmed that the strategically important bridge, which had been briefly closed on Monday, was attacked overnight for the second time in two days.

Videos and photos circulating on social media appeared to show the partial destruction of the bridge, with one section having collapsed into the water. CNBC was unable to independently verify the footage.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the attack as an "unprecedented operation" several weeks in the making, with Ukraine's defense forces, security services and weapons manufacturers involved.

"Russia strikes our infrastructure every day, including bridges in Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro, Kyiv, and the Odesa region," Zelenskyy said Tuesday on X.

"We are restoring our infrastructure. But we are also reminding Russia that war will always return to where it began. Ukraine's defensive capabilities are strong and will remain so, and we will never leave terror against our cities and people unanswered," he added.

Train and vehicle traffic was suspended due to the attack. No injuries have been reported.

Ukraine has repeatedly targeted the bridge since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in early 2022.

A 12-mile crossing of road and railways, the Kerch Bridge is one of Putin's signature projects. The crossing, sometimes referred to as the Crimean bridge, was built on his orders shortly after the Kremlin forcibly annexed Crimea in 2014 to support Moscow's claims to the territory.

Rail traffic on the bridge was opened on one track, Russia's Ministry of Transport said in a statement via Telegram on Tuesday, while restoration work continues on the second section.

The co-owner and chief engineer of Ukrainian missile and drone maker Fire Point, Denys Shtilierman, appeared to confirm the company's role in the attack, following reports that a Ukrainian Flamingo cruise missile was used in the strike.

"We dedicate this to the memory of our friends and colleagues Andriy and Yuriy, without whom this would not have been possible. R.I.P.," Shtilierman said via X on Tuesday. A spokesperson at Fire Point separately confirmed the company's role in the attack.

Analysts at the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, said Ukraine's attacks on the Kerch Bridge were likely part of Kyiv's ongoing and systematic strike campaign aimed at denying Russian forces the use of major ground lines of communication via Crimea.

Russian forces, meanwhile, struck two bridges crossing the Dnipro River in Kyiv.

Vitaliy Klitschko, the mayor of Ukraine's capital, said via Telegram on Tuesday that specialists were working to assess the extent of the damage to the North and South bridges.

Klitschko said Russian attacks on Kyiv overnight had also caused disruptions to water and heating supplies.

The strikes come ahead of Putin's trip to China this week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen, where a trilateral meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping is planned on Thursday.

Asked whether Ukraine's latest attacks might be connected to the upcoming trilateral summit, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said this could not be ruled out.

"Combat operations continue, and our military is striking targets that are somehow connected to Ukraine's military-industrial complex. And Ukraine is continuing its terrorist attacks," Peskov said, according to Russian state news outlet Ria Novosti.

#2953. Deutsche Bank shares sink as whistleblowers reveal Epstein payments, Trump tax leak, Russia bets

Deutsche Bank shares fell sharply in early trading on Tuesday after whistleblowers leaked about 15 million files from the German lender, with media reports revealing alleged historic failures across its risk management and financial crime controls.

These include suspicious payments linked to late financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and accidental leaks of President Donald Trump's tax statements.

The leaks contain board minutes, emails, internal investigations and other material that point to systemic failures across the Frankfurt-listed lender's business functions stretching back two decades.

Shares in Deutsche Bank were 4.7% lower by 9:20 a.m. E.T., having fallen more than 6% in early trade in Frankfurt.

Deutsche Bank processed $582 million in suspicious payments linked to Jeffrey Epstein, far more than previously known, the FT reported. Suspicious payments are not, by themselves, proof that every transaction was criminal.

The German lender also mistakenly leaked details of U.S. President Donald Trump's taxes in March 2017, during his first term in office, the FT said. The blunder — described by CEO Christian Sewing, who was then Deutsche's private banking head, as "an awful mistake" — was kept secret from the White House.

The wide-ranging investigation — which was led by a consortium of more than 200 journalists worldwide including the FT, Der Spiegel and Le Monde — also said Deutsche Bank had failed to offboard around 28,000 problematic investment bank clients who had been identified for removal by early 2018.

It also alleges that the bank concealed information around cost targets in 2021, when external monitors in New York reportedly warned that Deutsche's risk appetite was running ahead of controls.

The files also contain details of the bank's relationships with oligarchs and transactions that the investigation links to Russian money-laundering concerns. It was these ties that motivated whistleblowers to send the information to Indian journalist Josy Joseph and South African journalist Khadija Sharife.

The reports once again put Deutsche Bank's risk management practices and controls under the spotlight following years of regulatory scrutiny.

The bank — which has been raided multiple times by German officials this year — has, since 2012, paid out some 18.6 billion euros ($20.5 billion) in settlements over alleged market manipulation, money laundering, mis-selling and misrepresentation, among other things, the FT said.

In a statement, Deutsche Bank said the issues detailed in Tuesday's media reports go back many years.

"Where relevant, we reviewed these matters at the time and worked closely with regulators," the lender said.

The bank said it has undergone a "fundamental transformation" under CEO Christian Sewing, pointing to 7 billion euros of investment in its risk controls between 2019 and 2025.

"Deutsche Bank is a different bank today and remains focused on executing its strategy which has proven successful, as evidenced by record profits in 2025 as well as in recent quarters."

CNBC has reached out to BaFin, Germany's financial regulator, for comment.

#2951. Top Wall Street analysts are bullish on these 3 stocks for the long haul

The ongoing earnings season, Middle East tensions and buzz ahead of the U.S. midterm elections have been keeping investors busy. Further, worries about elevated artificial intelligence spending are weighing on investor sentiment.

Investors looking beyond the short-term noise and focusing on long-term returns can track top Wall Street analysts to pick the right stocks, backed by strong research.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

This week's first stock pick is Datadog, an AI-powered observability and security platform. The company will announce its results for the third quarter on Nov. 4. Datadog is seeing strong demand for its offerings, thanks to cloud migration and rapid AI adoption. Ikeda called Datadog and Atlassian his top picks, saying that companies that can show that AI is a tailwind to growth could see their valuation rerate, even at premium multiples. #2950. Demis Hassabis’ AI company raises $5 billion, months after he left as Google DeepMind CEO

Isomorphic Labs, an artificial intelligence drug discovery startup founded by former Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis, has raised a $5 billion Series C, the company said on Tuesday.

Isomorphic's round comes three-and-a-half months after Hassabis stepped back as CEO of DeepMind, Google's AI lab, which he co-founded before the Big Tech giant acquired it in 2014.

The round was co-led by Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital, alongside Andreessen Horowitz, with investment from Alphabet, Google's parent. The fresh funds will help fund the design and development of new medicines using AI.

Drug discovery startups have seen record funding poured into them by investors in 2026 as companies look to capitalize on advances in AI. OpenAI and Anthropic have also been investing in tools to develop new medicines using the technology.

Hassabis has been CEO of Isomorphic Labs since the startup spun out of DeepMind in 2021.

"When we founded Isomorphic, our conviction was that biology could be understood and modelled at the most fundamental molecular level and radically accelerated through AI," said Hassabis.

"This round enables us to accelerate our progress: building foundational biology models, deepening our systemic disease understanding, and driving our first therapeutic programs towards clinical trials to deliver tangible impact for patients," he added.

Isomorphic is building a proprietary drug design engine and therapeutic candidate pipeline designed with AI, which it says will help it deliver the next generation of medicines.

Anthropic announced it was launching an AI drug discovery program in June and OpenAI partnered with Novo Nordisk in April.

Drug discovery startups have raised $23.2 billion in 2026, according to deal-counting platform Dealroom, a record figure.

Isomorphic last raised in May, with a $2.1 billion Series B.

#2946. Federal Reserve Board finalizes changes to enhance the transparency and public accountability of its stress test and reduce volatility in its stress test-related capital requirements

An official website of the United States Government

Official websites use .govA .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPSA lock (LockLocked padlock icon) or https:// means you've safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

The Federal Reserve, the central bank of the United States, provides the nation with a safe, flexible, and stable monetary and financial system.

Review of Monetary Policy Strategy, Tools, and Communications

Mergers, Acquisitions, and Other Applications

Financial Stability Coordination & Actions

Financial Market Utilities & Infrastructures

For release at 9:00 a.m. EDT Share

The Federal Reserve Board on Wednesday finalized changes to enhance the transparency and public accountability of its stress test and reduce volatility in its stress test-related capital requirements. The two final rules are largely similar to the proposed rules from 2025. The Board also requested comment on a proposal to better capture differences in banks' business models to generate fee income.

The Board conducts stress tests to ensure that large banks are sufficiently capitalized and able to lend to households and businesses even in a severe recession. In December 2024, the Board announced it would modify the test to improve its resilience.

"The stress test is an essential component of our regulatory capital framework," said Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman. "Today's changes preserve its resilience by ensuring that it is transparent, granular, and risk-sensitive. The public will now have greater assurance that the risks banks take will be reflected appropriately in their stress test losses and their capital requirements."

The first final rule requires the Board to invite public input annually on the stress test scenarios and any material model changes. It also updates the framework that guides the design of the hypothetical scenarios and adopts the models that will be used for the 2027 stress test. In addition, the final rule makes several adjustments to the stress test calendar. The final rule also updates the global market shock component, which is a set of shocks to specific market components applied to banks with large trading books. These banks will now be tested against two global market shock components each year, and the Board will use the shock that produces the largest losses for each firm to calculate the firm's stress test results.

The second final rule requires the Board, when calculating stress capital buffer requirements, to average the results from the two most recent annual supervisory stress tests for firms subject to the stress test in both years. The Board will begin averaging stress capital buffer requirements in 2028 to ensure that only models incorporating public input are used in the calculation.

The proposal would request public comment on a revision to the Board's noninterest income model that would improve the stress test's ability to capture business model diversity across firms. If adopted, these adjustments would replace the current noninterest income model that projects each bank's fee income under stress. Comments are due 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

Together, the changes are likely to reduce year-over-year volatility in capital requirements by approximately 50 percent and are not expected to materially affect aggregate capital requirements.

#2941. Investors look to Nvidia's earnings and Anthropic's IPO to refresh the tech rally

I've spent the past 20 years pushing back against the periodically popular notion that markets are replaying the late-1990s and early-2000s tech bubble and bust.

We've simply never matched the levels of gross overvaluation, pervasive public greed, fevered IPO issuance, corporate malinvestment and Wall Street malfeasance that set up a generational market peak, a halving of the S&P 500 over two-and-a-half years and a lost decade for stocks.

We still haven't. Even if June was the peak in AI speculative fervor, as seems possible, and if Oct. 6 proves to have been a consequential broad-market top, the major indexes simply never stretched far enough into the thin air to make a potential retrenchment nearly as damaging as the early 2000s were.

Still, in a more muted fashion, markets have been behaving in ways that generate uncomfortable comparisons to past buying climaxes accompanying a technology revolution.

There is still room and time for the market to prove that the messy sell-down in AI-reliant growth stocks is simply a painful adjustment phase and the S&P 500's six-month purgatorial range a mid-cycle refresh. But it will need to start getting on with it.

Everyone wants to celebrate the way the market has absorbed the damage to semiconductors and other AI-buildout plays, rendering it a controlled demolition rather than indiscriminate destruction.

The Financial Times Unhedged newsletter on Monday called it "The perfect sell-off," the same day the Wall Street Journal cheered, "When Nvidia Stumbled, Equal-Weight Funds Delivered."

This is true, as far as it goes. A rush into defensive and "quality" stocks has largely offset the drag from Nvidia's $2 trillion market-cap loss from its October peak.

But recent defensive leadership, especially from low-growth consumer staples and Big Pharma, sends a less-reassuring macro message, and those groups lack the earnings momentum, narrative appeal or market-cap heft to carry a bull market to new heights.

BTIG technical strategist Jonathan Krinsky has noted echoes of the 2000 period when "boring" defensive stocks ripped as tech rolled over, supporting the tape for a while. Barclays equity desk noted Monday that the "quality factor" basket of stocks just had one of the best 100-day runs ever of the past 20 years.

And JP Morgan here plots the stampede into "low-volatility" stocks, mirroring the hasty retreat from "high-momentum" areas. There's room here for defensives to get even more popular before tripping multi-year extremes, but is that what an index investor should root for?

As for the ascendance of everyone's favorite, the equal-weighted S&P 500, Ned Davis Research analyst London Stockton this month noted that just over 50% of S&P 500 stocks were outperforming the index itself in 2026. Sounds healthy, right? Only to a point.

He explains: "Levels [of stocks outperforming the index] above 58% have most often occurred in and around years where there has been a large bear market." The current phase follows a period when leadership was extremely narrow, producing a "resemblance of the prior three years (2023-2025) to the two years prior to the last Tech bubble (1998-1999) with a very small percentage of companies outperforming the overall S&P 500.

"It is not likely that we are in a situation like in 2000," Stockton concludes, "but this highlights the importance that these large tech stocks at the very least do not decline substantially for the S&P 500 to continue rallying higher."

There are other straws in the wind that harken to prior tech busts:  The Federal Reserve is trying to restrain the corporate sector from overheating in the latter part of a cycle, same as in 1999. Retail traders have maniacally bought the cascading decline in Nvidia shares the past week or so, invoking the voracious dip-buying made famous in the late-'90s which worked until it failed spectacularly.  The market's refusal to pay up for sizzling earnings growth raises alarms about whether they are pulled forward, unsustainable or overstated; profits from 2000 were later revised down radically.

And Nvidia's alleged breach of chip-export rules and the forced departure of CEO Jensen Huang are a reminder that major corporate scandals were a key feature of the Tech Bubble's prolonged reckoning, though nothing resembling the multiple accounting frauds of that era are implied here.

Again, this is the kind of litany of worry and woe that gets recited each time a tech-propelled bull market breaks stride for a bit; more often than not a recovery follows to clear the gloom.

Perhaps Nvidia's results on Tuesday clearing the way for the company to restart stock buybacks and the final allocation of Anthropic's IPO shares will refresh the tech bid. With luck, the huge "hyperscaler" tech-platform stocks will move back to the fore as well-funded stewards of a more sober AI expansion.

Maybe, after weeks of Wall Street insisting that hedge-fund tech-stock positioning is scraping multi-year lows, this will finally presage an upside pain trade.

The vaunted seasonal, post-election tailwinds that the consensus was expecting to fill market's sails and lift the indexes from the floor of an enervating six-month trading range are running late. They need to arrive quite soon. Otherwise, the soggy tape - along with signs of ebbing liquidity reflected in Bitcoin weakness a strong dollar and jumpier equity volatility - will make those tech-bust echoes louder.

John Kolovos of Macro Risk Advisors on the latest reading: "Despite pervasive bearish sentiment and the average stock trading near new highs, our historical studies suggest the market remains vulnerable to disappointment. With defensive leadership still dominating, risk appetite weak, and financial conditions still tight, maintaining a short-term cautious/bearish stance still seems warranted."

-Twenty years ago this week, I wrote a cover story for Barron's that antagonized plenty of friends in the stock-trading profession by foretelling a future of fast, cheap electronic markets that has largely come to pass.

Called "Death of the Floor," the piece detailed the regulatory, technological and behavioral shifts that were ushering in high-frequency, low-touch trading and pressuring the old exchange model.

Reading it now, the conclusions seem utterly obvious and inevitable, though at the time there were still 2,500 NYSE floor brokers and specialists trying to remain in the middle of most trades.

"For the specialists who manage trading in individual stocks and for the floor brokers who depend on the in-person auction model, a tough challenge is becoming even tougher. To stay in the game, they must master cybertrading. For the small investor, this is almost entirely good news. Trading costs should continue to fall, while the likelihood of getting the best price should improve."

Happily, exchanges have adapted and evolved – to zero commissions, thousands of ETFs and microsecond executions - and we have a market that can handle multiples of the capital flow that was routine back then.

If I have one regret about the piece, it's that my good friend and former colleague Bob Pisani thought the CNBC reporter skeleton illustrating the article was meant to depict him.

I assured him, many times, that it was not.

-Almost every business relies heavily on its most loyal repeat customers. But this skew seems extreme for online-betting companies.

A Bloomberg piece picked up here by Yahoo Finance reports that one-third of all sports bettors produces some 97% of revenue at digital sportsbooks. It says the 1% most active gamblers on average lost 78 cents of each dollar bet, twice the loss rate of the norm among all customers.

One can view this as simply paying for entertainment (I "lose" 100 cents of every dollar I place on a movie ticket), but the social disapproval toward the industry seems to have grown.

Add it to the swirl of issues surrounding the legal and de-facto decriminalized wagering industry.

Perceived hostility of Congressional Democrats to prediction-markets venues taking sports bets in states that haven't explicitly approved sports gambling is seen as a plus for DraftKings and Flutter.

Meantime, Robinhood has blurred the lines between investing and gambling by aggressively expanding into prediction markets. And on Monday it was reported that Kalshi has looked to combine investing and betting from the opposite direction, acquiring a brokerage firm in order to offer stock trading to its prediction-markets clientele.

Adults should be free to behave unwisely with their money in search of a windfall. But brokers promoting the negative-sum game of wagering while professing to help the little guy accumulate long-term wealth sends a dissonant message.

The ducks that were quacking loudly ahead of SpaceX's June IPO are much quieter in advance of Anthropic's planned debut this week.

Here is the year-to-date performance of two ETFs that hold shares of recent new listings, Renaissance IPO and First Trust US Equity Opportunities, relative to the S&P 500.

As of June 12, when SpaceX priced, these funds had gone vertical as the public worked itself into an anticipatory lather, the Renaissance fund running ahead of the S&P by some 20 percentage points in the prior six months.

Since then, the IPO funds have deflated (both now have large positions in SpaceX, of course) and there's a bit more focus on whether Anthropic's target valuation is justified given the vast rethink of the AI-proliferation thesis.

All else being equal, a more favorable setup now versus then for a market being asked to swallow a new $1 trillion-plus ticker.

#2929. South Korea will suspend all aircraft operation for 35 minutes and markets will open late. Here’s why

South Korea will suspend all aircraft takeoffs and landings nationwide for 35 minutes on Thursday to minimize noise during the English listening portion of the country's highly competitive college entrance exam, the government said Tuesday.

The restrictions will be in place from 1:05 p.m. to 1:40 p.m. local time, affecting 130 flights, including 81 international and 49 domestic services, according to the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport.

Planes already in the air will be required to remain at least 3 kilometers above the ground during the exam, while emergency flights will be exempt from the restrictions.

The measures will also apply to helicopters, light aircraft and drones, with all drone flights prohibited nationwide during the 35 minutes. Violators could face criminal penalties, the ministry said.

The government will adjust the departure and arrival times of affected flights, while airlines will notify passengers of the revised schedules in advance.

The Korea Transportation Safety Authority will also send text messages to licensed drone operators, including those who have already received flight approvals, warning that drone flights will be prohibited during period regardless of prior authorization.

"We will thoroughly implement the necessary measures, including restrictions on aircraft operations, to ensure students can concentrate ton the English listening test in a table environment," said Jeong Chae-gyo, director general of aviation policy at the ministry.

Jeong also urged airlines and relevant authorities to cooperate in adjusting flight schedules and notifying passengers in advance, and to advise travelers to check their revised departure and arrival times with their airlines.

South Korea's college entrance exam, known as Suneung, is a high stakes annual test that plays a major role in determining students' university admissions.

The country's stock market will also open an hour later than usual on Thursday, at 10 a.m. local time, and close at 4:30 pm, as announced by the Korea Exchange.

Democrats' midterm election win has put the artificial intelligence trade in question, as voters clearly expressed opposition to the rapid buildout of data centers. The stock market could remain volatile amid AI trade concerns, macro uncertainties, and geopolitical tensions.

In this scenario, investors can add dividend-paying stocks to their portfolios to earn steady income. However, the extensive universe of dividend stocks can make selection challenging. Top Wall Street analysts' recommendations can help investors shortlist attractive dividend stocks, as these experts assign ratings after in-depth financial analysis.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Viper Energy (VNOM) is a subsidiary of Diamondback and owns and acquires mineral and royalty interests, primarily in the Permian Basin. The company reported upbeat third-quarter earnings, supported by recent acquisitions and continued development activity from Diamondback and third-party operators. Viper announced a base cash dividend of 50 cents per share for Q3 2026, payable on Nov. 19. Based on the base and variable dividends announced over the past 12 months, VNOM's dividend yield stands at 5.7%.

Following the Q3 results, TD Cowen analyst Aaron Bilkoski reiterated a buy rating on Viper Energy stock with a price target of $61. The analyst noted that the company delivered solid Q3 results, with production, including oil and natural gas liquids, exceeding both TD Cowen and consensus estimates.

The 5-star analyst highlighted that the key update was the announcement of two royalty acquisitions for $809 million in cash, including deferred consideration, and $82 million of newly issued shares.

Given the recently announced base dividend hike, Bilkoski expects Viper to direct incremental free cash flow toward buybacks. While the acquisitions increase leverage, the analyst believes that Viper has enough capacity for opportunistic buybacks.

Bilkoski noted that Viper has historically delivered one of the highest production per share growth profiles in his royalty coverage, but still trades at a notable discount to the royalty peer average and the company's historical FCF yield range. "In our view, its above-average growth warrants a higher valuation," said the analyst.

Bilkoski ranks No. 525 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 12.80%. See Viper Energy Stock Buybacks on TipRanks.

Exxon Mobil (XOM) reported robust Q3 2026 profits, as its U.S. refineries boosted production to capitalize on the high diesel fuel prices sparked by the conflict in the Middle East. The oil and gas giant announced a quarterly dividend of $1.07 per share, payable on Dec. 10, reflecting a 3.9% increase. This marks Exxon's 44th consecutive year of dividend increases. At an annualized dividend of $4.28 per share, XOM offers a yield of 2.53%.

Impressed by the Q3 print, TD Cowen analyst Jason Gabelman reiterated a buy rating on Exxon stock and raised his price target to $193 from $180 to reflect higher downstream earnings, with the expectation of increased mid-cycle margins.

Gabelman noted that the strength in Exxon's refining business continues to offset Middle East-related headwinds. He added that the company increased its ownership in LNG projects, which should reduce its Middle East concentration over time from 75% to 50% and lower the likelihood of diversification-focused mergers and acquisitions. Beyond LNG, Gabelman expects Exxon's growth in the 2030s to come from Guyana, Kashagan, Permian, and possibly Venezuela.

Gabelman noted that Exxon announced a dividend hike of nearly 4% and plans to maintain buybacks at $20 billion for 2027. "The decision to maintain reduces the pro-cyclicality nature of the buyback," said the analyst.

Gabelman ranks No. 347 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 66% of the time, delivering an average return of 16.90%. See Exxon Mobil Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Williams (WMB), which owns and operates energy infrastructure to deliver natural gas, reported strong third-quarter results. The company announced a quarterly dividend of $0.525 per share, or $2.10 per share annualized, payable on Dec. 28. WMB offers a dividend yield of 3.09%.

In reaction to the Q3 2026 results, CIBC analyst Robert Catellier reaffirmed a buy rating on Williams stock with a price target of $82. The analyst noted that Q3 results were essentially in line with expectations and reflected continued strength in execution across WMB's infrastructure portfolio.

Catellier said that Williams' Q3 performance was driven by higher transmission, storage, and power generation revenues, as well as contributions from the Momentum Midstream acquisition.

He noted that Williams maintained its full-year EBITDA guidance of $8.3 billion to $8.5 billion. In fact, results are tracking toward the higher end of the guidance range, backed by contributions from recently completed projects and the Momentum Midstream deal. WMB continues to target long-term EBITDA compound annual growth rate of at least 11% through 2030.

Catellier expects WMB's long-term targets to be supported by incremental transmission and storage opportunities, including Transco's Southeast Supply Enhancement II project and an 84 MMcf/d expansion of the Garden Connector project.

Catellier ranks No. 667 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 66% of the time, delivering an average return of 9.60%. See Williams Technical Analysis on TipRanks.
